<span typeof="mw:File"><span><img alt="Seal of the President of the United States" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/36/Seal_of_the_President_of_the_United_States.svg/70px-Seal_of_the_President_of_the_United_States.svg.png" decoding="async" width="70" height="70" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/36/Seal_of_the_President_of_the_United_States.svg/105px-Seal_of_the_President_of_the_United_States.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/36/Seal_of_the_President_of_the_United_States.svg/140px-Seal_of_the_President_of_the_United_States.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="2424" data-file-height="2425" /></span></span></td>
</tr><tr><td class="sidebar-navbar"><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1129693374"><style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r1063604349">.mw-parser-output .navbar{display:inline;font-size:88%;font-weight:normal}.mw-parser-output .navbar-collapse{float:left;text-align:left}.mw-parser-output .navbar-boxtext{word-spacing:0}.mw-parser-output .navbar ul{display:inline-block;white-space:nowrap;line-height:inherit}.mw-parser-output .navbar-brackets::before{margin-right:-0.125em;content:"[ "}.mw-parser-output .navbar-brackets::after{margin-left:-0.125em;content:" ]"}.mw-parser-output .navbar li{word-spacing:-0.125em}.mw-parser-output .navbar a>span,.mw-parser-output .navbar a>abbr{text-decoration:inherit}.mw-parser-output .navbar-mini abbr{font-variant:small-caps;border-bottom:none;text-decoration:none;cursor:inherit}.mw-parser-output .navbar-ct-full{font-size:114%;margin:0 7em}.mw-parser-output .navbar-ct-mini{font-size:114%;margin:0 4em}</style><div class="navbar plainlinks hlist navbar-mini"><ul><li class="nv-view"><a href="/wiki/Template:Theodore_Roosevelt_series" title="Template:Theodore Roosevelt series"><abbr title="View this template">v</abbr></a></li><li class="nv-talk"><a href="/w/index.php?title=Template_talk:Theodore_Roosevelt_series&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Template talk:Theodore Roosevelt series (page does not exist)"><abbr title="Discuss this template">t</abbr></a></li><li class="nv-edit"><a class="external text" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Template:Theodore_Roosevelt_series&amp;action=edit"><abbr title="Edit this template">e</abbr></a></li></ul></div></td></tr></tbody></table>
<p><b>Theodore  Roosevelt Jr.</b> (<span class="rt-commentedText nowrap"><span class="IPA nopopups noexcerpt" lang="en-fonipa"><a href="/wiki/Help:IPA/English" title="Help:IPA/English">/<span style="border-bottom:1px dotted"><span title="/ˈ/: primary stress follows">ˈ</span><span title="&#39;r&#39; in &#39;rye&#39;">r</span><span title="/oʊ/: &#39;o&#39; in &#39;code&#39;">oʊ</span><span title="&#39;z&#39; in &#39;zoom&#39;">z</span><span title="/ə/: &#39;a&#39; in &#39;about&#39;">ə</span><span title="&#39;v&#39; in &#39;vie&#39;">v</span><span title="/ɛ/: &#39;e&#39; in &#39;dress&#39;">ɛ</span><span title="&#39;l&#39; in &#39;lie&#39;">l</span><span title="&#39;t&#39; in &#39;tie&#39;">t</span></span>/</a></span></span> <a href="/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key" title="Help:Pronunciation respelling key"><i title="English pronunciation respelling"><span style="font-size:90%">ROH</span>-zə-velt</i></a>;<sup id="cite_ref-6" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-6">&#91;b&#93;</a></sup> October 27, 1858 – January 6, 1919), often referred to as <b>Teddy</b> or by his initials, <b>T. R.</b>, was an American politician, statesman, soldier, conservationist, naturalist, historian, and writer who served as the 26th <a href="/wiki/President_of_the_United_States" title="President of the United States">president of the United States</a> from 1901 to 1909. He previously served as the 25th <a href="/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_United_States" title="Vice President of the United States">vice president</a> under President <a href="/wiki/William_McKinley" title="William McKinley">William McKinley</a> from March to September 1901 and as the 33rd <a href="/wiki/Governor_of_New_York" title="Governor of New York">governor of New York</a> from 1899 to 1900. Assuming the presidency after <a href="/wiki/Assassination_of_William_McKinley" title="Assassination of William McKinley">McKinley's assassination</a>, Roosevelt emerged as a leader of the <a href="/wiki/History_of_the_Republican_Party_(United_States)" title="History of the Republican Party (United States)">Republican Party</a> and became a driving force for <a href="/wiki/United_States_antitrust_law" title="United States antitrust law">anti-trust</a> and <a href="/wiki/Progressive_Era" title="Progressive Era">Progressive</a> policies.
</p><p>A sickly child with debilitating asthma, he overcame his health problems as he grew by embracing <a href="/wiki/The_Strenuous_Life" title="The Strenuous Life">a strenuous lifestyle</a>. Roosevelt integrated his exuberant personality and a vast range of interests and achievements into a "cowboy" persona defined by robust masculinity. He was home-schooled and began a lifelong naturalist avocation before attending <a href="/wiki/Harvard_College" title="Harvard College">Harvard College</a>. His book <i><a href="/wiki/The_Naval_War_of_1812" title="The Naval War of 1812">The Naval War of 1812</a></i> (1882) established his reputation as a learned historian and popular writer. Upon entering politics, Roosevelt became the leader of the reform faction of Republicans in <a href="/wiki/New_York_State_Legislature" title="New York State Legislature">New York's state legislature</a>. His first wife and mother died on the same night, devastating him psychologically. He recuperated by buying and operating a cattle ranch in the Dakotas. Roosevelt served as <a href="/wiki/Assistant_Secretary_of_the_Navy" title="Assistant Secretary of the Navy">Assistant Secretary of the Navy</a> under President McKinley, and in 1898 helped plan the <a href="/wiki/Spanish%E2%80%93American_War" title="Spanish–American War">highly successful naval war against Spain</a>. He resigned to help form and lead the <a href="/wiki/Rough_Riders" title="Rough Riders">Rough Riders</a>, a unit that fought the <a href="/wiki/Spanish_Army" title="Spanish Army">Spanish Army</a> in Cuba to great publicity. Returning a war hero, Roosevelt was <a href="/wiki/1898_New_York_state_election" title="1898 New York state election">elected governor of New York</a> in 1898. The New York state party leadership disliked his ambitious agenda and convinced McKinley to choose him as his running mate in the <a href="/wiki/1900_United_States_presidential_election" title="1900 United States presidential election">1900 election</a>. Roosevelt campaigned vigorously and the McKinley–Roosevelt ticket won a landslide victory based on a platform of victory, peace, and prosperity.
</p><p>Roosevelt assumed the presidency at age 42, and remains the <a href="/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States_by_age" title="List of presidents of the United States by age">youngest person to become president of the United States</a>. As a leader of the <a href="/wiki/Progressivism_in_the_United_States" title="Progressivism in the United States">progressive movement</a> he championed his "<a href="/wiki/Square_Deal" title="Square Deal">Square Deal</a>" domestic policies. It called for fairness for all citizens, breaking of <a href="/wiki/Trust_(business)" title="Trust (business)">bad trusts</a>, regulation of railroads, and pure food and drugs. Roosevelt prioritized <a href="/wiki/Conservation_movement" title="Conservation movement">conservation</a> and established <a href="/wiki/List_of_national_parks_of_the_United_States" title="List of national parks of the United States">national parks</a>, <a href="/wiki/List_of_national_forests_of_the_United_States" title="List of national forests of the United States">forests</a>, and <a href="/wiki/List_of_national_monuments_of_the_United_States" title="List of national monuments of the United States">monuments</a> to preserve the nation's natural resources. In foreign policy, he <a href="/wiki/Roosevelt_Corollary" title="Roosevelt Corollary">focused on Central America</a>, where he began construction of the <a href="/wiki/Panama_Canal" title="Panama Canal">Panama Canal</a>. Roosevelt expanded the <a href="/wiki/United_States_Navy" title="United States Navy">Navy</a> and sent the <a href="/wiki/Great_White_Fleet" title="Great White Fleet">Great White Fleet</a> on a world tour to project American naval power. His successful efforts to broker the end of the <a href="/wiki/Russo-Japanese_War" title="Russo-Japanese War">Russo-Japanese War</a> won him the 1906 <a href="/wiki/Nobel_Peace_Prize" title="Nobel Peace Prize">Nobel Peace Prize</a>, making him the first American to ever win a <a href="/wiki/Nobel_Prize" title="Nobel Prize">Nobel Prize</a>. Roosevelt was elected to a full term in <a href="/wiki/1904_United_States_presidential_election" title="1904 United States presidential election">1904</a> and promoted policies more to the left, despite growing opposition from Republican leaders. During his presidency, he groomed his close ally <a href="/wiki/William_Howard_Taft" title="William Howard Taft">William Howard Taft</a> to succeed him in the <a href="/wiki/1908_United_States_presidential_election" title="1908 United States presidential election">1908 presidential election</a>.
</p><p>Roosevelt grew frustrated with Taft's conservatism and belatedly tried to win the <a href="/wiki/1912_Republican_Party_presidential_primaries" title="1912 Republican Party presidential primaries">1912 Republican nomination for president</a>. He failed, walked out, and founded the new <a href="/wiki/Progressive_Party_(United_States,_1912)" class="mw-redirect" title="Progressive Party (United States, 1912)">Progressive Party</a>. He ran in the <a href="/wiki/1912_United_States_presidential_election" title="1912 United States presidential election">1912 presidential election</a> and the split allowed the <a href="/wiki/History_of_the_Democratic_Party_(United_States)" title="History of the Democratic Party (United States)">Democratic</a> nominee <a href="/wiki/Woodrow_Wilson" title="Woodrow Wilson">Woodrow Wilson</a> to win the election. Following the defeat, Roosevelt led a <a href="/wiki/Roosevelt%E2%80%93Rondon_Scientific_Expedition" title="Roosevelt–Rondon Scientific Expedition">four-month expedition to the Amazon basin</a> where he nearly died of tropical disease. During <a href="/wiki/World_War_I" title="World War I">World War I</a>, he criticized Wilson for keeping the country out of the war, and his offer to lead volunteers to France was rejected. Roosevelt considered running for president again in <a href="/wiki/1920_United_States_presidential_election" title="1920 United States presidential election">1920</a>, but his health continued to deteriorate and he died in 1919. <a href="/wiki/Historical_rankings_of_presidents_of_the_United_States#Murray–Blessing_1982_survey" title="Historical rankings of presidents of the United States">Polls of historians and political scientists</a> rank him as one of the greatest presidents in American history.
</p>
<meta property="mw:PageProp/toc" />
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Early_life_and_family">Early life and family</span></h2>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:TR_Age_11_Paris.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/84/TR_Age_11_Paris.jpg/180px-TR_Age_11_Paris.jpg" decoding="async" width="180" height="195" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/84/TR_Age_11_Paris.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="209" data-file-height="226" /></a><figcaption>Theodore Roosevelt at age 11</figcaption></figure> 
<p>Theodore Roosevelt Jr. was born on October 27, 1858, at <a href="/wiki/Theodore_Roosevelt_Birthplace_National_Historic_Site" title="Theodore Roosevelt Birthplace National Historic Site">28 East 20th Street</a> in <a href="/wiki/Manhattan" title="Manhattan">Manhattan</a>, New York City.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMorris19793_7-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorris19793-7">&#91;5&#93;</a></sup> He was the second of four children born to socialite <a href="/wiki/Martha_Bulloch_Roosevelt" title="Martha Bulloch Roosevelt">Martha Stewart Bulloch</a> and businessman and philanthropist <a href="/wiki/Theodore_Roosevelt_Sr." title="Theodore Roosevelt Sr.">Theodore Roosevelt Sr.</a> He had an older sister (<a href="/wiki/Bamie_Roosevelt" title="Bamie Roosevelt">Anna</a>), a younger brother (<a href="/wiki/Elliott_Roosevelt_(socialite)" title="Elliott Roosevelt (socialite)">Elliott</a>) and a younger sister (<a href="/wiki/Corinne_Roosevelt_Robinson" title="Corinne Roosevelt Robinson">Corinne</a>).<sup id="cite_ref-8" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-8">&#91;6&#93;</a></sup> Elliott was later the father of <a href="/wiki/Anna_Eleanor_Roosevelt" class="mw-redirect" title="Anna Eleanor Roosevelt">Anna Eleanor Roosevelt</a> who married Theodore's distant cousin, <a href="/wiki/Franklin_D._Roosevelt" title="Franklin D. Roosevelt">Franklin Delano Roosevelt</a>. His paternal grandfather was of Dutch descent;<sup id="cite_ref-9" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-9">&#91;7&#93;</a></sup> his other ancestry included primarily Scottish and Scots-Irish, English<sup id="cite_ref-10" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-10">&#91;8&#93;</a></sup> and smaller amounts of German, Welsh, and French.<sup id="cite_ref-vought_11-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-vought-11">&#91;9&#93;</a></sup> Theodore Sr. was the fifth son of businessman <a href="/wiki/Cornelius_Roosevelt" title="Cornelius Roosevelt">Cornelius Van Schaack "C.&#160;V.&#160;S." Roosevelt</a> and Margaret Barnhill as well as a brother of <a href="/wiki/Robert_Roosevelt" title="Robert Roosevelt">Robert Roosevelt</a> and <a href="/wiki/James_A._Roosevelt" title="James A. Roosevelt">James A. Roosevelt</a>. Theodore's fourth cousin, <a href="/wiki/James_Roosevelt_I" title="James Roosevelt I">James Roosevelt I</a>, who was also a businessman, was the father of President Franklin Delano Roosevelt. Martha was the younger daughter of Major <a href="/wiki/James_Stephens_Bulloch" title="James Stephens Bulloch">James Stephens Bulloch</a> and Martha P. "Patsy" Stewart.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPutnam1958ch_1–2_12-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPutnam1958ch_1–2-12">&#91;10&#93;</a></sup> Through the Van Schaacks, Roosevelt was a descendant of the <a href="/wiki/Schuyler_family" title="Schuyler family">Schuyler family</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-13" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-13">&#91;11&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Roosevelt's youth was largely shaped by his poor health and debilitating <a href="/wiki/Asthma" title="Asthma">asthma</a>. He repeatedly experienced sudden nighttime asthma attacks that caused the experience of being smothered to death, which terrified both Theodore and his parents. Doctors had no cure.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcCullough1981&#91;httpsbooksgooglecombooksidnuzmvrqPvdICpgPA93_93–108&#93;_14-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCullough1981[httpsbooksgooglecombooksidnuzmvrqPvdICpgPA93_93–108]-14">&#91;12&#93;</a></sup> Nevertheless, he was energetic and mischievously inquisitive.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPutnam195823–27_15-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPutnam195823–27-15">&#91;13&#93;</a></sup> His lifelong interest in <a href="/wiki/Zoology" title="Zoology">zoology</a> began at age seven when he saw a dead <a href="/wiki/Pinniped" title="Pinniped">seal</a> at a local market; after obtaining the seal's head, Roosevelt and two cousins formed what they called the "Roosevelt Museum of Natural History". Having learned the rudiments of <a href="/wiki/Taxidermy" title="Taxidermy">taxidermy</a>, he filled his makeshift museum with animals that he killed or caught; he then studied the animals and prepared them for exhibition. At age nine, he recorded his observation of insects in a paper entitled "The Natural History of Insects".<sup id="cite_ref-environment_16-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-environment-16">&#91;14&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Roosevelt's father significantly influenced him. His father was a prominent leader in New York's cultural affairs; he helped to found the <a href="/wiki/Metropolitan_Museum_of_Art" title="Metropolitan Museum of Art">Metropolitan Museum of Art</a>, and had been especially active in mobilizing support for the Union during the <a href="/wiki/American_Civil_War" title="American Civil War">American Civil War</a>, even though his in-laws included Confederate leaders. Roosevelt said, "My father, Theodore Roosevelt, was the best man I ever knew. He combined strength and courage with gentleness, tenderness, and great unselfishness. He would not tolerate in us children selfishness or cruelty, idleness, cowardice, or untruthfulness."
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Lincoln_Funeral_Procession_Roosevelt_Mansion_Broadway.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cf/Lincoln_Funeral_Procession_Roosevelt_Mansion_Broadway.jpg/220px-Lincoln_Funeral_Procession_Roosevelt_Mansion_Broadway.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="227" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cf/Lincoln_Funeral_Procession_Roosevelt_Mansion_Broadway.jpg/330px-Lincoln_Funeral_Procession_Roosevelt_Mansion_Broadway.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cf/Lincoln_Funeral_Procession_Roosevelt_Mansion_Broadway.jpg/440px-Lincoln_Funeral_Procession_Roosevelt_Mansion_Broadway.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1988" data-file-height="2048" /></a><figcaption>6-year-old Theodore and 5-year-old Elliott watch Lincoln's funeral procession from the second-floor window of their grandfather's mansion (at top left, facing the camera), Manhattan, April 25, 1865.</figcaption></figure><p> Family trips abroad, including tours of <a href="/wiki/Europe" title="Europe">Europe</a> in 1869 and 1870, and <a href="/wiki/Egypt" title="Egypt">Egypt</a> in 1872, shaped his cosmopolitan perspective.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTERoosevelt191313_17-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoosevelt191313-17">&#91;15&#93;</a></sup> Hiking with his family in the <a href="/wiki/Alps" title="Alps">Alps</a> in 1869, Roosevelt found that he could keep pace with his father. He had discovered the significant benefits of physical exertion to minimize his asthma and bolster his spirits.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPutnam195863–70_18-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPutnam195863–70-18">&#91;16&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt began a heavy regime of exercise. After being manhandled by two older boys on a camping trip, he found a boxing coach to teach him to fight and strengthen his body.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEThayer191920_19-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThayer191920-19">&#91;17&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-20" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-20">&#91;18&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>A 6-year-old Roosevelt witnessed the <a href="/wiki/Funeral_and_burial_of_Abraham_Lincoln" title="Funeral and burial of Abraham Lincoln">funeral procession of Abraham Lincoln</a> from his grandfather Cornelius's mansion in <a href="/wiki/Union_Square_(Manhattan)" class="mw-redirect" title="Union Square (Manhattan)">Union Square</a>, New York City, where he was photographed in the window along with his brother Elliott, as confirmed by his second wife, Edith, who was also present.<sup id="cite_ref-21" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-21">&#91;19&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Education">Education</span></h3>
<p>Roosevelt was <a href="/wiki/Homeschooling" title="Homeschooling">homeschooled</a>, mostly by tutors and his parents.<sup id="cite_ref-22" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-22">&#91;20&#93;</a></sup> Biographer <a href="/wiki/H._W._Brands" title="H. W. Brands">H. W. Brands</a> argued that "The most obvious drawback to his home schooling was uneven coverage of the various areas of human knowledge."<sup id="cite_ref-23" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-23">&#91;21&#93;</a></sup> He was solid in geography and bright in history, biology, French, and German; however, he struggled in mathematics and the classical languages. When he entered Harvard College on September 27, 1876, his father advised: "Take care of your morals first, your health next, and finally your studies."<sup id="cite_ref-24" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-24">&#91;22&#93;</a></sup> His father's sudden death on February 9, 1878, devastated Roosevelt, but he eventually recovered and doubled his activities.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller199280–82_25-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller199280–82-25">&#91;23&#93;</a></sup> 
</p><p>His father, a devout Presbyterian, regularly led the family in prayers. While at Harvard, young Theodore emulated him by teaching Sunday School for more than three years at <a href="/wiki/Christ_Church_(Cambridge,_Massachusetts)" title="Christ Church (Cambridge, Massachusetts)">Christ Church</a> in Cambridge. When the minister at Christ Church, which was an Episcopal church, eventually insisted he become an Episcopalian to continue teaching in the Sunday School, Roosevelt declined, and instead began teaching a mission class in a poor section of Cambridge.<sup id="cite_ref-26" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-26">&#91;24&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>He did well in science, philosophy, and rhetoric courses but continued to struggle in Latin and Greek. He studied biology intently and was already an accomplished naturalist and a published <a href="/wiki/Ornithology" title="Ornithology">ornithologist</a>. He read prodigiously with an almost photographic memory.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands199762_27-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands199762-27">&#91;25&#93;</a></sup> While at Harvard, Roosevelt participated in rowing and <a href="/wiki/Harvard_Boxing_Club" title="Harvard Boxing Club">boxing</a>; he was once runner-up in an intramural boxing tournament.<sup id="cite_ref-28" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-28">&#91;26&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt was a member of the <a href="/wiki/Alpha_Delta_Phi" title="Alpha Delta Phi">Alpha Delta Phi</a> literary society (later the <a href="/wiki/Fly_Club" title="Fly Club">Fly Club</a>), the <a href="/wiki/Delta_Kappa_Epsilon" title="Delta Kappa Epsilon">Delta Kappa Epsilon</a> fraternity, and the prestigious <a href="/wiki/Porcellian_Club" title="Porcellian Club">Porcellian Club</a>; he was also an editor of <i><a href="/wiki/The_Harvard_Advocate" title="The Harvard Advocate">The Harvard Advocate</a></i>. In 1880, Roosevelt graduated <a href="/wiki/Phi_Beta_Kappa" title="Phi Beta Kappa">Phi Beta Kappa</a> (22nd of 177) from Harvard with an <a href="/wiki/Bachelors_of_Arts" class="mw-redirect" title="Bachelors of Arts">A.B.</a> <i><a href="/wiki/Magna_cum_laude" class="mw-redirect" title="Magna cum laude">magna cum laude</a></i>. Biographer <a href="/wiki/Henry_F._Pringle" title="Henry F. Pringle">Henry F. Pringle</a> states:
</p>
<style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r996844942">.mw-parser-output .templatequote{overflow:hidden;margin:1em 0;padding:0 40px}.mw-parser-output .templatequote .templatequotecite{line-height:1.5em;text-align:left;padding-left:1.6em;margin-top:0}</style><blockquote class="templatequote"><p>Roosevelt, attempting to analyze his college career and weigh the benefits he had received, felt that he had obtained little from Harvard. He had been depressed by the formalistic treatment of many subjects, by the rigidity, the attention to minutiae that were important in themselves, but which somehow were never linked up with the whole.<sup id="cite_ref-29" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-29">&#91;27&#93;</a></sup></p></blockquote>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Theodore_Roosevelt_Birthplace_from_west.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a0/Theodore_Roosevelt_Birthplace_from_west.jpg/180px-Theodore_Roosevelt_Birthplace_from_west.jpg" decoding="async" width="180" height="225" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a0/Theodore_Roosevelt_Birthplace_from_west.jpg/270px-Theodore_Roosevelt_Birthplace_from_west.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a0/Theodore_Roosevelt_Birthplace_from_west.jpg/360px-Theodore_Roosevelt_Birthplace_from_west.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1684" data-file-height="2109" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Theodore_Roosevelt_Birthplace_National_Historic_Site" title="Theodore Roosevelt Birthplace National Historic Site">Roosevelt's birthplace</a> at 28 East 20th Street in <a href="/wiki/Manhattan,_New_York_City" class="mw-redirect" title="Manhattan, New York City">Manhattan, New York City</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>After his father's death, Roosevelt had inherited $65,000 (equivalent to $1,971,069&#32;in 2022), enough wealth on which he could live comfortably for the rest of his life.<sup id="cite_ref-NYT14_30-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-NYT14-30">&#91;28&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt gave up his earlier plan of studying natural science and decided to attend <a href="/wiki/Columbia_Law_School" title="Columbia Law School">Columbia Law School</a> instead, moving back into his family's home in New York City. Although Roosevelt was an able law student, he often found law to be irrational. He spent much of his time writing a book on the <a href="/wiki/War_of_1812" title="War of 1812">War of 1812</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997110–212,_123–133._quote_p._126_31-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997110–212,_123–133._quote_p._126-31">&#91;29&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Determined to enter politics, Roosevelt began attending meetings at Morton Hall, the 59th Street headquarters of New York's 21st District Republican Association. Though Roosevelt's father had been a prominent member of the <a href="/wiki/History_of_the_Republican_Party_(United_States)" title="History of the Republican Party (United States)">Republican Party</a>, the younger Roosevelt made an unorthodox career choice for someone of his class, as most of Roosevelt's peers refrained from becoming too closely involved in politics. Roosevelt found allies in the local Republican Party and defeated an incumbent Republican state assemblyman tied to the political machine of Senator <a href="/wiki/Roscoe_Conkling" title="Roscoe Conkling">Roscoe Conkling</a> closely. After his election victory, Roosevelt decided to drop out of law school, later saying, "I intended to be one of the governing class."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997110–112,_123–133._quote_p._126_32-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997110–112,_123–133._quote_p._126-32">&#91;30&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Naval_history_and_strategy">Naval history and strategy</span></h3>
<p>While at Harvard, Roosevelt began a systematic study of the role played by the <a href="/wiki/United_States_Navy" title="United States Navy">United States Navy</a> in the <a href="/wiki/War_of_1812" title="War of 1812">War of 1812</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTERoosevelt191335_33-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoosevelt191335-33">&#91;31&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMorris1979565_34-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorris1979565-34">&#91;32&#93;</a></sup> Assisted by two uncles, he scrutinized original source materials and official U.S. Navy records, ultimately publishing <i><a href="/wiki/The_Naval_War_of_1812" title="The Naval War of 1812">The Naval War of 1812</a></i> in 1882. The book contained drawings of individual and combined ship maneuvers, charts depicting the differences in iron throw weights of cannon shot between rival forces, and analyses of the differences and similarities between British and American leadership down to the ship-to-ship level. Upon release, <i>The Naval War of 1812</i> was praised for its scholarship and style, and it remains a standard study of the war.<sup id="cite_ref-mjcrawford1_35-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-mjcrawford1-35">&#91;33&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>With the publication of <i><a href="/wiki/The_Influence_of_Sea_Power_upon_History" title="The Influence of Sea Power upon History">The Influence of Sea Power upon History</a></i> in 1890, Navy Captain <a href="/wiki/Alfred_Thayer_Mahan" title="Alfred Thayer Mahan">Alfred Thayer Mahan</a> was hailed as the world's outstanding naval theorist by the leaders of Europe immediately. Roosevelt paid very close attention to Mahan's emphasis that only a nation with the world's most powerful fleet could dominate the world's oceans, exert its diplomacy to the fullest, and defend its own borders.<sup id="cite_ref-36" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-36">&#91;34&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-37" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-37">&#91;35&#93;</a></sup> He incorporated Mahan's ideas into his views on naval strategy for the remainder of his career.<sup id="cite_ref-38" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-38">&#91;36&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-39" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-39">&#91;37&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="First_marriage_and_widowerhood">First marriage and widowerhood</span></h3>
<p>In 1880, Roosevelt married socialite <a href="/wiki/Alice_Hathaway_Lee_Roosevelt" title="Alice Hathaway Lee Roosevelt">Alice Hathaway Lee</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-40" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-40">&#91;38&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-41" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-41">&#91;39&#93;</a></sup> Their daughter, <a href="/wiki/Alice_Roosevelt_Longworth" title="Alice Roosevelt Longworth">Alice Lee Roosevelt</a>, was born on February 12, 1884. Two days later, the new mother died of undiagnosed <a href="/wiki/Kidney_failure" title="Kidney failure">kidney failure</a> that the pregnancy masked. In his diary, Roosevelt wrote a large "X" on the page and then, "The light has gone out of my life." His mother, Martha, had died of <a href="/wiki/Typhoid_fever" title="Typhoid fever">typhoid fever</a> eleven hours earlier at 3:00&#160;a.m., in the same house on <a href="/wiki/57th_Street_(Manhattan)" title="57th Street (Manhattan)">57th Street</a> in Manhattan. Distraught, Roosevelt left baby Alice in the care of his sister Bamie while he grieved; he assumed custody of Alice when she was three.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992154–158_42-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992154–158-42">&#91;40&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>After the deaths of his wife and mother, Roosevelt focused on his work, specifically by re-energizing a legislative investigation into corruption of the <a href="/wiki/New_York_City_government" class="mw-redirect" title="New York City government">New York City government</a>, which arose from a concurrent bill proposing that power be centralized in the mayor's office.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997166_43-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997166-43">&#91;41&#93;</a></sup> For the rest of his life, he rarely spoke about his wife Alice and did not write about her in his autobiography.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMorris1979232_44-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorris1979232-44">&#91;42&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Early_political_career">Early political career</span></h2>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="State_Assemblyman">State Assemblyman</span></h3>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:TR_NY_State_Assemblyman_1883_crop.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/48/TR_NY_State_Assemblyman_1883_crop.jpg/180px-TR_NY_State_Assemblyman_1883_crop.jpg" decoding="async" width="180" height="222" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/48/TR_NY_State_Assemblyman_1883_crop.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="230" data-file-height="284" /></a><figcaption>Roosevelt as New York State Assemblyman, 1883</figcaption></figure>
<p>Roosevelt was a member of the <a href="/wiki/New_York_State_Assembly" title="New York State Assembly">New York State Assembly</a> (New York Co., 21st D.) in <a href="/wiki/105th_New_York_State_Legislature" title="105th New York State Legislature">1882</a>, <a href="/wiki/106th_New_York_State_Legislature" title="106th New York State Legislature">1883</a>, and <a href="/wiki/107th_New_York_State_Legislature" title="107th New York State Legislature">1884</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-:1_45-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:1-45">&#91;43&#93;</a></sup> He began making his mark immediately handling in corporate corruption issues specifically.<sup id="cite_ref-:1_45-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:1-45">&#91;43&#93;</a></sup> He blocked a corrupt effort of financier <a href="/wiki/Jay_Gould" title="Jay Gould">Jay Gould</a> to lower his taxes. Roosevelt also exposed the suspected collusion of Gould and Judge <a href="/wiki/Theodoric_R._Westbrook" title="Theodoric R. Westbrook">Theodore Westbrook</a> and argued for and received approval for an investigation to proceed, aiming for the judge to be impeached. Although the investigation committee rejected the proposed impeachment, Roosevelt had exposed the potential corruption in <a href="/wiki/Albany,_New_York" title="Albany, New York">Albany</a> and assumed a high and positive political profile in multiple New York publications.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997134–140_46-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997134–140-46">&#91;44&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Roosevelt's anti-corruption efforts helped him win re-election in <a href="/wiki/1882_New_York_state_election" title="1882 New York state election">1882</a> by a margin greater than two-to-one, an achievement made even more impressive by the victory that Democratic gubernatorial candidate <a href="/wiki/Grover_Cleveland" title="Grover Cleveland">Grover Cleveland</a> won in Roosevelt's district.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992138–139_47-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992138–139-47">&#91;45&#93;</a></sup> With Conkling's <a href="/wiki/Stalwart_(politics)" class="mw-redirect" title="Stalwart (politics)">Stalwart</a> faction of the Republican Party in disarray following the assassination of President <a href="/wiki/James_Garfield" class="mw-redirect" title="James Garfield">James Garfield</a>, Roosevelt won election as the Republican party leader in the state assembly. He allied with Governor Cleveland to win passage of a civil service reform bill.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992140–142_48-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992140–142-48">&#91;46&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt won re-election a second time and sought the office of <a href="/wiki/Speaker_of_the_New_York_State_Assembly" class="mw-redirect" title="Speaker of the New York State Assembly">Speaker of the New York State Assembly</a>, but <a href="/wiki/Titus_Sheard" title="Titus Sheard">Titus Sheard</a> obtained the position in a 41 to 29 vote of the GOP caucus instead.<sup id="cite_ref-49" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-49">&#91;47&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992153_50-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992153-50">&#91;48&#93;</a></sup> In his final term, Roosevelt served as Chairman of the Committee on Affairs of Cities, during which he wrote more bills than any other legislator.<sup id="cite_ref-51" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-51">&#91;49&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Presidential_election_of_1884">Presidential election of 1884</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/1884_United_States_presidential_election" title="1884 United States presidential election">1884 United States presidential election</a></div>
<p>With numerous presidential hopefuls from whom to choose, Roosevelt supported Senator <a href="/wiki/George_F._Edmunds" title="George F. Edmunds">George F. Edmunds</a> of Vermont, a colorless reformer. The state GOP preferred the incumbent president, New York City's <a href="/wiki/Chester_Arthur" class="mw-redirect" title="Chester Arthur">Chester Arthur</a>, known for passing the <a href="/wiki/Pendleton_Civil_Service_Reform_Act" title="Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act">Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act</a>. Roosevelt fought for and succeeded in influencing the Manhattan delegates at the state convention in Utica. He then took control of the state convention, bargaining through the night and outmaneuvering the supporters of Arthur and <a href="/wiki/James_G._Blaine" title="James G. Blaine">James G. Blaine</a>; consequently, he gained a national reputation as a key politician in his state.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPutnam1958413–424_52-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPutnam1958413–424-52">&#91;50&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Roosevelt attended the 1884 <a href="/wiki/1884_Republican_National_Convention" title="1884 Republican National Convention">GOP National Convention</a> in Chicago and gave a speech convincing delegates to nominate <a href="/wiki/African_American" class="mw-redirect" title="African American">African American</a> <a href="/wiki/John_R._Lynch" title="John R. Lynch">John R. Lynch</a>, an Edmunds supporter, to be the temporary chair. Roosevelt fought alongside the <a href="/wiki/Mugwump" class="mw-redirect" title="Mugwump">Mugwump</a> reformers against Blaine. However, Blaine gained support from Arthur's and Edmunds's delegates, and won the nomination on the fourth ballot. In a crucial moment of his budding political career, Roosevelt resisted the demand of his fellow Mugwumps that he bolt from Blaine. He bragged about his one small success: "We achieved a victory in getting up a combination to beat the Blaine nominee for temporary chairman... To do this needed a mixture of skill, boldness and energy... to get the different factions to come in... to defeat the common foe."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997171_53-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997171-53">&#91;51&#93;</a></sup> He was also impressed by an invitation to speak before an audience of ten thousand, the largest crowd he had addressed up to that date. Having gotten a taste of national politics, Roosevelt felt less aspiration for advocacy on the state level; he then retired to his new "Chimney Butte Ranch" on the <a href="/wiki/Little_Missouri_River_(North_Dakota)" title="Little Missouri River (North Dakota)">Little Missouri River</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPutnam1958445–450_54-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPutnam1958445–450-54">&#91;52&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt refused to join other Mugwumps in supporting Grover Cleveland, the governor of New York and the <a href="/wiki/History_of_the_United_States_Democratic_Party" class="mw-redirect" title="History of the United States Democratic Party">Democratic</a> nominee in the general election. He debated the pros and cons of staying loyal with his political friend, <a href="/wiki/Henry_Cabot_Lodge" title="Henry Cabot Lodge">Henry Cabot Lodge</a>. After Blaine won the nomination, Roosevelt had said carelessly that he would give "hearty support to any decent Democrat". He distanced himself from the promise, saying that it had not been meant "for publication".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPringle195661_55-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPringle195661-55">&#91;53&#93;</a></sup> When a reporter asked if he would support Blaine, Roosevelt replied, "That question I decline to answer. It is a subject I do not care to talk about."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPutnam1958445_56-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPutnam1958445-56">&#91;54&#93;</a></sup> In the end, he realized that he had to support Blaine to maintain his role in the GOP and he did so in a press release on July 19.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPutnam1958467_57-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPutnam1958467-57">&#91;55&#93;</a></sup> Having lost the support of many reformers, Roosevelt decided to retire from politics and move to <a href="/wiki/North_Dakota" title="North Dakota">North Dakota</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992161_58-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992161-58">&#91;56&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Cattle_rancher_in_Dakota">Cattle rancher in Dakota</span></h2>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:TR_Buckskin_Tiffany_Knife.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/22/TR_Buckskin_Tiffany_Knife.jpg/180px-TR_Buckskin_Tiffany_Knife.jpg" decoding="async" width="180" height="225" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/22/TR_Buckskin_Tiffany_Knife.jpg/270px-TR_Buckskin_Tiffany_Knife.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/22/TR_Buckskin_Tiffany_Knife.jpg/360px-TR_Buckskin_Tiffany_Knife.jpg 2x" data-file-width="476" data-file-height="596" /></a><figcaption>Theodore Roosevelt as <a href="/wiki/Badlands" title="Badlands">Badlands</a> hunter in 1885. New York studio photo.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Roosevelt first visited the <a href="/wiki/Dakota_Territory" title="Dakota Territory">Dakota Territory</a> in 1883 to hunt <a href="/wiki/Bison" title="Bison">bison</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-59" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-59">&#91;57&#93;</a></sup> Exhilarated by the <a href="/wiki/Western_lifestyle" title="Western lifestyle">western lifestyle</a> and with the cattle business booming in the territory, Roosevelt invested $14,000 ($439,700 in 2022) in hopes of becoming a prosperous cattle rancher. For the next several years, he shuttled between his home in New York and his ranch in Dakota.<sup id="cite_ref-60" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-60">&#91;58&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Following the <a href="/wiki/1884_United_States_presidential_election" title="1884 United States presidential election">1884 United States presidential election</a>, Roosevelt built a <a href="/wiki/Elkhorn_Ranch" title="Elkhorn Ranch">ranch named Elkhorn</a>, which was 35&#160;mi (56&#160;km) north of the boomtown of <a href="/wiki/Medora,_North_Dakota" title="Medora, North Dakota">Medora, North Dakota</a>. Roosevelt learned to ride western style, rope, and hunt on the banks of the <a href="/wiki/Little_Missouri_River_(North_Dakota)" title="Little Missouri River (North Dakota)">Little Missouri</a>. Though he earned the respect of the authentic <a href="/wiki/Cowboy" title="Cowboy">cowboys</a>, they were not overly impressed.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997182_61-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997182-61">&#91;59&#93;</a></sup> However, he identified with the herdsman of history, a man he said possesses "few of the emasculated, milk-and-water moralities admired by the pseudo-philanthropists; but he does possess, to a very high degree, the stern, manly qualities that are invaluable to a nation".<sup id="cite_ref-62" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-62">&#91;60&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-63" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-63">&#91;61&#93;</a></sup> He reoriented and began writing about frontier life for national magazines; he also published three books: <i>Hunting Trips of a Ranchman</i>, <i>Ranch Life and the Hunting-Trail</i>, and <i>The Wilderness Hunter</i>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997191_64-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997191-64">&#91;62&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Roosevelt successfully led efforts to organize ranchers there to address the problems of overgrazing and other shared concerns, which resulted in the formation of the Little Missouri Stockmen's Association. He felt compelled to promote conservation and was able to form the <a href="/wiki/Boone_and_Crockett_Club" title="Boone and Crockett Club">Boone and Crockett Club</a>, whose primary goal was the conservation of large game animals and their habitats.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997189_65-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997189-65">&#91;63&#93;</a></sup> In 1886, Roosevelt served as a <a href="/wiki/Sheriffs_in_the_United_States" title="Sheriffs in the United States">deputy sheriff</a> in <a href="/wiki/Billings_County,_North_Dakota" title="Billings County, North Dakota">Billings County, North Dakota</a>. During this time, he and two ranch hands hunted down three boat thieves.<sup id="cite_ref-66" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-66">&#91;64&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The uniquely severe U.S. <a href="/wiki/Winter_of_1886%E2%80%931887" title="Winter of 1886–1887">winter of 1886–1887</a> wiped out his herd of cattle and those of his competitors and over half of his $80,000 investment ($2.61&#160;million in 2022). <sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMorris1979376_67-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorris1979376-67">&#91;65&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-68" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-68">&#91;66&#93;</a></sup> He ended his ranching life and returned to New York, where he escaped the damaging label of an ineffectual intellectual.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992163–164_69-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992163–164-69">&#91;67&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Second_marriage">Second marriage</span></h2>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Smithsonian_-_NPG_-_Roosevelt_-_NPG_81_126.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a3/Smithsonian_-_NPG_-_Roosevelt_-_NPG_81_126.jpg/290px-Smithsonian_-_NPG_-_Roosevelt_-_NPG_81_126.jpg" decoding="async" width="290" height="217" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a3/Smithsonian_-_NPG_-_Roosevelt_-_NPG_81_126.jpg/435px-Smithsonian_-_NPG_-_Roosevelt_-_NPG_81_126.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a3/Smithsonian_-_NPG_-_Roosevelt_-_NPG_81_126.jpg/580px-Smithsonian_-_NPG_-_Roosevelt_-_NPG_81_126.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4000" data-file-height="2993" /></a><figcaption>Theodore Roosevelt and family. From left to right: Ethel Kermit Carow, Kermit, Quentin, Edith Kermit Carow, Theodore Roosevelt, Jr., Theodore Roosevelt, Archibald Bulloch, Alice Lee Roosevelt Longworth, Nicholas Longworth</figcaption></figure>
<p>On December 2, 1886, Roosevelt married his childhood friend, <a href="/wiki/Edith_Roosevelt" title="Edith Roosevelt">Edith Kermit Carow</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-70" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-70">&#91;68&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt felt deeply troubled that his second marriage had taken place very quickly after the death of his first wife and he also faced resistance from his sisters.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992181–182_71-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992181–182-71">&#91;69&#93;</a></sup> Nonetheless, the couple married at <a href="/wiki/St_George%27s,_Hanover_Square" title="St George&#39;s, Hanover Square">St George's, Hanover Square</a>, in London, England.<sup id="cite_ref-72" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-72">&#91;70&#93;</a></sup> The couple had five children: <a href="/wiki/Theodore_Roosevelt_Jr." title="Theodore Roosevelt Jr.">Theodore "Ted" III</a> in 1887, <a href="/wiki/Kermit_Roosevelt" title="Kermit Roosevelt">Kermit</a> in 1889, <a href="/wiki/Ethel_Roosevelt_Derby" title="Ethel Roosevelt Derby">Ethel</a> in 1891, <a href="/wiki/Archibald_Roosevelt" title="Archibald Roosevelt">Archibald</a> in 1894, and <a href="/wiki/Quentin_Roosevelt" title="Quentin Roosevelt">Quentin</a> in 1897. They also raised Roosevelt's daughter from his first marriage, Alice, who often clashed with her stepmother.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992193–194_73-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992193–194-73">&#91;71&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Reentering_public_life">Reentering public life</span></h2>
<p>Upon Roosevelt's return to New York in 1886, Republican leaders quickly approached him about running for <a href="/wiki/Mayor_of_New_York_City" title="Mayor of New York City">mayor of New York City</a> in the <a href="/wiki/1886_New_York_City_mayoral_election" title="1886 New York City mayoral election">1886 election</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-74" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-74">&#91;72&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt accepted the nomination despite having little hope of winning the race against <a href="/wiki/Labor_Party_(United_States,_19th_century)" title="Labor Party (United States, 19th century)">United Labor Party</a> candidate <a href="/wiki/Henry_George" title="Henry George">Henry George</a> and Democratic candidate <a href="/wiki/Abram_Hewitt" title="Abram Hewitt">Abram Hewitt</a>. Roosevelt campaigned hard for the position, but Hewitt won with 41% (90,552 votes), taking the votes of many Republicans who feared George's radical policies.<sup id="cite_ref-everything_75-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-everything-75">&#91;73&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992183–185_76-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992183–185-76">&#91;74&#93;</a></sup> George was held to 31% (68,110 votes), and Roosevelt took third place with 27% (60,435 votes). Fearing that his political career might never recover, Roosevelt turned his attention to writing <i>The Winning of the West</i>, a historical work tracking the westward movement of Americans; the book was a great success for Roosevelt, earning favorable reviews and selling numerous<sup class="noprint Inline-Template" style="margin-left:0.1em; white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify" title="Wikipedia:Please clarify"><span title="The text near this tag may need clarification or removal of jargon. (December 2022)">clarification needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup> copies.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992197–200_77-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992197–200-77">&#91;75&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Civil_Service_Commission">Civil Service Commission</span></h3>
<p>After <a href="/wiki/Benjamin_Harrison" title="Benjamin Harrison">Benjamin Harrison</a> unexpectedly defeated Blaine for the presidential nomination at the <a href="/wiki/1888_Republican_National_Convention" title="1888 Republican National Convention">1888 Republican National Convention</a>, Roosevelt gave <a href="/wiki/Stump_speech_(politics)" class="mw-redirect" title="Stump speech (politics)">stump speeches</a> in the Midwest in support of Harrison.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992201_78-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992201-78">&#91;76&#93;</a></sup> On the insistence of <a href="/wiki/Henry_Cabot_Lodge" title="Henry Cabot Lodge">Henry Cabot Lodge</a>, President Harrison appointed Roosevelt to the <a href="/wiki/United_States_Civil_Service_Commission" title="United States Civil Service Commission">United States Civil Service Commission</a>, where he served until 1895.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992203_79-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992203-79">&#91;77&#93;</a></sup> While many of his predecessors had approached the office as a <a href="/wiki/Sinecure" title="Sinecure">sinecure</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992206–207_80-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992206–207-80">&#91;78&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt vigorously fought the <a href="/wiki/Spoils_system" title="Spoils system">spoilsmen</a> and demanded enforcement of civil service laws.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEThayer19191–2ch._VI_81-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThayer19191–2ch._VI-81">&#91;79&#93;</a></sup> <i><a href="/wiki/The_Sun_(New_York)" class="mw-redirect" title="The Sun (New York)">The Sun</a></i> then described Roosevelt as "irrepressible, belligerent, and enthusiastic".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBishop2007&#91;httpsbooksgooglecombooksidKPMEAAAAYAAJqTheodoreRooseveltandHisTimeShowninHisOwnLetters_51&#93;_82-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBishop2007[httpsbooksgooglecombooksidKPMEAAAAYAAJqTheodoreRooseveltandHisTimeShowninHisOwnLetters_51]-82">&#91;80&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt frequently clashed with Postmaster General <a href="/wiki/John_Wanamaker" title="John Wanamaker">John Wanamaker</a>, who handed out numerous patronage positions to Harrison supporters, and Roosevelt's attempt to force out several postal workers damaged Harrison politically.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992216–221_83-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992216–221-83">&#91;81&#93;</a></sup> Despite Roosevelt's support for Harrison's reelection bid in the <a href="/wiki/1892_U.S._presidential_election" class="mw-redirect" title="1892 U.S. presidential election">presidential election of 1892</a>, the eventual winner, Grover Cleveland, reappointed him to the same post.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBishop2007&#91;httpsbooksgooglecombooksidKPMEAAAAYAAJqTheodoreRooseveltandHisTimeShowninHisOwnLetters_53&#93;_84-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBishop2007[httpsbooksgooglecombooksidKPMEAAAAYAAJqTheodoreRooseveltandHisTimeShowninHisOwnLetters_53]-84">&#91;82&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt's close friend and biographer, <a href="/wiki/Joseph_Bucklin_Bishop" title="Joseph Bucklin Bishop">Joseph Bucklin Bishop</a>, described his assault on the spoils system:
</p>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r996844942"><blockquote class="templatequote"><p> The very citadel of spoils politics, the hitherto impregnable fortress that had existed unshaken since it was erected on the foundation laid by <a href="/wiki/Andrew_Jackson" title="Andrew Jackson">Andrew Jackson</a>, was tottering to its fall under the assaults of this audacious and irrepressible young man... Whatever may have been the feelings of the (fellow Republican party) President (Harrison)—and there is little doubt that he had no idea when he appointed Roosevelt that he would prove to be so veritable a bull in a china shop—he refused to remove him and stood by him firmly till the end of his term.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBishop2007&#91;httpsbooksgooglecombooksidKPMEAAAAYAAJqTheodoreRooseveltandHisTimeShowninHisOwnLetters_51&#93;_82-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBishop2007[httpsbooksgooglecombooksidKPMEAAAAYAAJqTheodoreRooseveltandHisTimeShowninHisOwnLetters_51]-82">&#91;80&#93;</a></sup></p></blockquote>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="New_York_City_Police_Commissioner">New York City Police Commissioner</span></h3>
<p>In 1894, a group of reform Republicans approached Roosevelt about running for Mayor of New York again; he declined, mostly due to his wife's resistance to being removed from the Washington social set. Soon after he declined, he realized that he had missed an opportunity to reinvigorate a dormant political career. He retreated to the Dakotas for a time; his wife Edith regretted her role in the decision and vowed that there would be no repeat of it.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997265–268_85-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997265–268-85">&#91;83&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p><a href="/wiki/William_Lafayette_Strong" title="William Lafayette Strong">William Lafayette Strong</a>, a reform-minded Republican, won the 1894 mayoral election and offered Roosevelt a position on the board of the <a href="/wiki/New_York_City_Police_Commissioner" title="New York City Police Commissioner">New York City Police Commissioners</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992201_78-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992201-78">&#91;76&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-86" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-86">&#91;84&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt became president of the board of commissioners and radically reformed the police force. Roosevelt implemented regular inspections of firearms and annual physical exams, appointed recruits based on their physical and mental qualifications rather than political affiliation, established <a href="/wiki/Meritorious_Service_Medal_(United_States)" title="Meritorious Service Medal (United States)">Meritorious Service Medals</a>, and closed corrupt police hostelries. During his tenure, a Municipal Lodging House was established by the Board of Charities, and Roosevelt required officers to register with the Board; he also had telephones installed in station houses.<sup id="cite_ref-87" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-87">&#91;85&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In 1894, Roosevelt met <a href="/wiki/Jacob_Riis" title="Jacob Riis">Jacob Riis</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Muckraker" title="Muckraker">muckraking</a> <i><a href="/wiki/The_Sun_(New_York_City)" title="The Sun (New York City)">Evening Sun</a></i> newspaper journalist who was opening the eyes of New Yorkers to the terrible conditions of the city's millions of poor immigrants with such books as <i><a href="/wiki/How_the_Other_Half_Lives" title="How the Other Half Lives">How the Other Half Lives</a>.</i> Riis described how his book affected Roosevelt:
</p>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r996844942"><blockquote class="templatequote"><p>When Roosevelt read [my] book, he came... No one ever helped as he did. For two years we were brothers in (New York City's crime-ridden) <a href="/wiki/Mulberry_Street_(Manhattan)" title="Mulberry Street (Manhattan)">Mulberry Street</a>. When he left I had seen its golden age... There is very little ease where Theodore Roosevelt leads, as we all of us found out. The lawbreaker found it out who predicted scornfully that he would "knuckle down to politics the way they all did", and lived to respect him, though he swore at him, as the one of them all who was stronger than pull... that was what made the age golden, that for the first time a moral purpose came into the street. In the light of it everything was transformed.<sup id="cite_ref-88" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-88">&#91;86&#93;</a></sup></p></blockquote>
<p>Roosevelt made a habit of walking officers' <a href="/wiki/Beat_(police)" title="Beat (police)">beats</a> late at night and early in the morning to make sure that they were on duty.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997277_89-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997277-89">&#91;87&#93;</a></sup> He made a concerted effort to uniformly enforce New York's <a href="/wiki/Raines_law" title="Raines law">Sunday closing law</a>; in this, he ran up against boss <a href="/wiki/Thomas_C._Platt" title="Thomas C. Platt">Tom Platt</a> as well as <a href="/wiki/Tammany_Hall" title="Tammany Hall">Tammany Hall</a>—he was notified that the Police Commission was being legislated out of existence. His crackdowns led to protests and demonstrations. Invited to one large demonstration, not only did he surprisingly accept, but he also delighted in the insults, caricatures, and lampoons directed at him, and earned some good will.<sup id="cite_ref-Bully_Pulpit_90-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Bully_Pulpit-90">&#91;88&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt chose to defer rather than split with his party.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997293_91-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997293-91">&#91;89&#93;</a></sup> As Governor of New York State, he would later sign an act replacing the Police Commission with a single Police Commissioner.<sup id="cite_ref-92" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-92">&#91;90&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Emergence_as_a_national_figure">Emergence as a national figure</span></h2>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Assistant_Secretary_of_the_Navy">Assistant Secretary of the Navy</span></h3>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:LC-USZC4-701_(17518506711).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4f/LC-USZC4-701_%2817518506711%29.jpg/220px-LC-USZC4-701_%2817518506711%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="150" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4f/LC-USZC4-701_%2817518506711%29.jpg/330px-LC-USZC4-701_%2817518506711%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4f/LC-USZC4-701_%2817518506711%29.jpg/440px-LC-USZC4-701_%2817518506711%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1354" data-file-height="923" /></a><figcaption>The <a href="/wiki/Asiatic_Squadron" title="Asiatic Squadron">Asiatic Squadron</a> destroying the Spanish fleet in the <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Manila_Bay" title="Battle of Manila Bay">Battle of Manila Bay</a> on May 1, 1898</figcaption></figure>
<p>In the <a href="/wiki/1896_United_States_presidential_election" title="1896 United States presidential election">1896 presidential election</a>, Roosevelt backed Speaker of the House <a href="/wiki/Thomas_Brackett_Reed" title="Thomas Brackett Reed">Thomas Brackett Reed</a> for the Republican nomination, but <a href="/wiki/William_McKinley" title="William McKinley">William McKinley</a> won the nomination and defeated <a href="/wiki/William_Jennings_Bryan" title="William Jennings Bryan">William Jennings Bryan</a> in the general election.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992242–243_93-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992242–243-93">&#91;91&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt strongly opposed Bryan's <a href="/wiki/Free_silver" title="Free silver">free silver</a> platform, viewing many of Bryan's followers as dangerous fanatics. He gave scores of campaign speeches for McKinley.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992243–246_94-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992243–246-94">&#91;92&#93;</a></sup> Urged by Senator <a href="/wiki/Henry_Cabot_Lodge" title="Henry Cabot Lodge">Henry Cabot Lodge</a>, President McKinley appointed Roosevelt as the <a href="/wiki/Assistant_Secretary_of_the_Navy" title="Assistant Secretary of the Navy">Assistant Secretary of the Navy</a> in 1897.<sup id="cite_ref-95" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-95">&#91;93&#93;</a></sup> Secretary of the Navy <a href="/wiki/John_D._Long" class="mw-redirect" title="John D. Long">John D. Long</a> was more concerned about formalities than functions, was in poor health, and left many major decisions to Roosevelt. Influenced by <a href="/wiki/Alfred_Thayer_Mahan" title="Alfred Thayer Mahan">Alfred Thayer Mahan</a>, Roosevelt called for a build-up in the country's naval strength, particularly the construction of <a href="/wiki/Battleship" title="Battleship">battleships</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992253_96-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992253-96">&#91;94&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt also began pressing his national security views regarding the Pacific and the Caribbean on McKinley and was particularly adamant that Spain be ejected from Cuba.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997310–212_97-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997310–212-97">&#91;95&#93;</a></sup> He explained his priorities to one of the Navy's planners in late 1897:
</p>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r996844942"><blockquote class="templatequote"><p>I would regard war with Spain from two viewpoints: first, the advisability on the grounds both of humanity and self-interest of interfering on behalf of the Cubans, and of taking one more step toward the complete freeing of America from European dominion; second, the benefit done our people by giving them something to think of which is not material gain, and especially the benefit done our military forces by trying both the Navy and Army in actual practice.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTERoosevelt2001157–158_98-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoosevelt2001157–158-98">&#91;96&#93;</a></sup></p></blockquote>
<p>On February 15, 1898, <a href="/wiki/USS_Maine_(ACR-1)" class="mw-redirect" title="USS Maine (ACR-1)">USS&#160;<i>Maine</i></a>, an armored cruiser, exploded in the harbor of <a href="/wiki/Havana,_Cuba" class="mw-redirect" title="Havana, Cuba">Havana, Cuba</a>, killing hundreds of crew members. While Roosevelt and many other Americans blamed Spain for the explosion, McKinley sought a diplomatic solution.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992267–268_99-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992267–268-99">&#91;97&#93;</a></sup> Without approval from Long or McKinley, Roosevelt sent out orders to several naval vessels, directing them to prepare for war.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992267–268_99-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992267–268-99">&#91;97&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997325–326_100-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997325–326-100">&#91;98&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/George_Dewey" title="George Dewey">George Dewey</a>, who had received an appointment to lead the <a href="/wiki/Asiatic_Squadron" title="Asiatic Squadron">Asiatic Squadron</a> with the backing of Roosevelt, later credited his victory at the <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Manila_Bay" title="Battle of Manila Bay">Battle of Manila Bay</a> to Roosevelt's orders.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992261,_268_101-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992261,_268-101">&#91;99&#93;</a></sup> After finally giving up hope of a peaceful solution, McKinley asked Congress to declare war upon Spain, beginning the <a href="/wiki/Spanish%E2%80%93American_War" title="Spanish–American War">Spanish–American War</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992271–272_102-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992271–272-102">&#91;100&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="War_in_Cuba">War in Cuba</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Rough_Riders" title="Rough Riders">Rough Riders</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Theodore_Rooseveltnewtry.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e2/Theodore_Rooseveltnewtry.jpg/220px-Theodore_Rooseveltnewtry.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="325" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e2/Theodore_Rooseveltnewtry.jpg/330px-Theodore_Rooseveltnewtry.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e2/Theodore_Rooseveltnewtry.jpg/440px-Theodore_Rooseveltnewtry.jpg 2x" data-file-width="880" data-file-height="1300" /></a><figcaption>Colonel Theodore Roosevelt</figcaption></figure>
<p>With the beginning of the Spanish–American War in late April 1898, Roosevelt resigned from his post as Assistant Secretary of the Navy. Along with Army Colonel <a href="/wiki/Leonard_Wood" title="Leonard Wood">Leonard Wood</a>, he formed the <a href="/wiki/Rough_Riders" title="Rough Riders">First U.S. Volunteer Cavalry Regiment</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-LOC_103-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-LOC-103">&#91;101&#93;</a></sup> His wife and many of his friends begged Roosevelt to remain in his post in Washington, but Roosevelt was determined to see battle. When the newspapers reported the formation of the new regiment, Roosevelt and Wood were flooded with applications from all over the country.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992272–274_104-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992272–274-104">&#91;102&#93;</a></sup> Referred to by the press as the "Rough Riders", the regiment was one of many temporary units active only for the duration of the war.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESamuels1997148_105-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESamuels1997148-105">&#91;103&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The regiment trained for several weeks in <a href="/wiki/San_Antonio,_Texas" class="mw-redirect" title="San Antonio, Texas">San Antonio, Texas</a>, and in his autobiography, Roosevelt wrote that his prior experience with the <a href="/wiki/New_York_National_Guard" class="mw-redirect" title="New York National Guard">New York National Guard</a> had been invaluable, in that it enabled him to immediately begin teaching his men basic soldiering skills.<sup id="cite_ref-106" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-106">&#91;104&#93;</a></sup> The Rough Riders used some standard issue gear and some of their own design, purchased with gift money. Diversity characterized the regiment, which included <a href="/wiki/Ivy_League" title="Ivy League">Ivy Leaguers</a>, professional and amateur athletes, upscale gentlemen, cowboys, frontiersmen, <a href="/wiki/Native_Americans_in_the_United_States" title="Native Americans in the United States">Native Americans</a>, hunters, miners, prospectors, former soldiers, tradesmen, and sheriffs. The Rough Riders were part of the cavalry division commanded by former Confederate general <a href="/wiki/Joseph_Wheeler" title="Joseph Wheeler">Joseph Wheeler</a>, which itself was one of three divisions in the V Corps under Major General <a href="/wiki/William_Rufus_Shafter" title="William Rufus Shafter">William Rufus Shafter</a>. Roosevelt and his men landed in <a href="/wiki/Daiquir%C3%AD" title="Daiquirí">Daiquirí</a>, Cuba, on June 23, 1898, and marched to <a href="/wiki/Siboney,_Cuba" title="Siboney, Cuba">Siboney</a>. Wheeler sent parts of the 1st and 10th Regular Cavalry on the lower road northwest and sent the "Rough Riders" on the parallel road running along a ridge up from the beach. To throw off his infantry rival, Wheeler left one regiment of his Cavalry Division, the 9th, at Siboney so that he could claim that his move north was only a limited reconnaissance if things went wrong. Roosevelt was promoted to colonel and took command of the regiment when Wood was put in command of the brigade. The Rough Riders had a short, minor skirmish known as the <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Las_Guasimas" title="Battle of Las Guasimas">Battle of Las Guasimas</a>; they fought their way through Spanish resistance and, together with the Regulars, forced the Spaniards to abandon their positions.<sup id="cite_ref-The_Rough_Riders_107-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-The_Rough_Riders-107">&#91;105&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:TR_San_Juan_Hill_1898.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/58/TR_San_Juan_Hill_1898.jpg/290px-TR_San_Juan_Hill_1898.jpg" decoding="async" width="290" height="234" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/58/TR_San_Juan_Hill_1898.jpg/435px-TR_San_Juan_Hill_1898.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/58/TR_San_Juan_Hill_1898.jpg/580px-TR_San_Juan_Hill_1898.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1144" data-file-height="925" /></a><figcaption>Colonel Roosevelt and the Rough Riders after capturing <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_San_Juan_Hill#Kettle_Hill" title="Battle of San Juan Hill">Kettle Hill</a> in <a href="/wiki/Cuba" title="Cuba">Cuba</a> in July 1898, along with members of the 3rd Volunteers and the regular Army black <a href="/wiki/10th_Cavalry_Regiment_(United_States)" title="10th Cavalry Regiment (United States)">10th Cavalry</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>Under Roosevelt's leadership, the Rough Riders became famous for the charge up <a href="/wiki/Kettle_Hill" class="mw-redirect" title="Kettle Hill">Kettle Hill</a> on July 1, 1898, while supporting the regulars. Roosevelt had the only horse and rode back and forth between rifle pits at the forefront of the advance up Kettle Hill, an advance that he urged despite the absence of any orders from superiors. He was forced to walk up the last part of Kettle Hill because his horse had been entangled in <a href="/wiki/Barbed_wire" title="Barbed wire">barbed wire</a>. The victories came at a cost of 200 killed and 1,000 wounded.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997356_108-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997356-108">&#91;106&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In August, Roosevelt and other officers demanded that the soldiers be returned home. Roosevelt always recalled the Battle of Kettle Hill (part of the San Juan Heights) as "the great day of my life" and "my crowded hour". In 2001, Roosevelt was posthumously awarded the <a href="/wiki/Medal_of_Honor" title="Medal of Honor">Medal of Honor</a> for his actions;<sup id="cite_ref-MoH2001_109-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-MoH2001-109">&#91;107&#93;</a></sup> he had been nominated during the war, but Army officials, annoyed at his grabbing the headlines, blocked it.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESamuels1997&#91;httpsbooksgooglecombooksid1v7PSGbzhDwCpgPA266_266&#93;_110-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESamuels1997[httpsbooksgooglecombooksid1v7PSGbzhDwCpgPA266_266]-110">&#91;108&#93;</a></sup> After returning to civilian life, Roosevelt preferred to be known as "Colonel Roosevelt" or "The Colonel", though "Teddy" remained much more popular with the public, even though Roosevelt openly despised that moniker. Men working closely with Roosevelt customarily called him "Colonel" or "Theodore".<sup id="cite_ref-HandyBook_111-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-HandyBook-111">&#91;109&#93;</a></sup><sup class="noprint Inline-Template" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing_sources" title="Wikipedia:Citing sources"><span title="This citation requires a reference to the specific page or range of pages in which the material appears. (September 2021)">page&#160;needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup> 
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Governor_of_New_York">Governor of New York</span></h3>
<p>After leaving Cuba in August 1898, the Rough Riders were transported to a camp at <a href="/wiki/Montauk_County_Park" title="Montauk County Park">Montauk Point</a>, <a href="/wiki/Long_Island" title="Long Island">Long Island</a>, where Roosevelt and his men were briefly quarantined due to the War Department's fear of spreading <a href="/wiki/Yellow_fever" title="Yellow fever">yellow fever</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992308–310_112-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992308–310-112">&#91;110&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Sister_Regina_Purtell" class="mw-redirect" title="Sister Regina Purtell">Sister Regina Purtell</a> was one of the nurses sent to this camp, and she was so competent during outbreaks and so beloved by the Rough Riders that she became friends with Roosevelt himself; a few years later he would ask for her to personally care for him when he was in St. Vincent's hospital.<sup id="cite_ref-113" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-113">&#91;111&#93;</a></sup> Shortly after Roosevelt's return to the United States, Republican Congressman <a href="/wiki/Lemuel_E._Quigg" title="Lemuel E. Quigg">Lemuel E. Quigg</a>, a lieutenant of party boss Tom Platt, asked Roosevelt to run in the <a href="/wiki/1898_New_York_state_election" title="1898 New York state election">1898 gubernatorial election</a>. Prospering politically from the <a href="/wiki/Platt_machine" title="Platt machine">Platt machine</a>, Roosevelt's gradual rise to power was marked by the pragmatic decisions of New York machine boss <a href="/wiki/Thomas_C._Platt" title="Thomas C. Platt">T. C. "Tom" Platt</a>, who served as a U.S. senator from the state.<sup id="cite_ref-114" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-114">&#91;112&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-115" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-115">&#91;113&#93;</a></sup> The demonstrated willingness of Platt to compromise with the GOP progressive wing led by Roosevelt and <a href="/wiki/Benjamin_B._Odell_Jr." class="mw-redirect" title="Benjamin B. Odell Jr.">Benjamin B. Odell Jr.</a>, resulted, over time, in their growth of political strength at the expense of the "easy boss," whose machine faced collapse in 1903 at the hands of Odell.<sup id="cite_ref-116" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-116">&#91;114&#93;</a></sup>
Platt disliked Roosevelt personally, feared that Roosevelt would oppose Platt's interests in office, and was reluctant to propel Roosevelt to the forefront of national politics. However, Platt also needed a strong candidate due to the unpopularity of the incumbent Republican governor, <a href="/wiki/Frank_S._Black" title="Frank S. Black">Frank S. Black</a>. Roosevelt agreed to become the nominee and to try not to "make war" with the Republican establishment once in office. Roosevelt defeated Black in the Republican caucus by a vote of 753 to 218, and faced Democrat <a href="/wiki/Augustus_Van_Wyck" title="Augustus Van Wyck">Augustus Van Wyck</a>, a well-respected judge, in the general election.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992309–311,_318_117-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992309–311,_318-117">&#91;115&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt campaigned vigorously on his war record, winning the election by a margin of just one percent.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMorris1979674–687_118-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorris1979674–687-118">&#91;116&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>As governor, Roosevelt learned much about ongoing economic issues and political techniques that later proved valuable in his presidency. He studied the problems of trusts, monopolies, labor relations, and conservation. Chessman argues that Roosevelt's program "rested firmly upon the concept of the square deal by a neutral state". The rules for the Square Deal were "honesty in public affairs, an equitable sharing of privilege and responsibility, and subordination of party and local concerns to the interests of the state at large".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChessman19656_119-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChessman19656-119">&#91;117&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>By holding twice-daily press conferences—which was an innovation—Roosevelt remained connected with his middle-class political base.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMorris1979693_120-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorris1979693-120">&#91;118&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt successfully pushed the Ford Franchise-Tax bill, which taxed public franchises granted by the state and controlled by corporations, declaring that "a corporation which derives its powers from the State, should pay to the State a just percentage of its earnings as a return for the privileges it enjoys".<sup id="cite_ref-121" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-121">&#91;119&#93;</a></sup> He rejected "boss" Thomas C. Platt's worries that this approached Bryanite Socialism, explaining that without it, New York voters might get angry and adopt public ownership of streetcar lines and other franchises.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997378–379_122-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997378–379-122">&#91;120&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The New York state government affected many interests, and the power to make appointments to policy-making positions was a key role for the governor. Platt insisted that he be consulted on major appointments; Roosevelt appeared to comply, but then made his own decisions. Historians marvel that Roosevelt managed to appoint so many first-rate men with Platt's approval.
