He even enlisted Platt's help in securing reform, such as in the spring of 1899, when Platt pressured state senators to vote for a civil service bill that the secretary of the Civil Service Reform Association called "superior to any civil service statute heretofore secured in America".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChessman196579_123-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChessman196579-123">&#91;121&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>G. Wallace Chessman argues that as governor, Roosevelt developed the principles that shaped his presidency, especially insistence upon the public responsibility of large corporations, publicity as a first remedy for trusts, regulation of railroad rates, mediation of the conflict of capital and labor, conservation of natural resources and protection of the less fortunate members of society.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChessman19656_119-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChessman19656-119">&#91;117&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt sought to position himself against the excesses of large corporations on the one hand and radical movements on the other.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992322_124-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992322-124">&#91;122&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>As the chief executive of the most populous state in the union, Roosevelt was widely considered a potential future presidential candidate, and supporters such as <a href="/wiki/William_Allen_White" title="William Allen White">William Allen White</a> encouraged him to run for president.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992331–333_125-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992331–333-125">&#91;123&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt had no interest in challenging McKinley for the Republican nomination in 1900 and was denied his preferred post of <a href="/wiki/Secretary_of_War" class="mw-redirect" title="Secretary of War">Secretary of War</a>. As his term progressed, Roosevelt pondered a 1904 presidential run, but was uncertain about whether he should seek re-election as governor in 1900.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992333–334_126-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992333–334-126">&#91;124&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span id="Vice_presidency_.281901.29"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Vice_presidency_(1901)">Vice presidency (1901)</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/1900_United_States_presidential_election" title="1900 United States presidential election">1900 United States presidential election</a></div>
<p>In November 1899, Vice President <a href="/wiki/Garret_Hobart" title="Garret Hobart">Garret Hobart</a> died of heart failure, leaving an open spot on the 1900 Republican national ticket. Though <a href="/wiki/Henry_Cabot_Lodge" title="Henry Cabot Lodge">Henry Cabot Lodge</a> and others urged him to run for vice president in 1900, Roosevelt was reluctant to take the powerless position and issued a public statement saying that he would not accept the nomination.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992333–334,_338_127-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992333–334,_338-127">&#91;125&#93;</a></sup> Additionally, Roosevelt was informed by President McKinley and campaign manager <a href="/wiki/Mark_Hanna" title="Mark Hanna">Mark Hanna</a> that he was not being considered for the role of vice president due to his actions prior to the Spanish–American War<sup class="noprint Inline-Template" style="margin-left:0.1em; white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify" title="Wikipedia:Please clarify"><span title="The text near this tag may need clarification or removal of jargon. (December 2022)">clarification needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup>. Eager to be rid of Roosevelt, Platt nonetheless began a newspaper campaign in favor of Roosevelt's nomination for the vice presidency.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992338_128-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992338-128">&#91;126&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt attended the <a href="/wiki/1900_Republican_National_Convention" title="1900 Republican National Convention">1900 Republican National Convention</a> as a state delegate and struck a bargain with Platt: Roosevelt would accept the nomination for vice president if the convention offered it to him but would otherwise serve another term as governor. Platt asked Pennsylvania party boss <a href="/wiki/Matthew_Quay" title="Matthew Quay">Matthew Quay</a> to lead the campaign for Roosevelt's nomination, and Quay outmaneuvered Hanna at the convention to put Roosevelt on the ticket.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992340–341_129-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992340–341-129">&#91;127&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt won the nomination unanimously.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992342_130-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992342-130">&#91;128&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Roosevelt's vice-presidential campaigning proved highly energetic and an equal match for Democratic presidential nominee William Jennings Bryan's famous barnstorming style of campaigning. In a whirlwind campaign that displayed his energy to the public, Roosevelt made 480 stops in 23 states. He denounced the radicalism of Bryan, contrasting it with the heroism of the soldiers and sailors who fought and won the war against Spain. Bryan had strongly supported the war itself, but he denounced the annexation of the <a href="/wiki/Philippines" title="Philippines">Philippines</a> as <a href="/wiki/Imperialism" title="Imperialism">imperialism</a>, which would spoil America's innocence. Roosevelt countered that it was best for the <a href="/wiki/Filipinos" title="Filipinos">Filipinos</a> to have stability and the Americans to have a proud place in the world. With the nation basking in peace and prosperity, the voters gave McKinley an even larger victory than that which he had achieved in 1896.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997388–405_131-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997388–405-131">&#91;129&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-132" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-132">&#91;130&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>After the campaign, Roosevelt took office as vice president in March 1901. The office of vice president was a powerless sinecure and did not suit Roosevelt's aggressive temperament.<sup id="cite_ref-133" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-133">&#91;131&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt's six months as vice president were uneventful and boring for a man of action. He had no power; he presided over the Senate for a mere four days before it adjourned.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992346_134-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992346-134">&#91;132&#93;</a></sup> On September 2, 1901, Roosevelt first publicized an <a href="/wiki/Aphorism" title="Aphorism">aphorism</a> that thrilled his supporters: "<a href="/wiki/Big_Stick_ideology" class="mw-redirect" title="Big Stick ideology">Speak softly and carry a big stick, and you will go far."</a><sup id="cite_ref-135" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-135">&#91;133&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span id="Presidency_.281901.E2.80.931909.29"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Presidency_(1901–1909)">Presidency (1901–1909)</span></h2>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Presidency_of_Theodore_Roosevelt" title="Presidency of Theodore Roosevelt">Presidency of Theodore Roosevelt</a></div>
<figure typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Theodore_Roosevelt_by_John_Singer_Sargent,_1903.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/22/Theodore_Roosevelt_by_John_Singer_Sargent%2C_1903.jpg/180px-Theodore_Roosevelt_by_John_Singer_Sargent%2C_1903.jpg" decoding="async" width="180" height="270" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/22/Theodore_Roosevelt_by_John_Singer_Sargent%2C_1903.jpg/269px-Theodore_Roosevelt_by_John_Singer_Sargent%2C_1903.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/22/Theodore_Roosevelt_by_John_Singer_Sargent%2C_1903.jpg/359px-Theodore_Roosevelt_by_John_Singer_Sargent%2C_1903.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1997" data-file-height="3000" /></a><figcaption>Official <a href="/wiki/White_House" title="White House">White House</a> Portrait by artist <a href="/wiki/John_Singer_Sargent" title="John Singer Sargent">John Singer Sargent</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>On September 6, 1901, President McKinley was attending the <a href="/wiki/Pan-American_Exposition" title="Pan-American Exposition">Pan-American Exposition</a> in <a href="/wiki/Buffalo,_New_York" title="Buffalo, New York">Buffalo, New York</a> when he <a href="/wiki/Assassination_of_William_McKinley" title="Assassination of William McKinley">was shot</a> by anarchist <a href="/wiki/Leon_Czolgosz" title="Leon Czolgosz">Leon Czolgosz</a>. Roosevelt was vacationing in <a href="/wiki/Isle_La_Motte,_Vermont" class="mw-redirect" title="Isle La Motte, Vermont">Isle La Motte, Vermont</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-136" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-136">&#91;134&#93;</a></sup> and traveled to Buffalo to visit McKinley in the hospital. It appeared that McKinley would recover, so Roosevelt resumed his vacation in the <a href="/wiki/Adirondack_Mountains" title="Adirondack Mountains">Adirondack Mountains</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-137" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-137">&#91;135&#93;</a></sup> When McKinley's condition worsened, Roosevelt again rushed back to Buffalo. McKinley died on September 14, and Roosevelt was informed while he was in <a href="/wiki/North_Creek,_New_York" title="North Creek, New York">North Creek</a>; he continued on to Buffalo and was <a href="/wiki/First_inauguration_of_Theodore_Roosevelt" title="First inauguration of Theodore Roosevelt">sworn in as the nation's 26th president</a> at the <a href="/wiki/Theodore_Roosevelt_Inaugural_National_Historic_Site" title="Theodore Roosevelt Inaugural National Historic Site">Ansley Wilcox House</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992348–352_138-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992348–352-138">&#91;136&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>McKinley's supporters were nervous about the new president, and Ohio Senator <a href="/wiki/Mark_Hanna" title="Mark Hanna">Mark Hanna</a> was particularly bitter that the man he had opposed so vigorously at the convention had succeeded McKinley. Roosevelt assured party leaders that he intended to adhere to McKinley's policies, and he retained McKinley's Cabinet. Nonetheless, Roosevelt sought to position himself as the party's undisputed leader, seeking to bolster the role of the president and position himself for the 1904 election.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992354–356_139-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992354–356-139">&#91;137&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Shortly after taking office, Roosevelt invited <a href="/wiki/Booker_T._Washington" title="Booker T. Washington">Booker T. Washington</a> to dinner at the <a href="/wiki/White_House" title="White House">White House</a>. This sparked a bitter, and at times vicious, reaction among whites across the heavily segregated South.<sup id="cite_ref-140" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-140">&#91;138&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt reacted with astonishment and protest, saying that he looked forward to many future dinners with Washington. Upon further reflection, Roosevelt wanted to ensure that this had no effect on political support in the white South, and further dinner invitations to Washington were avoided;<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997422–423_141-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997422–423-141">&#91;139&#93;</a></sup> their next meeting was scheduled as typical business at 10:00&#160;a.m. instead.<sup id="cite_ref-142" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-142">&#91;140&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Domestic_policies:_The_Square_Deal">Domestic policies: The Square Deal</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <a href="/wiki/Square_Deal" title="Square Deal">Square Deal</a></div>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Trust_busting_and_regulation">Trust busting and regulation</span></h4>
<p>For his aggressive use of the 1890 <a href="/wiki/Sherman_Antitrust_Act" title="Sherman Antitrust Act">Sherman Antitrust Act</a>, compared to his predecessors, Roosevelt was hailed as the "trust-buster".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTERuddy2016_143-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTERuddy2016-143">&#91;141&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt viewed big business as a necessary part of the American economy and sought only to prosecute the "bad trusts" that restrained trade and charged unfair prices.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992365–366_144-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992365–366-144">&#91;142&#93;</a></sup> He brought 44 antitrust suits, breaking up the <a href="/wiki/Northern_Securities_Company" title="Northern Securities Company">Northern Securities Company</a>, the largest railroad monopoly; and regulating <a href="/wiki/Standard_Oil" title="Standard Oil">Standard Oil</a>, the largest oil company.<sup id="cite_ref-145" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-145">&#91;143&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTERuddy2016_143-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTERuddy2016-143">&#91;141&#93;</a></sup> Presidents Benjamin Harrison, Grover Cleveland, and William McKinley combined had prosecuted only 18 antitrust violations under the Sherman Antitrust Act.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTERuddy2016_143-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTERuddy2016-143">&#91;141&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Bolstered by his party's winning large majorities in the <a href="/wiki/1902_United_States_elections" title="1902 United States elections">1902 elections</a>, Roosevelt proposed the creation of the <a href="/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Commerce_and_Labor" title="United States Department of Commerce and Labor">United States Department of Commerce and Labor</a>, which would include the <a href="/wiki/Bureau_of_Corporations" title="Bureau of Corporations">Bureau of Corporations</a>. While Congress was receptive to the Department of Commerce and Labor, it was more skeptical of the antitrust powers that Roosevelt sought to endow within the Bureau of Corporations. Roosevelt successfully appealed to the public to pressure Congress, and Congress overwhelmingly voted to pass Roosevelt's version of the bill.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992378–381_146-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992378–381-146">&#91;144&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In a moment of frustration, House Speaker <a href="/wiki/Joseph_Gurney_Cannon" title="Joseph Gurney Cannon">Joseph Gurney Cannon</a> commented on Roosevelt's desire for executive branch control in domestic policymaking: "That fellow at the other end of the avenue wants everything from the birth of Christ to the death of the devil." Biographer Brands states, "Even his friends occasionally wondered whether there wasn't any custom or practice too minor for him to try to regulate, update or otherwise improve."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997552–553_147-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997552–553-147">&#91;145&#93;</a></sup> In fact, Roosevelt's willingness to exercise his power included attempted rule changes in the game of <a href="/wiki/American_football" title="American football">football</a>; at the <a href="/wiki/U.S._Naval_Academy" class="mw-redirect" title="U.S. Naval Academy">U.S. Naval Academy</a>, he sought to force retention of martial arts classes and to revise disciplinary rules. He even ordered changes made in the minting of a coin whose design he disliked and ordered the Government Printing Office to adopt simplified spellings for a core list of 300 words, according to reformers on the <a href="/wiki/Simplified_Spelling_Board" title="Simplified Spelling Board">Simplified Spelling Board</a>. He was forced to rescind the latter after substantial ridicule from the press and a resolution of protest from the <a href="/wiki/U.S._House_of_Representatives" class="mw-redirect" title="U.S. House of Representatives">U.S. House of Representatives</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997553–556_148-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997553–556-148">&#91;146&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Coal_strike">Coal strike</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Coal_strike_of_1902" class="mw-redirect" title="Coal strike of 1902">Coal strike of 1902</a></div>
<p>In May 1902, <a href="/wiki/United_Mine_Workers" class="mw-redirect" title="United Mine Workers">anthracite coal miners</a> went on strike, threatening a national energy shortage. After threatening the coal operators with intervention by federal troops, Roosevelt won their agreement to dispute arbitration by a commission, which succeeded in stopping the strike. The accord with <a href="/wiki/J._P._Morgan" title="J. P. Morgan">J. P. Morgan</a> resulted in the miners getting more pay for fewer hours, but with no union recognition.<sup id="cite_ref-149" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-149">&#91;147&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997450–483_150-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997450–483-150">&#91;148&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt said, "My action on labor should always be considered in connection with my action as regards capital, and both are reducible to my favorite formula—a square deal for every man."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997509_151-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997509-151">&#91;149&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt was the first president to help settle a labor dispute.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992376–377_152-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992376–377-152">&#91;150&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Prosecuted_misconduct">Prosecuted misconduct</span></h4>
<p>During Roosevelt's second year in office, it was discovered there was corruption in the <a href="/wiki/Bureau_of_Indian_Affairs" title="Bureau of Indian Affairs">Indian Service</a>, the <a href="/wiki/General_Land_Office" title="General Land Office">Land Office</a>, and the <a href="/wiki/United_States_Postal_Service" title="United States Postal Service">Post Office Department</a>. Roosevelt investigated and prosecuted corrupt Indian agents who had cheated the <a href="/wiki/Muscogee" title="Muscogee">Creeks</a> and various <a href="/wiki/Native_American_tribes" class="mw-redirect" title="Native American tribes">Native American tribes</a> out of land parcels. Land fraud and speculation were found involving Oregon federal timberlands. In November 1902, Roosevelt and Secretary <a href="/wiki/Ethan_A._Hitchcock_(Interior)" title="Ethan A. Hitchcock (Interior)">Ethan A. Hitchcock</a> forced <a href="/wiki/Binger_Hermann" title="Binger Hermann">Binger Hermann</a>, the General Land Office Commissioner, to resign from office. On November 6, 1903, <a href="/wiki/Francis_J._Heney" title="Francis J. Heney">Francis J. Heney</a> was appointed special prosecutor and obtained 146 indictments involving an <a href="/wiki/Oregon" title="Oregon">Oregon</a> Land Office bribery ring. U.S. Senator <a href="/wiki/John_H._Mitchell" title="John H. Mitchell">John H. Mitchell</a> was indicted for bribery to expedite illegal land patents, found guilty in July 1905, and sentenced to six months in prison.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChambers1974207_153-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChambers1974207-153">&#91;151&#93;</a></sup> More corruption was found in the Postal Department, that brought on the indictments of 44 government employees on charges of bribery and fraud.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChambers1974208_154-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChambers1974208-154">&#91;152&#93;</a></sup> Historians generally agree that Roosevelt moved "quickly and decisively" to prosecute misconduct in his administration.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChambers1974209_155-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChambers1974209-155">&#91;153&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Railroads">Railroads</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Hepburn_Act" title="Hepburn Act">Hepburn Act</a></div>
<p>Merchants complained that some railroad rates were too high. In the 1906 <a href="/wiki/Hepburn_Act" title="Hepburn Act">Hepburn Act</a>, Roosevelt sought to give the <a href="/wiki/Interstate_Commerce_Commission" title="Interstate Commerce Commission">Interstate Commerce Commission</a> the power to regulate rates, but the Senate, led by conservative <a href="/wiki/Nelson_Aldrich" class="mw-redirect" title="Nelson Aldrich">Nelson Aldrich</a>, fought back. Roosevelt worked with the Democratic Senator <a href="/wiki/Benjamin_Tillman" title="Benjamin Tillman">Benjamin Tillman</a> to pass the bill. Roosevelt and Aldrich ultimately reached a compromise that gave the ICC the power to replace existing rates with "just-and-reasonable" maximum rates, but allowed railroads to appeal to the federal courts on what was "reasonable".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992453–459_156-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992453–459-156">&#91;154&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-157" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-157">&#91;155&#93;</a></sup> In addition to rate-setting, the Hepburn Act also granted the ICC regulatory power over pipeline fees, storage contracts, and several other aspects of railroad operations.<sup id="cite_ref-158" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-158">&#91;156&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Pure_food_and_drugs">Pure food and drugs</span></h4>
<p>Roosevelt responded to public anger over the abuses in the food packing industry by pushing Congress to pass the <a href="/wiki/Meat_Inspection_Act" class="mw-redirect" title="Meat Inspection Act">Meat Inspection Act</a> of 1906 and the <a href="/wiki/Pure_Food_and_Drug_Act" title="Pure Food and Drug Act">Pure Food and Drug Act</a>. Though conservatives initially opposed the bill, <a href="/wiki/Upton_Sinclair" title="Upton Sinclair">Upton Sinclair</a>'s <i><a href="/wiki/The_Jungle" title="The Jungle">The Jungle</a></i>, published in 1906, helped galvanize support for reform.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992459–460_159-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992459–460-159">&#91;157&#93;</a></sup> The Meat Inspection Act of 1906 banned misleading labels and <a href="/wiki/Preservatives" class="mw-redirect" title="Preservatives">preservatives</a> that contained harmful chemicals. The Pure Food and Drug Act banned food and drugs that were impure or falsely labeled from being made, sold, and shipped. Roosevelt also served as honorary president of the <a href="/wiki/American_School_Hygiene_Association" title="American School Hygiene Association">American School Hygiene Association</a> from 1907 to 1908, and in 1909 he convened the first <a href="/wiki/White_House" title="White House">White House</a> Conference on the Care of Dependent Children.<sup id="cite_ref-ProgHealth21_160-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ProgHealth21-160">&#91;158&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Conservation">Conservation</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Presidency_of_Theodore_Roosevelt#Conservation" title="Presidency of Theodore Roosevelt">Presidency of Theodore Roosevelt §&#160;Conservation</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:President_Theodore_Roosevelt_Driving_Through_the_Wawona_Tunnel_Tree,_in_Yellowstone_National_Park_(14994749857).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c5/President_Theodore_Roosevelt_Driving_Through_the_Wawona_Tunnel_Tree%2C_in_Yellowstone_National_Park_%2814994749857%29.jpg/180px-President_Theodore_Roosevelt_Driving_Through_the_Wawona_Tunnel_Tree%2C_in_Yellowstone_National_Park_%2814994749857%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="180" height="227" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c5/President_Theodore_Roosevelt_Driving_Through_the_Wawona_Tunnel_Tree%2C_in_Yellowstone_National_Park_%2814994749857%29.jpg/270px-President_Theodore_Roosevelt_Driving_Through_the_Wawona_Tunnel_Tree%2C_in_Yellowstone_National_Park_%2814994749857%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c5/President_Theodore_Roosevelt_Driving_Through_the_Wawona_Tunnel_Tree%2C_in_Yellowstone_National_Park_%2814994749857%29.jpg/360px-President_Theodore_Roosevelt_Driving_Through_the_Wawona_Tunnel_Tree%2C_in_Yellowstone_National_Park_%2814994749857%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="728" data-file-height="920" /></a><figcaption>Roosevelt driving through a <a href="/wiki/Sequoiadendron_giganteum" title="Sequoiadendron giganteum">sequoia</a> <a href="/wiki/Wawona_Tree" title="Wawona Tree">tree tunnel</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>Of all Roosevelt's achievements, he was proudest of his work in the conservation of natural resources and extending federal protection to land and wildlife.<sup id="cite_ref-161" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-161">&#91;159&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt worked closely with Interior Secretary <a href="/wiki/James_Rudolph_Garfield" title="James Rudolph Garfield">James Rudolph Garfield</a> and Chief of the United States Forest Service <a href="/wiki/Gifford_Pinchot" title="Gifford Pinchot">Gifford Pinchot</a> to enact a series of conservation programs that often met with resistance from Western members of Congress, such as <a href="/wiki/Charles_William_Fulton" class="mw-redirect" title="Charles William Fulton">Charles William Fulton</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992469–471_162-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992469–471-162">&#91;160&#93;</a></sup> Nonetheless, Roosevelt established the <a href="/wiki/United_States_Forest_Service" title="United States Forest Service">United States Forest Service</a>, signed into law the creation of five <a href="/wiki/National_parks_(United_States)" class="mw-redirect" title="National parks (United States)">National Parks</a>, and signed the 1906 <a href="/wiki/Antiquities_Act" title="Antiquities Act">Antiquities Act</a>, under which he proclaimed 18 new <a href="/wiki/U.S._National_Monument" class="mw-redirect" title="U.S. National Monument">U.S. National Monuments</a>. He also established the first 51 <a href="/wiki/Bird_reserve" title="Bird reserve">bird reserves</a>, four <a href="/wiki/Game_preservation" title="Game preservation">game preserves</a>, and 150 <a href="/wiki/United_States_National_Forest" class="mw-redirect" title="United States National Forest">National Forests</a>. The area of the United States that he placed under public protection totals approximately 230&#160;million acres (930,000 square kilometers).<sup id="cite_ref-163" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-163">&#91;161&#93;</a></sup> In part due to his dedication to conservation, Roosevelt was voted in as the first honorary member of the <a href="/wiki/Camp_Fire_Club" title="Camp Fire Club">Camp-Fire Club of America</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-164" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-164">&#91;162&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Roosevelt extensively used <a href="/wiki/Executive_order_(United_States)" class="mw-redirect" title="Executive order (United States)">executive orders</a> on a number of occasions to protect forest and wildlife lands during his tenure as president.<sup id="cite_ref-165" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-165">&#91;163&#93;</a></sup> By the end of his second term in office, Roosevelt used executive orders to establish 150&#160;million acres (600,000 square kilometers) of reserved forestry land.<sup id="cite_ref-Take_up_Your_Pen_166-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Take_up_Your_Pen-166">&#91;164&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt was unapologetic about his extensive use of executive orders to protect the environment, despite the perception in Congress that he was encroaching on too many lands.<sup id="cite_ref-Take_up_Your_Pen_166-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Take_up_Your_Pen-166">&#91;164&#93;</a></sup> Eventually, Senator <a href="/wiki/Charles_William_Fulton" class="mw-redirect" title="Charles William Fulton">Charles Fulton</a> (R-OR) attached an amendment to an agricultural appropriations bill that effectively prevented the president from reserving any further land.<sup id="cite_ref-Take_up_Your_Pen_166-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Take_up_Your_Pen-166">&#91;164&#93;</a></sup> Before signing that bill into law, Roosevelt used executive orders to establish an additional 21 forest reserves, waiting until the last minute to sign the bill into law.<sup id="cite_ref-ReferenceA_167-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ReferenceA-167">&#91;165&#93;</a></sup> In total, Roosevelt used executive orders to establish 121 forest reserves in 31 states.<sup id="cite_ref-ReferenceA_167-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ReferenceA-167">&#91;165&#93;</a></sup> Prior to Roosevelt, only one president had issued over 200 executive orders, Grover Cleveland (253). The first 25 presidents issued a total of 1,262 executive orders; Roosevelt issued 1,081.<sup id="cite_ref-executiveorders_168-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-executiveorders-168">&#91;166&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Business_panic_of_1907">Business panic of 1907</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <a href="/wiki/Panic_of_1907" title="Panic of 1907">Panic of 1907</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Theodore_Roosevelt_by_Harris_%26_Ewing_Studio,_1907.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/22/Theodore_Roosevelt_by_Harris_%26_Ewing_Studio%2C_1907.jpg/220px-Theodore_Roosevelt_by_Harris_%26_Ewing_Studio%2C_1907.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="300" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/22/Theodore_Roosevelt_by_Harris_%26_Ewing_Studio%2C_1907.jpg/330px-Theodore_Roosevelt_by_Harris_%26_Ewing_Studio%2C_1907.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/22/Theodore_Roosevelt_by_Harris_%26_Ewing_Studio%2C_1907.jpg/440px-Theodore_Roosevelt_by_Harris_%26_Ewing_Studio%2C_1907.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2938" data-file-height="4000" /></a><figcaption>Roosevelt portrait by <a href="/wiki/Harris_%26_Ewing" title="Harris &amp; Ewing">Harris &amp; Ewing</a>, 1907</figcaption></figure>
<p>In 1907, Roosevelt faced the greatest domestic economic crisis since the <a href="/wiki/Panic_of_1893" title="Panic of 1893">Panic of 1893</a>. Wall Street's stock market entered a slump in early 1907, and many investors blamed Roosevelt's regulatory policies for the decline in stock prices.<sup id="cite_ref-169" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-169">&#91;167&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt helped calm the crisis by meeting on November 4, 1907, with the leaders of <a href="/wiki/U.S._Steel" title="U.S. Steel">U.S. Steel</a> and approving their plan to purchase a Tennessee steel company near bankruptcy—its failure would ruin a major New York bank. He thus approved the growth of one of the largest and most hated trusts, while the public announcement calmed the markets.<sup id="cite_ref-170" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-170">&#91;168&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>
Roosevelt exploded in anger at the super-rich for the economic malfeasance, calling them "malefactors of great wealth". in a major speech in August entitled, "The Puritan Spirit and the Regulation of Corporations". Trying to restore confidence, he blamed the crisis primarily on Europe, but then, after saluting the unbending rectitude of the Puritans, he went on:<sup id="cite_ref-171" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-171">&#91;169&#93;</a></sup> </p><blockquote><p>It may well be that the determination of the government...to punish certain malefactors of great wealth, has been responsible for something of the trouble; at least to the extent of having caused these men to combine to bring about as much financial stress as possible, in order to discredit the policy of the government and thereby secure a reversal of that policy, so that they may enjoy unmolested the fruits of their own evil-doing.</p></blockquote>
<p>Regarding the very wealthy, Roosevelt privately scorned, "...their entire unfitness to govern the country, and ... the lasting damage they do by much of what they think are the legitimate big business operations of the day".<sup id="cite_ref-172" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-172">&#91;170&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Foreign_policy">Foreign policy</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Foreign_policy_of_the_Theodore_Roosevelt_administration" title="Foreign policy of the Theodore Roosevelt administration">Foreign policy of the Theodore Roosevelt administration</a></div>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Japan">Japan</span></h4>
<p>The American <a href="/wiki/Newlands_Resolution" title="Newlands Resolution">annexation of Hawaii</a> in 1898 was stimulated in part by fear that otherwise Japan would dominate or seize the Hawaiian Republic.<sup id="cite_ref-173" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-173">&#91;171&#93;</a></sup> Similarly, Germany was the alternative to American takeover of the Philippines in 1900, and Tokyo strongly preferred the U.S. to take over. As the U.S. became a naval world power, it needed to find a way to avoid a military confrontation in the Pacific with Japan.<sup id="cite_ref-174" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-174">&#91;172&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In the 1890s, Roosevelt had been an ardent <a href="/wiki/American_imperialism" title="American imperialism">imperialist</a> and vigorously defended the permanent acquisition of the Philippines in the 1900 campaign. After the <a href="/wiki/Philippine%E2%80%93American_War" title="Philippine–American War">local insurrection</a> ended in 1902, Roosevelt wished to have a strong U.S. presence in the region as a symbol of democratic values, but he did not envision any new acquisitions. One of Roosevelt's priorities during his presidency and afterwards, was the maintenance of friendly relations with Japan.<sup id="cite_ref-175" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-175">&#91;173&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-176" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-176">&#91;174&#93;</a></sup> From 1904 to 1905 <a href="/wiki/Russo-Japanese_War" title="Russo-Japanese War">Japan and Russia were at war</a>. Both sides asked Roosevelt to mediate a peace conference, held successfully in <a href="/wiki/Portsmouth,_New_Hampshire" title="Portsmouth, New Hampshire">Portsmouth, New Hampshire</a>. Roosevelt won the <a href="/wiki/Nobel_Peace_Prize" title="Nobel Peace Prize">Nobel Peace Prize</a> for his efforts.<sup id="cite_ref-177" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-177">&#91;175&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Though he proclaimed that the United States would be neutral during the <a href="/wiki/Russo-Japanese_War" title="Russo-Japanese War">Russo-Japanese War</a>, Roosevelt secretly favored Imperial Japan to emerge victorious against the Russian Empire. He wanted the influence of the Russians to weaken in order to take them out in the Pacific diplomatic equation, with the Japanese emerging to their spot as the Russian replacement.<sup id="cite_ref-178" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-178">&#91;176&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In California, <a href="/wiki/Anti-Japanese_sentiment_in_the_United_States" title="Anti-Japanese sentiment in the United States">anti-Japanese hostility was growing</a>, and Tokyo protested. Roosevelt <a href="/wiki/Gentlemen%27s_Agreement_of_1907" title="Gentlemen&#39;s Agreement of 1907">negotiated a "Gentleman's Agreement" in 1907</a>. It ended explicit discrimination against the Japanese, and Japan agreed not to allow unskilled immigrants into the United States.<sup id="cite_ref-179" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-179">&#91;177&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Great_White_Fleet" title="Great White Fleet">Great White Fleet</a> of American battleships visited Japan in 1908 during its round-the-world tour. Roosevelt intended to emphasize the superiority of the American fleet over the smaller Japanese navy, but instead of resentment the visitors arrived to a joyous welcome by Japanese elite as well as the general public. This good-will facilitated the <a href="/wiki/Root%E2%80%93Takahira_Agreement" title="Root–Takahira Agreement">Root–Takahira Agreement</a> of November 1908 which reaffirmed the status quo of Japanese control of Korea and American control of the Philippines.<sup id="cite_ref-180" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-180">&#91;178&#93;</a></sup>
<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997614–616_181-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997614–616-181">&#91;179&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Europe">Europe</span></h4>
<p>Success in the war against Spain and the new empire, plus having the largest economy in the world, meant that the United States had emerged as a world power.<sup id="cite_ref-182" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-182">&#91;180&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt searched for ways to win recognition for the position abroad.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992382–383_183-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992382–383-183">&#91;181&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Roosevelt also played a major role in mediating the <a href="/wiki/First_Moroccan_Crisis" title="First Moroccan Crisis">First Moroccan Crisis</a> by calling the <a href="/wiki/Algeciras_Conference" title="Algeciras Conference">Algeciras Conference</a>, which averted war between France and Germany.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992450–451_184-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992450–451-184">&#91;182&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Roosevelt's presidency saw the strengthening of ties with Great Britain. <a href="/wiki/The_Great_Rapprochement" class="mw-redirect" title="The Great Rapprochement">The Great Rapprochement</a> had begun with British support of the United States during the Spanish–American War, and it continued as Britain withdrew its fleet from the Caribbean in favor of focusing on the rising <a href="/wiki/Anglo-German_naval_arms_race" title="Anglo-German naval arms race">German naval threat</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992387–388_185-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992387–388-185">&#91;183&#93;</a></sup> In 1901, Britain and the United States signed the <a href="/wiki/Hay%E2%80%93Pauncefote_Treaty" title="Hay–Pauncefote Treaty">Hay–Pauncefote Treaty</a>, abrogating the <a href="/wiki/Clayton%E2%80%93Bulwer_Treaty" title="Clayton–Bulwer Treaty">Clayton–Bulwer Treaty</a>, which had prevented the United States from constructing a canal connecting the Pacific and the Atlantic Ocean.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992399–400_186-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992399–400-186">&#91;184&#93;</a></sup> The long-standing <a href="/wiki/Alaska_boundary_dispute" title="Alaska boundary dispute">Alaska boundary dispute</a> was settled on terms favorable to the United States, as Great Britain was unwilling to alienate the United States over what it considered to be a secondary issue. As Roosevelt later put it, the resolution of the Alaskan boundary dispute "settled the last serious trouble between the British Empire and ourselves."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992397–398_187-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992397–398-187">&#91;185&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Latin_America_and_Panama_Canal">Latin America and Panama Canal</span></h4>
<p>As president, he primarily focused the nation's overseas ambitions on the Caribbean, especially locations that had a bearing on the defense of his pet project, the <a href="/wiki/Panama_Canal" title="Panama Canal">Panama Canal</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997615–616_188-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997615–616-188">&#91;186&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt also increased the size of the navy, and by the end of his second term the United States had more battleships than any other country besides Britain. The Panama Canal, when it opened in 1914, allowed the U.S. Navy to rapidly move back and forth from the Pacific to the Caribbean to European waters.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992384_189-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992384-189">&#91;187&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In December 1902, the Germans, British, and Italians blockaded the ports of <a href="/wiki/Venezuela" title="Venezuela">Venezuela</a> in order to force the repayment of delinquent loans. Roosevelt was particularly concerned with the motives of German Emperor <a href="/wiki/Wilhelm_II,_German_Emperor" title="Wilhelm II, German Emperor">Wilhelm II</a>. He succeeded in getting the three nations to agree to arbitration by tribunal at <a href="/wiki/The_Hague" title="The Hague">The Hague</a>, and successfully defused the <a href="/wiki/Venezuela_Crisis_of_1902%E2%80%931903" class="mw-redirect" title="Venezuela Crisis of 1902–1903">crisis</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997464_190-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997464-190">&#91;188&#93;</a></sup> The latitude granted to the Europeans by the arbiters was in part responsible for the "<a href="/wiki/Roosevelt_Corollary" title="Roosevelt Corollary">Roosevelt Corollary</a>" to the <a href="/wiki/Monroe_Doctrine" title="Monroe Doctrine">Monroe Doctrine</a>, which the President issued in 1904: "Chronic wrongdoing or an impotence which results in a general loosening of the ties of civilized society, may in America, as elsewhere, ultimately require intervention by some civilized nation, and in the Western Hemisphere, the adherence of the United States to the Monroe doctrine may force the United States, however reluctantly, in flagrant cases of such wrongdoing or impotence, to the exercise of an international police power."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997527_191-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997527-191">&#91;189&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Panama_canal_cartooon_1903.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ac/Panama_canal_cartooon_1903.jpg/220px-Panama_canal_cartooon_1903.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="118" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ac/Panama_canal_cartooon_1903.jpg/330px-Panama_canal_cartooon_1903.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ac/Panama_canal_cartooon_1903.jpg/440px-Panama_canal_cartooon_1903.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1500" data-file-height="805" /></a><figcaption>The U.S.'s intentions to influence the area (especially the <a href="/wiki/Panama_Canal" title="Panama Canal">Panama Canal</a> construction and control) led to the <a href="/wiki/Separation_of_Panama_from_Colombia" title="Separation of Panama from Colombia">separation of Panama from Colombia</a> in 1903.</figcaption></figure>
<p>The pursuit of an <a href="/wiki/History_of_the_Panama_Canal" title="History of the Panama Canal">isthmus canal</a> in Central America during this period focused on two possible routes—<a href="/wiki/Nicaragua" title="Nicaragua">Nicaragua</a> and Panama, which was then a rebellious district within <a href="/wiki/Colombia" title="Colombia">Colombia</a>. Roosevelt convinced Congress to approve the Panamanian alternative, and a treaty was approved, only to be rejected by the Colombian government. When the Panamanians learned of this, a rebellion followed, was supported by Roosevelt, and succeeded. A <a href="/wiki/Hay%E2%80%93Bunau-Varilla_Treaty" title="Hay–Bunau-Varilla Treaty">treaty</a> with the new Panama government for construction of the canal was then reached in 1903.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997482–486_192-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997482–486-192">&#91;190&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt received criticism for paying the bankrupt Panama Canal Company and the New Panama Canal Company $40,000,000 (equivalent to $13.03&#160;billion in 2022) for the rights and equipment to build the canal.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChambers1974209_155-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChambers1974209-155">&#91;153&#93;</a></sup> Critics charged that an American investor syndicate allegedly divided the large payment among themselves. There was also controversy over whether a French company engineer influenced Roosevelt in choosing the Panama route for the canal over the Nicaragua route. Roosevelt denied charges of corruption concerning the canal in a January 8, 1906, message to Congress. In January 1909, Roosevelt, in an unprecedented move, brought criminal libel charges against the <i><a href="/wiki/New_York_World" title="New York World">New York World</a></i> and the <i><a href="/wiki/Indianapolis_News" title="Indianapolis News">Indianapolis News</a></i> known as the "Roosevelt-Panama Libel Cases".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChambers1974209–210_193-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChambers1974209–210-193">&#91;191&#93;</a></sup> Both cases were dismissed by U.S. District Courts, and on January 3, 1911, the U.S. Supreme Court, upon federal appeal, upheld the lower courts' rulings.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChambers1974213–214_194-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChambers1974213–214-194">&#91;192&#93;</a></sup> Historians are sharply critical of Roosevelt's criminal prosecutions of the <i>World</i> and the <i>News</i> but are divided on whether actual corruption in acquiring and building the Panama Canal took place.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChambers1974215_195-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChambers1974215-195">&#91;193&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In 1906, following a disputed election, an insurrection ensued in Cuba; Roosevelt sent Taft, the Secretary of War, to monitor the situation; he was convinced that he had the authority to unilaterally authorize Taft to deploy Marines, if necessary, without congressional approval.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997570_196-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997570-196">&#91;194&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Examining the work of numerous scholars, Ricard (2014) reports that:
</p>
<blockquote><p>The most striking evolution in the twenty-first-century historiography of Theodore Roosevelt is the switch from a partial arraignment of the imperialist to a quasi-unanimous celebration of the master diplomatist.... [Recent works] have underlined cogently Roosevelt's exceptional statesmanship in the construction of the nascent twentieth-century "special relationship". ...The twenty-sixth president's reputation as a brilliant diplomatist and real politician has undeniably reached new heights in the twenty-first century...yet, his Philippine policy still prompts criticism.<sup id="cite_ref-197" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-197">&#91;195&#93;</a></sup></p></blockquote>
<p>On November 6, 1906, Roosevelt was the first president to depart the continental United States on an official diplomatic trip. Roosevelt made a 17-day trip to Panama and Puerto Rico. Roosevelt checked on the progress of the Canal's construction and talked to workers about the importance of the project. In Puerto Rico, he recommended that Puerto Ricans become U.S. citizens.<sup id="cite_ref-198" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-198">&#91;196&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-199" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-199">&#91;197&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Media">Media</span></h3>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Go_Away_Little_Man_Charles_Green_Bush.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c3/Go_Away_Little_Man_Charles_Green_Bush.jpg/180px-Go_Away_Little_Man_Charles_Green_Bush.jpg" decoding="async" width="180" height="183" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c3/Go_Away_Little_Man_Charles_Green_Bush.jpg/270px-Go_Away_Little_Man_Charles_Green_Bush.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c3/Go_Away_Little_Man_Charles_Green_Bush.jpg/360px-Go_Away_Little_Man_Charles_Green_Bush.jpg 2x" data-file-width="507" data-file-height="515" /></a><figcaption>1903 cartoon: <i>"Go Away, Little Man, and Don't Bother Me".</i> Roosevelt intimidating <a href="/wiki/Colombia" title="Colombia">Colombia</a> to acquire the <a href="/wiki/Panama_Canal_Zone" title="Panama Canal Zone">Panama Canal Zone</a>.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Building on McKinley's effective use of the press, Roosevelt made the White House the center of news every day, providing interviews and photo opportunities. After noticing the reporters huddled outside the White House in the rain one day, he gave them their own room inside, effectively inventing the presidential <a href="/wiki/Press_briefing" class="mw-redirect" title="Press briefing">press briefing</a>. The grateful press, with unprecedented access to the White House, rewarded Roosevelt with ample coverage.<sup id="cite_ref-american_chronicle_200-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-american_chronicle-200">&#91;198&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Roosevelt normally enjoyed very close relationships with the press, which he used to keep in daily contact with his middle-class base. While out of office, he made a living as a writer and magazine editor. He loved talking with intellectuals, authors, and writers. He drew the line, however, at exposé-oriented scandal-mongering journalists who, during his term, sent magazine subscriptions soaring by their attacks on corrupt politicians, mayors, and corporations. Roosevelt himself was not usually a target, but a speech of his from 1906 coined the term "<a href="/wiki/Muckraker" title="Muckraker">muckraker</a>" for unscrupulous journalists making wild charges. "The liar", he said, "is no whit better than the thief, and if his mendacity takes the form of slander he may be worse than most thieves."<sup id="cite_ref-201" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-201">&#91;199&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The press did briefly target Roosevelt in one instance. After 1904, he was periodically criticized for the manner in which he facilitated the construction of the <a href="/wiki/Panama_Canal" title="Panama Canal">Panama Canal</a>. According to biographer Brands, Roosevelt, near the end of his term, demanded that the <a href="/wiki/U.S._Justice_Department" class="mw-redirect" title="U.S. Justice Department">U.S. Justice Department</a> bring charges of criminal libel against <a href="/wiki/Joseph_Pulitzer" title="Joseph Pulitzer">Joseph Pulitzer</a>'s <i>New York World</i>. The publication had accused him of "deliberate misstatements of fact" in defense of family members who were criticized as a result of the Panama affair. Though an indictment was obtained, the case was ultimately dismissed in federal court—it was not a federal offense, but one enforceable in state courts. The Justice Department had predicted that result and had also advised Roosevelt accordingly.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997633–634_202-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997633–634-202">&#91;200&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Election_of_1904">Election of 1904</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/1904_United_States_presidential_election" title="1904 United States presidential election">1904 United States presidential election</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:ElectoralCollege1904.svg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/aa/ElectoralCollege1904.svg/300px-ElectoralCollege1904.svg.png" decoding="async" width="300" height="174" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/aa/ElectoralCollege1904.svg/450px-ElectoralCollege1904.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/aa/ElectoralCollege1904.svg/600px-ElectoralCollege1904.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="1020" data-file-height="593" /></a><figcaption>1904 election results</figcaption></figure>
<p>The control and management of the Republican Party lay in the hands of Ohio Senator and Republican Party chairman Mark Hanna until McKinley's death. Roosevelt and Hanna frequently cooperated during Roosevelt's first term, but Hanna left open the possibility of a challenge to Roosevelt for the 1904 Republican nomination. Roosevelt and Ohio's other Senator, <a href="/wiki/Joseph_B._Foraker" title="Joseph B. Foraker">Joseph B. Foraker</a>, forced Hanna's hand by calling for Ohio's state Republican convention to endorse Roosevelt for the 1904 nomination.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992436–437_203-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992436–437-203">&#91;201&#93;</a></sup> Unwilling to break with the president, Hanna was forced to publicly endorse Roosevelt. Hanna and Pennsylvania Senator <a href="/wiki/Matthew_Quay" title="Matthew Quay">Matthew Quay</a> both died in early 1904, and with the waning of Thomas Platt's power, Roosevelt faced little effective opposition for the 1904 nomination.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992437–438_204-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992437–438-204">&#91;202&#93;</a></sup> In deference to Hanna's conservative loyalists, Roosevelt at first offered the party chairmanship to <a href="/wiki/Cornelius_Bliss" class="mw-redirect" title="Cornelius Bliss">Cornelius Bliss</a>, but he declined. Roosevelt turned to his own man, <a href="/wiki/George_B._Cortelyou" title="George B. Cortelyou">George B. Cortelyou</a> of New York, the first Secretary of Commerce and Labor. To buttress his hold on the party's nomination, Roosevelt made it clear that anyone opposing Cortelyou would be considered to be opposing the President.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997501–503_205-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997501–503-205">&#91;203&#93;</a></sup> The President secured his own nomination, but his preferred vice-presidential running mate, <a href="/wiki/Robert_R._Hitt" title="Robert R. Hitt">Robert R. Hitt</a>, was not nominated.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997504_206-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997504-206">&#91;204&#93;</a></sup> Senator <a href="/wiki/Charles_W._Fairbanks" title="Charles W. Fairbanks">Charles Warren Fairbanks</a> of Indiana, a favorite of conservatives, gained the nomination.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992437–438_204-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992437–438-204">&#91;202&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>While Roosevelt followed the tradition of incumbents in not actively campaigning on the stump, he sought to control the campaign's message through specific instructions to Cortelyou. He also attempted to manage the press's release of White House statements by forming the <a href="/wiki/Ananias_Club" title="Ananias Club">Ananias Club</a>. Any journalist who repeated a statement made by the president without approval was penalized by restriction of further access.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997507_207-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997507-207">&#91;205&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The Democratic Party's nominee in 1904 was <a href="/wiki/Alton_B._Parker" title="Alton B. Parker">Alton Brooks Parker</a>. Democratic newspapers charged that Republicans were extorting large campaign contributions from corporations, putting ultimate responsibility on Roosevelt, himself.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChambers1974215–216_208-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChambers1974215–216-208">&#91;206&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt denied corruption while at the same time he ordered Cortelyou to return $100,000 (equivalent to $3.3&#160;million in 2022) of a campaign contribution from <a href="/wiki/Standard_Oil" title="Standard Oil">Standard Oil</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChambers1974216_209-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChambers1974216-209">&#91;207&#93;</a></sup> Parker said that Roosevelt was accepting corporate donations to keep damaging information from the <a href="/wiki/Bureau_of_Corporations" title="Bureau of Corporations">Bureau of Corporations</a> from going public.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChambers1974216_209-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChambers1974216-209">&#91;207&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt strongly denied Parker's charge and responded that he would "go into the Presidency unhampered by any pledge, promise, or understanding of any kind, sort, or description...".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChambers1974216–217_210-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChambers1974216–217-210">&#91;208&#93;</a></sup> Allegations from Parker and the Democrats, however, had little impact on the election, as Roosevelt promised to give every American a "<a href="/wiki/Square_Deal" title="Square Deal">square deal</a>".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChambers1974216–217_210-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChambers1974216–217-210">&#91;208&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt won 56% of the popular vote, and Parker received 38%; Roosevelt also won the <a href="/wiki/Electoral_College_(United_States)" class="mw-redirect" title="Electoral College (United States)">Electoral College</a> vote, 336 to 140. Before his inauguration ceremony, Roosevelt declared that he would not serve another term.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997513–514_211-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997513–514-211">&#91;209&#93;</a></sup> Democrats afterwards would continue to charge Roosevelt and the Republicans of being influenced by corporate donations during Roosevelt's second term.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChambers1974217–218_212-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChambers1974217–218-212">&#91;210&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Second_term">Second term</span></h3>
<p>As his second term progressed, Roosevelt moved to the left of his Republican Party base and called for a series of reforms, most of which Congress failed to pass.<sup id="cite_ref-213" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-213">&#91;211&#93;</a></sup> In his last year in office, he was assisted by his friend <a href="/wiki/Archibald_Butt" title="Archibald Butt">Archibald Butt</a> (who later perished in the sinking of <a href="/wiki/RMS_Titanic" class="mw-redirect" title="RMS Titanic">RMS <i>Titanic</i></a>).<sup id="cite_ref-Obit_214-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Obit-214">&#91;212&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt's influence waned as he approached the end of his second term, as his promise to forego a third term made him a <a href="/wiki/Lame_duck_(politics)" title="Lame duck (politics)">lame duck</a> and his concentration of power provoked a backlash from many Congressmen.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992463–464_215-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992463–464-215">&#91;213&#93;</a></sup> He sought a national <a href="/wiki/Incorporation_(business)" title="Incorporation (business)">incorporation</a> law (at a time when all corporations had state charters), called for a federal <a href="/wiki/Income_tax_in_the_United_States" title="Income tax in the United States">income tax</a> (despite the Supreme Court's ruling in <i><a href="/wiki/Pollock_v._Farmers%27_Loan_%26_Trust_Co." title="Pollock v. Farmers&#39; Loan &amp; Trust Co.">Pollock v. Farmers' Loan &amp; Trust Co.</a></i>), and an <a href="/wiki/Estate_tax_in_the_United_States" title="Estate tax in the United States">inheritance tax</a>. In the area of labor legislation, Roosevelt called for limits on the use of court injunctions against labor unions during strikes; injunctions were a powerful weapon that mostly helped business. He wanted an employee liability law for industrial injuries (pre-empting state laws) and an <a href="/wiki/Eight-hour_day" title="Eight-hour day">eight-hour work day</a> for federal employees. In other areas he also sought a <a href="/wiki/Postal_savings_system" title="Postal savings system">postal savings system</a> (to provide competition for local banks), and he asked for campaign reform laws.<sup id="cite_ref-216" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-216">&#91;214&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The election of 1904 continued to be a source of contention between Republicans and Democrats. A Congressional investigation in 1905 revealed that corporate executives donated tens of thousands of dollars in 1904 to the <a href="/wiki/Republican_National_Committee" title="Republican National Committee">Republican National Committee</a>. In 1908, a month before the general presidential election, Governor <a href="/wiki/Charles_N._Haskell" title="Charles N. Haskell">Charles N. Haskell</a> of Oklahoma, former Democratic Treasurer, said that Senators beholden to Standard Oil lobbied Roosevelt, in the summer of 1904, to authorize the leasing of Indian oil lands by Standard Oil subsidiaries. He said Roosevelt overruled his <a href="/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Interior" class="mw-redirect" title="United States Secretary of Interior">Secretary of the Interior</a> <a href="/wiki/Ethan_A._Hitchcock_(Interior)" title="Ethan A. Hitchcock (Interior)">Ethan A. Hitchcock</a> and granted a pipeline franchise to run through the <a href="/wiki/Osage_Nation" title="Osage Nation">Osage lands</a> to the Prairie Oil and Gas Company. The New York <i>Sun</i> made a similar accusation and said that Standard Oil, a refinery who financially benefited from the pipeline, had contributed $150,000 to the Republicans in 1904 (equivalent to $4.9&#160;million in 2022) after Roosevelt's alleged reversal allowing the pipeline franchise. Roosevelt branded Haskell's allegation as "a lie, pure and simple" and obtained a denial from Treasury Secretary <a href="/wiki/L._M._Shaw" title="L. M. Shaw">Shaw</a> that Roosevelt had neither coerced Shaw nor overruled him.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChambers1974219_217-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChambers1974219-217">&#91;215&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Rhetoric_of_righteousness">Rhetoric of righteousness</span></h4><p>
Roosevelt's rhetoric was characterized by an intense moralism of personal righteousness.<sup id="cite_ref-218" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-218">&#91;216&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-219" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-219">&#91;217&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-220" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-220">&#91;218&#93;</a></sup> The tone was typified by his denunciation of "predatory wealth" in a message he sent Congress in January 1908 calling for passage of new labor laws: </p><blockquote><p>Predatory wealth--of the wealth accumulated on a giant scale by all forms of iniquity, ranging from the oppression of wageworkers to unfair and unwholesome methods of crushing out competition, and to defrauding the public by stock jobbing and the manipulation of securities. Certain wealthy men of this stamp, whose conduct should be abhorrent to every man of ordinarily decent conscience, and who commit the hideous wrong of teaching our young men that phenomenal business success must ordinarily be based on dishonesty, have during the last few months made it apparent that they have banded together to work for a reaction. Their endeavor is to overthrow and discredit all who honestly administer the law, to prevent any additional legislation which would check and restrain them, and to secure if possible a freedom from all restraint which will permit every unscrupulous wrongdoer to do what he wishes unchecked provided he has enough money....The methods by which the Standard Oil people and those engaged in the other combinations of which I have spoken above have achieved great fortunes can only be justified by the advocacy of a system of morality which would also justify every form of criminality on the part of a labor union, and every form of violence, corruption, and fraud, from murder to bribery and ballot box stuffing in politics.<sup id="cite_ref-221" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-221">&#91;219&#93;</a></sup> </p></blockquote>
<h2><span id="Post-presidency_.281909.E2.80.931919.29"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Post-presidency_(1909–1919)">Post-presidency (1909–1919)</span></h2>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Election_of_1908">Election of 1908</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/1908_United_States_presidential_election" title="1908 United States presidential election">1908 United States presidential election</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:TR_smiling_in_automobile.tif" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e7/TR_smiling_in_automobile.tif/lossy-page1-220px-TR_smiling_in_automobile.tif.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="179" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e7/TR_smiling_in_automobile.tif/lossy-page1-330px-TR_smiling_in_automobile.tif.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e7/TR_smiling_in_automobile.tif/lossy-page1-440px-TR_smiling_in_automobile.tif.jpg 2x" data-file-width="5845" data-file-height="4746" /></a><figcaption>Roosevelt shortly after leaving office, October 1910</figcaption></figure>
<p>Roosevelt enjoyed being president and was still relatively youthful but felt that a limited number of terms provided a check against dictatorship. Roosevelt ultimately decided to stick to his 1904 pledge not to run for a third term. He personally favored Secretary of State <a href="/wiki/Elihu_Root" title="Elihu Root">Elihu Root</a> as his successor, but Root's ill health made him an unsuitable candidate. New York Governor <a href="/wiki/Charles_Evans_Hughes" title="Charles Evans Hughes">Charles Evans Hughes</a> loomed as a potentially strong candidate and shared Roosevelt's progressivism, but Roosevelt disliked him and considered him to be too independent. Instead, Roosevelt settled on his Secretary of War, William Howard Taft, who had ably served under Presidents Harrison, McKinley, and Roosevelt in various positions. Roosevelt and Taft had been friends since 1890, and Taft had consistently supported President Roosevelt's policies.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992483–485_222-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992483–485-222">&#91;220&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt was determined to install the successor of his choice, and wrote the following to Taft: "Dear Will: Do you want any action about those federal officials? I will break their necks with the utmost cheerfulness if you say the word!". Just weeks later he branded as "false and malicious" the charge that he was using the offices at his disposal to favor Taft.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997626_223-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997626-223">&#91;221&#93;</a></sup> At the 1908 Republican convention, many chanted for "four years more" of a Roosevelt presidency, but Taft won the nomination after Henry Cabot Lodge made it clear that Roosevelt was not interested in a third term.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992488–489_224-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992488–489-224">&#91;222&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In the <a href="/wiki/1908_United_States_presidential_election" title="1908 United States presidential election">1908 election</a>, Taft easily defeated the Democratic nominee, three-time candidate <a href="/wiki/William_Jennings_Bryan" title="William Jennings Bryan">William Jennings Bryan</a>. Taft promoted a progressivism that stressed the rule of law; he preferred that judges rather than administrators or politicians make the basic decisions about fairness. Taft usually proved to be a less adroit politician than Roosevelt and lacked the energy and personal magnetism, along with the publicity devices, the dedicated supporters, and the broad base of public support that made Roosevelt so formidable. When Roosevelt realized that lowering the tariff would risk creating severe tensions inside the Republican Party by pitting producers (manufacturers, industrial workers, and farmers) against merchants and consumers, he stopped talking about the issue. Taft ignored the risks and tackled the tariff boldly, encouraging reformers to fight for lower rates, and then cutting deals with conservative leaders that kept overall rates high. The resulting <a href="/wiki/Payne-Aldrich_tariff" class="mw-redirect" title="Payne-Aldrich tariff">Payne-Aldrich tariff</a> of 1909, signed into law early in President Taft's tenure, was too high for most reformers, and Taft's handling of the tariff alienated all sides. While the crisis was building inside the Party, Roosevelt was touring Africa and Europe, to allow Taft space to be his own man.<sup id="cite_ref-225" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-225">&#91;223&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span id="Africa_and_Europe_.281909.E2.80.931910.29"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Africa_and_Europe_(1909–1910)">Africa and Europe (1909–1910)</span></h3>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Roosevelt_safari_elephant.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8c/Roosevelt_safari_elephant.jpg/220px-Roosevelt_safari_elephant.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="159" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8c/Roosevelt_safari_elephant.jpg/330px-Roosevelt_safari_elephant.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8c/Roosevelt_safari_elephant.jpg/440px-Roosevelt_safari_elephant.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3647" data-file-height="2631" /></a><figcaption>Roosevelt standing next to the elephant he shot on safari</figcaption></figure>
<p>In March 1909, the ex-president left the country for the <a href="/wiki/Smithsonian-Roosevelt_African_Expedition" class="mw-redirect" title="Smithsonian-Roosevelt African Expedition">Smithsonian-Roosevelt African Expedition</a>, a safari in <a href="/wiki/East_Africa" title="East Africa">east</a> and <a href="/wiki/Central_Africa" title="Central Africa">central Africa</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Science1908_226-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Science1908-226">&#91;224&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt's party landed in <a href="/wiki/Mombasa" title="Mombasa">Mombasa</a>, <a href="/wiki/British_East_Africa" class="mw-redirect" title="British East Africa">East Africa</a> (now <a href="/wiki/Kenya" title="Kenya">Kenya</a>) and traveled to the <a href="/wiki/Belgian_Congo" title="Belgian Congo">Belgian Congo</a> (now <a href="/wiki/Democratic_Republic_of_the_Congo" title="Democratic Republic of the Congo">Democratic Republic of the Congo</a>) before following the Nile River to <a href="/wiki/Khartoum" title="Khartoum">Khartoum</a> in modern <a href="/wiki/Sudan" title="Sudan">Sudan</a>. Well-financed by <a href="/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie" title="Andrew Carnegie">Andrew Carnegie</a> and by his own writings, Roosevelt's large party hunted for specimens for the <a href="/wiki/Smithsonian_Institution" title="Smithsonian Institution">Smithsonian Institution</a> and for the <a href="/wiki/American_Museum_of_Natural_History" title="American Museum of Natural History">American Museum of Natural History</a> in New York.<sup id="cite_ref-SIA_227-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-SIA-227">&#91;225&#93;</a></sup> The group, led by the hunter-tracker R.J. Cunninghame, included scientists from the Smithsonian, and was joined from time to time by <a href="/wiki/Frederick_Selous" title="Frederick Selous">Frederick Selous</a>, the famous big game hunter and explorer. Participants on the expedition included <a href="/wiki/Kermit_Roosevelt" title="Kermit Roosevelt">Kermit Roosevelt</a>, <a href="/wiki/Edgar_Alexander_Mearns" title="Edgar Alexander Mearns">Edgar Alexander Mearns</a>, <a href="/wiki/Edmund_Heller" title="Edmund Heller">Edmund Heller</a>, and <a href="/wiki/John_Alden_Loring" title="John Alden Loring">John Alden Loring</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-228" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-228">&#91;226&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The team killed or trapped 11,400 animals,<sup id="cite_ref-SIA_227-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-SIA-227">&#91;225&#93;</a></sup> from insects and moles to hippopotamuses and elephants. The 1,000 large animals included 512 <a href="/wiki/Big-game_hunting" title="Big-game hunting">big game</a> animals, including six rare <a href="/wiki/White_rhinoceros" title="White rhinoceros">white rhinos</a>. Tons of salted carcases and skins were shipped to Washington; it took years to mount them all, and the Smithsonian shared duplicate specimens with other museums. Regarding the large number of animals taken, Roosevelt said, "I can be condemned only if the existence of the <a href="/wiki/National_Museum_of_Natural_History" title="National Museum of Natural History">National Museum</a>, the <a href="/wiki/American_Museum_of_Natural_History" title="American Museum of Natural History">American Museum of Natural History</a>, and all similar zoological institutions are to be condemned".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEO&#39;Toole200567_229-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEO&#39;Toole200567-229">&#91;227&#93;</a></sup> He wrote a detailed account of the safari in the book <i>African Game Trails</i>, recounting the excitement of the chase, the people he met, and the flora and fauna he collected in the name of science.<sup id="cite_ref-230" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-230">&#91;228&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>After his safari, Roosevelt traveled north to embark on a tour of Europe. Stopping first in Egypt, he commented favorably on British rule of the region, giving his opinion that Egypt was not yet ready for independence.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992505_231-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992505-231">&#91;229&#93;</a></sup> He refused a meeting with the <a href="/wiki/Pope_Pius_X" title="Pope Pius X">Pope</a> due to a dispute over a group of <a href="/wiki/Methodists" class="mw-redirect" title="Methodists">Methodists</a> active in Rome. He met with Emperor <a href="/wiki/Franz_Joseph" class="mw-redirect" title="Franz Joseph">Franz Joseph</a> of <a href="/wiki/Austria-Hungary" title="Austria-Hungary">Austria-Hungary</a>, Kaiser Wilhelm II of Germany, King <a href="/wiki/George_V" title="George V">George V</a> of Great Britain, and other European leaders. In Oslo, Norway, Roosevelt delivered a speech calling for limitations on naval armaments, a strengthening of the <a href="/wiki/Permanent_Court_of_Arbitration" title="Permanent Court of Arbitration">Permanent Court of Arbitration</a>, and the creation of a "League of Peace" among the world powers.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992505–509_232-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992505–509-232">&#91;230&#93;</a></sup> He also delivered the <a href="/wiki/Romanes_Lecture" title="Romanes Lecture">Romanes Lecture</a> at Oxford, in which he denounced those who sought parallels between the evolution of animal life and the development of society.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992511_233-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992511-233">&#91;231&#93;</a></sup> Though Roosevelt attempted to avoid domestic politics, he quietly met with <a href="/wiki/Gifford_Pinchot" title="Gifford Pinchot">Gifford Pinchot</a>, who related his own disappointment with the Taft Administration.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992506–507_234-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992506–507-234">&#91;232&#93;</a></sup> Pinchot had been forced to resign as head of the forest service after clashing with Taft's Interior Secretary, <a href="/wiki/Richard_Ballinger" class="mw-redirect" title="Richard Ballinger">Richard Ballinger</a>, who had prioritized development over conservation. Roosevelt returned to the United States in June 1910<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992503,_511_235-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992503,_511-235">&#91;233&#93;</a></sup> where he was shortly thereafter honored with a reception luncheon on the roof of the Waldorf-Astoria Hotel in New York City hosted by the <a href="/wiki/Camp_Fire_Club" title="Camp Fire Club">Camp-Fire Club of America</a>, of which he was a member.<sup id="cite_ref-236" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-236">&#91;234&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In October 1910, Roosevelt became the first U.S. president to fly in an airplane, staying aloft for four minutes in a <a href="/wiki/Wright_Brothers" class="mw-redirect" title="Wright Brothers">Wright Brothers</a>-designed craft <a href="/wiki/Kinloch,_Missouri" title="Kinloch, Missouri">near St. Louis</a>, Missouri.<sup id="cite_ref-237" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-237">&#91;235&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Republican_Party_schism">Republican Party schism</span></h3>
<p>Roosevelt had attempted to refashion Taft into a copy of himself, but he recoiled as Taft began to display his individuality. He was offended on election night when Taft indicated that his success had been possible not just through the efforts of Roosevelt, but also Taft's half-brother <a href="/wiki/Charles_Phelps_Taft" title="Charles Phelps Taft">Charles P. Taft</a>. Roosevelt was further alienated when Taft, intent on becoming his own man, did not consult him about cabinet appointments.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997665–666_238-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997665–666-238">&#91;236&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt and other progressives were ideologically dissatisfied over Taft's conservation policies and his handling of the tariff when he concentrated more power in the hands of conservative party leaders in Congress.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992502–503_239-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992502–503-239">&#91;237&#93;</a></sup> Stanley Solvick argues that as President Taft abided by the goals and procedures of the "<a href="/wiki/Square_Deal" title="Square Deal">Square Deal</a>" promoted by Roosevelt in his first term.
