The problem was that Roosevelt and the more radical progressives had moved on to more aggressive goals, such as curbing the judiciary, which Taft rejected.<sup id="cite_ref-240" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-240">&#91;238&#93;</a></sup> Regarding radicalism and liberalism, Roosevelt wrote a British friend in 1911:
</p>
<dl><dd>Fundamentally it is the radical liberal with whom I sympathize. He is at least working toward the end for which I think we should all of us strive; and when he adds sanity in moderation to courage and enthusiasm for high ideals he develops into the kind of statesman whom alone I can wholeheartedly support.<sup id="cite_ref-241" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-241">&#91;239&#93;</a></sup></dd></dl>
<p>Roosevelt urged progressives to take control of the Republican Party at the state and local level and to avoid splitting the party in a way that would hand the presidency to the Democrats in 1912. To that end Roosevelt publicly expressed optimism about the Taft Administration after meeting with the president in June 1910.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992512–513_242-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992512–513-242">&#91;240&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In August 1910, Roosevelt escalated the rivalry with a speech at <a href="/wiki/Osawatomie,_Kansas" title="Osawatomie, Kansas">Osawatomie, Kansas</a>, which was the most radical of his career. It marked his public break with Taft and the conservative Republicans. Advocating a program he called the "<a href="/wiki/New_Nationalism_(Theodore_Roosevelt)" title="New Nationalism (Theodore Roosevelt)">New Nationalism</a>", Roosevelt emphasized the priority of labor over capital interests, and the need to control corporate creation and combination. He called for a ban on corporate political contributions.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997675_243-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997675-243">&#91;241&#93;</a></sup> Returning to New York, Roosevelt began a battle to take control of the state Republican party from <a href="/wiki/William_Barnes_Jr." title="William Barnes Jr.">William Barnes Jr.</a>, Tom Platt's successor as the state party boss. Taft had pledged his support to Roosevelt in this endeavor, and Roosevelt was outraged when Taft's support failed to materialize at the 1910 state convention.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992515–516_244-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992515–516-244">&#91;242&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt campaigned for the Republicans in the <a href="/wiki/1910_United_States_elections" title="1910 United States elections">1910 elections</a>, in which the Democrats gained control of the House for the first time since 1892. Among the newly elected Democrats was New York state senator <a href="/wiki/Franklin_Delano_Roosevelt" class="mw-redirect" title="Franklin Delano Roosevelt">Franklin Delano Roosevelt</a>, who argued that he represented his distant cousin's policies better than his Republican opponent.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992517_245-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992517-245">&#91;243&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The Republican progressives interpreted the 1910 defeats as a compelling argument for the complete reorganization of the party in 1911.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997683_246-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997683-246">&#91;244&#93;</a></sup> Senator <a href="/wiki/Robert_M._La_Follette" title="Robert M. La Follette">Robert M. La Follette</a> of Wisconsin joined with Pinchot, William White, and California Governor <a href="/wiki/Hiram_Johnson" title="Hiram Johnson">Hiram Johnson</a> to create the National Progressive Republican League; their objectives were to defeat the power of political bossism at the state level and to replace Taft at the national level.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992518_247-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992518-247">&#91;245&#93;</a></sup> Despite his skepticism of La Follette's new league, Roosevelt expressed general support for progressive principles. Between January and April 1911, Roosevelt wrote a series of articles for <i>The Outlook</i>, defending what he called "the great movement of our day, the progressive nationalist movement against special privilege, and in favor of an honest and efficient political and <a href="/wiki/Industrial_democracy" title="Industrial democracy">industrial democracy</a>".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997684_248-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997684-248">&#91;246&#93;</a></sup> With Roosevelt apparently uninterested in running in 1912, La Follette declared his own candidacy in June 1911.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992518_247-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992518-247">&#91;245&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt continually criticized Taft after the 1910 elections, and the break between the two men became final after the Justice Department filed an <a href="/wiki/Antitrust" class="mw-redirect" title="Antitrust">antitrust</a> lawsuit against US Steel in September 1911; Roosevelt was humiliated by this suit because he had personally approved of an acquisition that the Justice Department was now challenging. However, Roosevelt was still unwilling to run against Taft in 1912; he instead hoped to run in 1916 against whichever Democrat beat Taft in 1912.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992519_249-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992519-249">&#91;247&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Battling_Taft_over_arbitration_treaties">Battling Taft over arbitration treaties</span></h4>
<p>Taft was world leader for arbitration as a guarantee of world peace. In 1911 he and his Secretary of State <a href="/wiki/Philander_C._Knox" title="Philander C. Knox">Philander C. Knox</a> negotiated major treaties with Great Britain and France providing that differences be arbitrated. Disputes had to be submitted to the <a href="/wiki/Hague_Conventions_of_1899_and_1907#Hague_Convention_of_1907" title="Hague Conventions of 1899 and 1907">Hague Court</a> or another tribunal. These were signed in August 1911 but had to be ratified by a two-thirds vote of the Senate. Neither Taft nor Knox consulted with leaders of the Senate during the negotiating process. By then many Republicans were opposed to Taft, and the president felt that lobbying too hard for the treaties might cause their defeat. He made some speeches supporting the treaties in October, but the Senate added amendments Taft could not accept, killing the agreements.<sup id="cite_ref-250" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-250">&#91;248&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The arbitration issue revealed a deep philosophical dispute among American progressives. One faction, led by Taft looked to legal arbitration as the best alternative to warfare. Taft was a constitutional lawyer with a deep understanding of the legal issues.<sup id="cite_ref-251" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-251">&#91;249&#93;</a></sup> Taft's political base was the conservative business community that largely supported peace movements before 1914. However, he failed to mobilize that base. The businessmen believed that economic rivalries were the cause of war, and that extensive trade led to an interdependent world that would make war a very expensive and useless anachronism.<sup id="cite_ref-252" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-252">&#91;250&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>However, an opposing faction of progressives, led by Roosevelt, ridiculed arbitration as foolhardy idealism, and insisted on the realism of warfare as the only solution to serious international disputes. Roosevelt worked with his close friend Senator <a href="/wiki/Henry_Cabot_Lodge" title="Henry Cabot Lodge">Henry Cabot Lodge</a> to impose those amendments that ruined the goals of the treaties. Lodge's motivation was that he complained the treaties impinged too much on senatorial prerogatives.<sup id="cite_ref-253" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-253">&#91;251&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt, however, was acting to sabotage Taft's campaign promises.<sup id="cite_ref-254" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-254">&#91;252&#93;</a></sup> At a deeper level, Roosevelt truly believed that arbitration was a naïve solution and the great issues had to be decided by warfare. The Rooseveltian approach incorporated a near-mystical faith of the ennobling nature of war. It endorsed jingoistic nationalism as opposed to the businessmen's calculation of profit and national interest.<sup id="cite_ref-255" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-255">&#91;253&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-256" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-256">&#91;254&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Election_of_1912">Election of 1912</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/1912_United_States_presidential_election" title="1912 United States presidential election">1912 United States presidential election</a> and <a href="/wiki/Progressive_Party_(United_States,_1912)" class="mw-redirect" title="Progressive Party (United States, 1912)">Progressive Party (United States, 1912)</a></div>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Republican_primaries_and_convention">Republican primaries and convention</span></h4>
<p>In November 1911, a group of Ohio Republicans endorsed Roosevelt for the party's nomination for president; the endorsers included James R. Garfield and Dan Hanna. This endorsement was made by leaders of President Taft's home state. Roosevelt conspicuously declined to make a statement—requested by Garfield—that he would flatly refuse a nomination. Soon thereafter, Roosevelt said, "I am really sorry for Taft... I am sure he means well, but he means well feebly, and he does not know how! He is utterly unfit for leadership and this is a time when we need leadership." In January 1912, Roosevelt declared "if the people make a draft on me I shall not decline to serve".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997698_257-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997698-257">&#91;255&#93;</a></sup> Later that year, Roosevelt spoke before the Constitutional Convention in Ohio, openly identifying as a progressive and endorsing progressive reforms—even endorsing popular review of state judicial decisions.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997703_258-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997703-258">&#91;256&#93;</a></sup> In reaction to Roosevelt's proposals for popular overrule of court decisions, Taft said, "Such extremists are not progressives—they are political emotionalists or neurotics".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997709_259-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997709-259">&#91;257&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:For_Auld_Lang_Syne_-_Leonard_Raven-Hill.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fb/For_Auld_Lang_Syne_-_Leonard_Raven-Hill.jpg/220px-For_Auld_Lang_Syne_-_Leonard_Raven-Hill.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="282" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fb/For_Auld_Lang_Syne_-_Leonard_Raven-Hill.jpg/330px-For_Auld_Lang_Syne_-_Leonard_Raven-Hill.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fb/For_Auld_Lang_Syne_-_Leonard_Raven-Hill.jpg/440px-For_Auld_Lang_Syne_-_Leonard_Raven-Hill.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1109" data-file-height="1421" /></a><figcaption><i>Punch</i> in May 1912 depicts no-holds-barred fight between Taft and Roosevelt.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Roosevelt began to envision himself as the savior of the Republican Party from defeat in the upcoming presidential election. In February 1912, Roosevelt announced in Boston, "I will accept the nomination for president if it is tendered to me. I hope that so far as possible the people may be given the chance through direct primaries to express who shall be the nominee.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997705_260-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997705-260">&#91;258&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-gloriousr_261-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-gloriousr-261">&#91;259&#93;</a></sup> Elihu Root and Henry Cabot Lodge thought that division of the party would lead to its defeat in the next election, while Taft believed that he would be defeated either in the Republican primary or in the general election.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997706_262-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997706-262">&#91;260&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The 1912 primaries represented the first extensive use of the <a href="/wiki/United_States_presidential_primary" title="United States presidential primary">presidential primary</a>, a reform achievement of the progressive movement.<sup id="cite_ref-263" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-263">&#91;261&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Republican_Party_presidential_primaries,_1912" class="mw-redirect" title="Republican Party presidential primaries, 1912">Republican primaries</a> in the South, where party regulars dominated, went for Taft, as did results in New York, Indiana, Michigan, Kentucky, and Massachusetts. Meanwhile, Roosevelt won in Illinois, Minnesota, Nebraska, South Dakota, California, Maryland, and Pennsylvania. The greatest primary fight came in Ohio, Taft's base. Both the Taft and Roosevelt campaigns worked furiously, and La Follette joined in. Each team sent in big name speakers. Roosevelt's train went 1,800 miles back and forth in the one state, where he made 75 speeches. Taft's train went 3,000 miles criss-crossing Ohio and he made over 100 speeches.Roosevelt swept the state, convincing Roosevelt that he should intensify his campaigning, and letting Taft know he should work from the White House not the stump.<sup id="cite_ref-264" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-264">&#91;262&#93;</a></sup> Only a third of the states held primaries; elsewhere the state organization chose the delegations to the national convention, and they favored Taft. The final credentials of the state delegates at the national convention were determined by the national committee, which was controlled by Taft men.<sup id="cite_ref-265" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-265">&#91;263&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-266" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-266">&#91;264&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Prior to the <a href="/wiki/1912_Republican_National_Convention" title="1912 Republican National Convention">1912 Republican National Convention</a> in Chicago, Roosevelt expressed doubt about his prospects for victory, noting that Taft had more delegates and control of the credentials committee. His only hope was to convince party leaders that the nomination of Taft would hand the election to the Democrats, but party leaders were determined not to cede their leadership to Roosevelt.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992524_267-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992524-267">&#91;265&#93;</a></sup> The credentials committee awarded 235 contested delegates to Taft and 19 to Roosevelt. Taft won the nomination on the first ballot with 561 votes against 107 for Roosevelt and 41 for La Follette. Of the Roosevelt delegates, 344 refused to vote so they would not be committed to the Republican ticket.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992524–526_268-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992524–526-268">&#91;266&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-269" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-269">&#91;267&#93;</a></sup> Black delegates from the South played a key role: they voted heavily for Taft and put him over the top.<sup id="cite_ref-270" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-270">&#91;268&#93;</a></sup> La Follette hoped that a deadlocked convention would result in his own nomination and refused to release his delegates to support Roosevelt.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992524–526_268-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992524–526-268">&#91;266&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Roosevelt_denounces_the_election">Roosevelt denounces the election</span></h4><p>
According to <a href="/wiki/Lewis_L._Gould" title="Lewis L. Gould">Lewis L. Gould</a>, in 1912 </p><blockquote><p>   Roosevelt saw Taft as the agent of "the forces of reaction and of political crookedness".... Roosevelt had become the most dangerous man in American history, said Taft, "because of his hold upon the less intelligent voters and the discontented." The Republican National Committee, dominated by the Taft forces, awarded 235 delegates to the president and 19 to Roosevelt, thereby ensuring Taft's renomination. Roosevelt believed himself entitled to 72 delegates from Arizona, California, Texas and Washington that had been given to Taft. Firm in his conviction that the nomination was being stolen from him, Roosevelt ....told cheering supporters that there was "a great moral issue" at stake and he should have "sixty to eighty lawfully elected delegates" added to his total....Roosevelt ended his speech declaring: "Fearless of the future; unheeding of our individual fates; with unflinching hearts and undimmed eyes; we stand at Armageddon, and we battle for the Lord!"<sup id="cite_ref-271" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-271">&#91;269&#93;</a></sup>
</p></blockquote>
<h4><span id="The_Progressive_.28.22Bull_Moose.22.29_Party"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="The_Progressive_(&quot;Bull_Moose&quot;)_Party">The Progressive ("Bull Moose") Party</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/New_Nationalism_(Theodore_Roosevelt)" title="New Nationalism (Theodore Roosevelt)">New Nationalism (Theodore Roosevelt)</a> and <a href="/wiki/Progressive_Party_(United_States,_1912)" class="mw-redirect" title="Progressive Party (United States, 1912)">Progressive Party (United States, 1912)</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1134653256"><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1096940132"><div class="side-box side-box-right listen noprint"><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1126788409">
<div class="side-box-flex">
<div class="side-box-image"><figure class="mw-halign-center" typeof="mw:File"><span><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg/50px-Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg.png" decoding="async" width="50" height="50" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg/75px-Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg/100px-Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="160" data-file-height="160" /></span><figcaption></figcaption></figure></div>
<div class="side-box-text plainlist"><div class="haudio">
<div class="listen-file-header"><a href="/wiki/File:Right_of_the_People.ogg" title="File:Right of the People.ogg">"The right of the people to rule"</a></div>
<div><span typeof="mw:File"><span><audio id="mwe_player_1" controls="" preload="none" class="mw-file-element" width="232" style="width:232px;" data-durationhint="248" data-mwtitle="Right_of_the_People.ogg" data-mwprovider="wikimediacommons"><source src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/a9/Right_of_the_People.ogg" type="audio/ogg; codecs=&quot;vorbis&quot;" data-title="Original Ogg file (66 kbps)" data-shorttitle="Ogg source" data-width="0" data-height="0" /><source src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/a/a9/Right_of_the_People.ogg/Right_of_the_People.ogg.mp3" type="audio/mpeg" data-title="MP3" data-shorttitle="MP3" data-transcodekey="mp3" data-width="0" data-height="0" /></audio></span></span></div>
<div class="description">Excerpts from a speech given by Theodore Roosevelt at <a href="/wiki/Carnegie_Hall" title="Carnegie Hall">Carnegie Hall</a>, March 12, 1912. Recorded August 1912 by <a href="/wiki/Thomas_Edison" title="Thomas Edison">Thomas Edison</a>. Duration 4:07.</div></div></div></div>
<div class="side-box-abovebelow"><hr /><i class="selfreference">Problems playing this file? See <a href="/wiki/Help:Media" title="Help:Media">media help</a>.</i></div>
</div>
<p>Once his defeat at the Republican convention appeared probable, Roosevelt announced that he would "accept the progressive nomination on a progressive platform and I shall fight to the end, win or lose". At the same time, Roosevelt prophetically said, "My feeling is that the Democrats will probably win if they nominate a progressive".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997717_272-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997717-272">&#91;270&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Roosevelt left the Republican Party and created the Progressive Party, structuring it as a permanent organization that would field complete tickets at the presidential and state level. The new party included many reformers, including <a href="/wiki/Jane_Addams" title="Jane Addams">Jane Addams</a>. Although many Republican politicians had announced for Roosevelt before Taft won the nomination, he was stunned to discover that very few incumbent politicians followed him into the new party. The main exception was California, where the Progressive faction took control of the Republican Party. Loyalty to the old party was a powerful factor for incumbents; only five senators now supported Roosevelt.<sup id="cite_ref-273" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-273">&#91;271&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-274" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-274">&#91;272&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt's daughter Alice had a White House marriage to Congressman <a href="/wiki/Nicholas_Longworth" title="Nicholas Longworth">Nicholas Longworth</a>, who represented Taft's base in Cincinnati. Roosevelt reassured him in 1912 that of course he had to endorse Taft. However, Alice was her father's biggest cheerleader—the public conflict between spouses ruined the marriage.<sup id="cite_ref-275" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-275">&#91;273&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Perkins-pinchot.JPG" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2d/Perkins-pinchot.JPG/220px-Perkins-pinchot.JPG" decoding="async" width="220" height="264" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2d/Perkins-pinchot.JPG/330px-Perkins-pinchot.JPG 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2d/Perkins-pinchot.JPG/440px-Perkins-pinchot.JPG 2x" data-file-width="662" data-file-height="795" /></a><figcaption>1912 editorial cartoon showing George Perkins (left, with checkbook symbolizing control of money) and <a href="/wiki/Amos_Pinchot" title="Amos Pinchot">Amos Pinchot</a> (wielding an endorsement from Roosevelt campaign manager, Senator <a href="/wiki/Joseph_M._Dixon" title="Joseph M. Dixon">Joseph M. Dixon</a>) in battle for Progressive party control</figcaption></figure>
<p>The leadership of the new party included a wide range of reformers. Jane Addams campaigned vigorously for the new party as a breakthrough in social reform.<sup id="cite_ref-276" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-276">&#91;274&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Gifford_Pinchot" title="Gifford Pinchot">Gifford Pinchot</a> represented the environmentalists and anti-trust crusaders. Publisher <a href="/wiki/Frank_Munsey" title="Frank Munsey">Frank Munsey</a> provided much of the cash.<sup id="cite_ref-277" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-277">&#91;275&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/George_Walbridge_Perkins" title="George Walbridge Perkins">George W. Perkins</a>, a leading Wall Street financier and senior partner of <a href="/wiki/J.P._Morgan_%26_Co." title="J.P. Morgan &amp; Co.">J.P. Morgan bank</a> came from the <a href="/wiki/Efficiency_movement" title="Efficiency movement">efficiency movement</a>. He handled the new party's finances efficiently but was deeply distrusted by many reformers.<sup id="cite_ref-278" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-278">&#91;276&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The new party was popularly known as the "Bull Moose Party" after Roosevelt told reporters, "I'm as fit as a bull moose".<sup id="cite_ref-279" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-279">&#91;277&#93;</a></sup> At the <a href="/wiki/1912_Progressive_National_Convention" title="1912 Progressive National Convention">1912 Progressive National Convention</a>, Roosevelt cried out, "We stand at <a href="/wiki/Armageddon" title="Armageddon">Armageddon</a> and we battle for the Lord." Governor <a href="/wiki/Hiram_Johnson" title="Hiram Johnson">Hiram Johnson</a> controlled the California party, forcing out the Taft supporters. He was nominated as Roosevelt's running mate.<sup id="cite_ref-280" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-280">&#91;278&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Roosevelt's platform echoed his radical 1907–1908 proposals, calling for vigorous government intervention to protect the people from selfish interests:
</p>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r996844942"><blockquote class="templatequote"><p>To destroy this invisible Government, to dissolve the <a href="https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/unholy_alliance" class="extiw" title="wikt:unholy alliance">unholy alliance</a> between corrupt business and corrupt politics is the first task of the statesmanship of the day.<sup id="cite_ref-281" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-281">&#91;279&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTERoosevelt1913&#91;httpwwwbartlebycom5515bhtml_XV._The_Peace_of_Righteousness,_Appendix_B&#93;_282-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoosevelt1913[httpwwwbartlebycom5515bhtml_XV._The_Peace_of_Righteousness,_Appendix_B]-282">&#91;280&#93;</a></sup> This country belongs to the people. Its resources, its business, its laws, its institutions, should be utilized, maintained, or altered in whatever manner will best promote the general interest. This assertion is explicit... Mr. Wilson must know that every monopoly in the United States opposes the Progressive party... I challenge him... to name the monopoly that did support the Progressive party, whether... the Sugar Trust, the US Steel Trust, the Harvester Trust, the Standard Oil Trust, the Tobacco Trust, or any other... Ours was the only program to which they objected, and they supported either Mr. Wilson or Mr. Taft.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEThayer191925–31Chapter_XXII_283-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThayer191925–31Chapter_XXII-283">&#91;281&#93;</a></sup></p></blockquote>
<p>Though many Progressive party activists in the North opposed the steady loss of civil rights for blacks, Roosevelt ran a "<a href="/wiki/Lily-white_movement" title="Lily-white movement">lily-white</a>" campaign in the South. Rival all-white and all-black delegations from four southern states arrived at the Progressive national convention, and Roosevelt decided to seat the all-white delegations.<sup id="cite_ref-284" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-284">&#91;282&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-285" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-285">&#91;283&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-286" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-286">&#91;284&#93;</a></sup> Nevertheless, he won few votes outside a few traditional Republican strongholds. Out of 1,100 counties in the South, Roosevelt won two counties in Alabama, one in Arkansas, seven in North Carolina, three in Georgia, 17 in Tennessee, two in Texas, one in Virginia, and none in Florida, Louisiana, Mississippi, or South Carolina.<sup id="cite_ref-287" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-287">&#91;285&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Assassination_attempt">Assassination attempt</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Attempted_assassination_of_Theodore_Roosevelt" title="Attempted assassination of Theodore Roosevelt">Attempted assassination of Theodore Roosevelt</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Theodore_Roosevelt%27s_medical_x-ray_on_October_14,_1912_assassination_attempt_showing_bullet_to_remain_inside_his_body_for_life,_from-_X-Ray_of_Roosevelt_(shows_bullet)_LCCN2014690853_(cropped).tif" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f4/Theodore_Roosevelt%27s_medical_x-ray_on_October_14%2C_1912_assassination_attempt_showing_bullet_to_remain_inside_his_body_for_life%2C_from-_X-Ray_of_Roosevelt_%28shows_bullet%29_LCCN2014690853_%28cropped%29.tif/lossy-page1-220px-thumbnail.tif.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="156" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f4/Theodore_Roosevelt%27s_medical_x-ray_on_October_14%2C_1912_assassination_attempt_showing_bullet_to_remain_inside_his_body_for_life%2C_from-_X-Ray_of_Roosevelt_%28shows_bullet%29_LCCN2014690853_%28cropped%29.tif/lossy-page1-330px-thumbnail.tif.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f4/Theodore_Roosevelt%27s_medical_x-ray_on_October_14%2C_1912_assassination_attempt_showing_bullet_to_remain_inside_his_body_for_life%2C_from-_X-Ray_of_Roosevelt_%28shows_bullet%29_LCCN2014690853_%28cropped%29.tif/lossy-page1-440px-thumbnail.tif.jpg 2x" data-file-width="5150" data-file-height="3647" /></a><figcaption>Theodore Roosevelt's medical x-ray on October 14, 1912, after the assassination attempt, showing the bullet that would remain inside his body for life</figcaption></figure>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:TR_Assassination_Bullet_Damage.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/58/TR_Assassination_Bullet_Damage.jpg/260px-TR_Assassination_Bullet_Damage.jpg" decoding="async" width="260" height="260" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/58/TR_Assassination_Bullet_Damage.jpg/390px-TR_Assassination_Bullet_Damage.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/58/TR_Assassination_Bullet_Damage.jpg/520px-TR_Assassination_Bullet_Damage.jpg 2x" data-file-width="750" data-file-height="750" /></a><figcaption>The bullet-damaged speech and eyeglass case on display at the <a href="/wiki/Theodore_Roosevelt_Birthplace_National_Historic_Site" title="Theodore Roosevelt Birthplace National Historic Site">Theodore Roosevelt Birthplace</a> in <a href="/wiki/Manhattan" title="Manhattan">Manhattan</a>, <a href="/wiki/New_York_City" title="New York City">New York City</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>On October 14, 1912, while arriving at a campaign event in <a href="/wiki/Milwaukee,_Wisconsin" class="mw-redirect" title="Milwaukee, Wisconsin">Milwaukee, Wisconsin</a>, Roosevelt was shot from seven feet away in front of the Gilpatrick Hotel by a delusional saloonkeeper named <a href="/wiki/John_Flammang_Schrank" class="mw-redirect" title="John Flammang Schrank">John Flammang Schrank</a>, who believed that the ghost of assassinated president William McKinley had directed him to kill Roosevelt.<sup id="cite_ref-288" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-288">&#91;286&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-289" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-289">&#91;287&#93;</a></sup> The bullet lodged in his chest after penetrating his steel eyeglass case and passing through a 50-page-thick single-folded copy of the speech titled "<a href="https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Progressive_Cause_Greater_Than_Any_Individual" class="extiw" title="s:Progressive Cause Greater Than Any Individual">Progressive Cause Greater Than Any Individual</a>", which he was carrying in his jacket.<sup id="cite_ref-290" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-290">&#91;288&#93;</a></sup> Schrank was immediately disarmed (by <a href="/wiki/Czech_people" class="mw-redirect" title="Czech people">Czech</a> immigrant Frank Bukovsky), captured, and might have been lynched had Roosevelt not shouted for Schrank to remain unharmed.<sup id="cite_ref-291" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-291">&#91;289&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-292" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-292">&#91;290&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt assured the crowd he was all right, then ordered police to take charge of Schrank and to make sure no violence was done to him.<sup id="cite_ref-remey_293-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-remey-293">&#91;291&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>As an experienced hunter and anatomist, Roosevelt correctly concluded that since he was not coughing blood, the bullet had not reached his lung. He declined suggestions to go to the hospital immediately and instead delivered a <a href="https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/I_have_just_been_shot" class="extiw" title="s:I have just been shot">90-minute speech</a> with blood seeping into his shirt.<sup id="cite_ref-294" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-294">&#91;292&#93;</a></sup><sup class="noprint Inline-Template" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Reliable_sources" title="Wikipedia:Reliable sources"><span title="The material near this tag may rely on an unreliable source. (September 2021)">unreliable source?</span></a></i>&#93;</sup> His opening comments to the gathered crowd were, "Ladies and gentlemen, I don't know whether you fully understand that I have just been shot, but it takes more than that to kill a Bull Moose."<sup id="cite_ref-295" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-295">&#91;293&#93;</a></sup><sup class="noprint Inline-Template" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Reliable_sources" title="Wikipedia:Reliable sources"><span title="The material near this tag may rely on an unreliable source. (September 2021)">unreliable source?</span></a></i>&#93;</sup> Only after finishing his address did he accept medical attention.
</p><p>Subsequent probes and an <a href="/wiki/X-ray" title="X-ray">x-ray</a> showed that the bullet had lodged in Roosevelt's chest muscle but did not penetrate the <a href="/wiki/Pleura" class="mw-redirect" title="Pleura">pleura</a>. Doctors concluded that it would be less dangerous to leave it in place than to attempt to remove it, and Roosevelt carried the bullet with him for the rest of his life.<sup id="cite_ref-296" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-296">&#91;294&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-297" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-297">&#91;295&#93;</a></sup> Both Taft and Democratic nominee Woodrow Wilson suspended their own campaigning until Roosevelt recovered and resumed his. When asked if the shooting would affect his election campaign, he said to the reporter "I'm fit as a bull moose." The bull moose became a symbol of both Roosevelt and the Progressive Party, and it often was referred to as simply the Bull Moose Party. He spent two weeks recuperating before returning to the campaign trail. He later wrote a friend about the bullet inside him, "I do not mind it any more than if it were in my waistcoat pocket."<sup id="cite_ref-298" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-298">&#91;296&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Democratic_victory">Democratic victory</span></h4>
<p>After the Democrats nominated Governor <a href="/wiki/Woodrow_Wilson" title="Woodrow Wilson">Woodrow Wilson</a> of New Jersey, Roosevelt did not expect to win the general election, as Wilson had compiled a record attractive to many progressive Democrats who might have otherwise considered voting for Roosevelt.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992529_299-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992529-299">&#91;297&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt still campaigned vigorously, and the election developed into a two-person contest despite Taft's quiet presence in the race. Roosevelt respected Wilson, but the two differed on various issues; Wilson opposed any federal intervention regarding <a href="/wiki/Women%27s_suffrage" title="Women&#39;s suffrage">women's suffrage</a> or <a href="/wiki/Child_labor" class="mw-redirect" title="Child labor">child labor</a> (he viewed these as state issues) and attacked Roosevelt's tolerance of large businesses.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992529–530_300-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992529–530-300">&#91;298&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Roosevelt won 4.1&#160;million votes (27%), compared to Taft's 3.5&#160;million (23%) and Wilson's gained 6.3&#160;million (42%). Wilson scored a massive landslide in the <a href="/wiki/Electoral_College_(United_States)" class="mw-redirect" title="Electoral College (United States)">Electoral College</a>, with 435 electoral votes; Roosevelt won 88 electoral votes, while Taft won 8. Pennsylvania was the only eastern state won by Roosevelt; in the Midwest, he carried Michigan, Minnesota, and South Dakota; in the West, California, and Washington.<sup id="cite_ref-301" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-301">&#91;299&#93;</a></sup> Wilson's victory was the first for a Democrat since Cleveland in <a href="/wiki/1892_United_States_presidential_election" title="1892 United States presidential election">1892</a>. It was the party's best <a href="/wiki/List_of_United_States_presidential_elections_by_Electoral_College_margin" title="List of United States presidential elections by Electoral College margin">performance in the Electoral College</a> since <a href="/wiki/1852_United_States_presidential_election" title="1852 United States presidential election">1852</a>. Roosevelt, meanwhile, garnered a <a href="/wiki/List_of_third_party_performances_in_United_States_presidential_elections" title="List of third party performances in United States presidential elections">higher share of the popular vote</a> than any other third-party presidential candidate in history and won the most states of any third-party candidate after the Civil War.<sup id="cite_ref-cnnthirdparty1_302-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-cnnthirdparty1-302">&#91;300&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span id="South_American_expedition_.281913.E2.80.931914.29"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="South_American_expedition_(1913–1914)">South American expedition (1913–1914)</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Roosevelt%E2%80%93Rondon_Scientific_Expedition" title="Roosevelt–Rondon Scientific Expedition">Roosevelt–Rondon Scientific Expedition</a></div>
<p>In 1907 a friend of Roosevelt's, <a href="/wiki/John_Augustine_Zahm" title="John Augustine Zahm">John Augustine Zahm</a>, a professor at the University of Notre Dame, invited Roosevelt to help plan a research expedition to South America. Now was the time to escape politics. To finance it, Roosevelt obtained support from the <a href="/wiki/American_Museum_of_Natural_History" title="American Museum of Natural History">American Museum of Natural History</a> in return for promising to bring back many new animal specimens. Roosevelt's popular book, <i>Through the Brazilian Wilderness</i><sup id="cite_ref-303" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-303">&#91;301&#93;</a></sup> describes his expedition into the Brazilian jungle in 1913 as a member of the <a href="/wiki/Roosevelt-Rondon_Scientific_Expedition" class="mw-redirect" title="Roosevelt-Rondon Scientific Expedition">Roosevelt-Rondon Scientific Expedition</a>, co-named after its leader, Brazilian explorer <a href="/wiki/C%C3%A2ndido_Rondon" title="Cândido Rondon">Cândido Rondon</a>.
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:River-doubt-team.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fa/River-doubt-team.jpg/220px-River-doubt-team.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fa/River-doubt-team.jpg/330px-River-doubt-team.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fa/River-doubt-team.jpg/440px-River-doubt-team.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1039" data-file-height="694" /></a><figcaption>From left to right (seated): fr. John Augustine Zahm, Cândido Rondon, Kermit Roosevelt, Cherrie, Miller, four Brazilians, Roosevelt, Fiala. Only Roosevelt, Kermit, Cherrie, Rondon, and the Brazilians traveled down the River of Doubt.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Once in South America, a new, far more ambitious goal was added: to find the headwaters of the Rio da Duvida (Portuguese for "River of Doubt") and trace it north to the <a href="/wiki/Madeira_River" title="Madeira River">Madeira</a> and thence to the <a href="/wiki/Amazon_River" title="Amazon River">Amazon River</a>. It was later renamed <a href="/wiki/Roosevelt_River" title="Roosevelt River">Roosevelt River</a> in honor of the former president. Roosevelt's crew consisted of his son <a href="/wiki/Kermit_Roosevelt" title="Kermit Roosevelt">Kermit</a>, Colonel Rondon, naturalist <a href="/wiki/George_Kruck_Cherrie" title="George Kruck Cherrie">George Kruck Cherrie</a> (sent by the American Museum of Natural History), Brazilian Lieutenant João Lira, team physician José Antonio Cajazeira, and 16 skilled paddlers and porters. Roosevelt also identified Leo Miller (another AMNH recommendation), <a href="/wiki/Anthony_Fiala" title="Anthony Fiala">Anthony Fiala</a>, Frank Harper, and Jacob Sigg as crew members.<sup id="cite_ref-304" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-304">&#91;302&#93;</a></sup> The initial expedition started somewhat tenuously on December 9, 1913, at the height of the rainy season. The trip down the River of Doubt started on February 27, 1914.<sup id="cite_ref-Millard,_2009_305-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Millard,_2009-305">&#91;303&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>During the trip down the river, Roosevelt suffered a minor leg wound after he jumped into the river to try to prevent two canoes from smashing against the rocks. The flesh wound he received, however, soon gave him <a href="/wiki/Tropical_fever" class="mw-redirect" title="Tropical fever">tropical fever</a> that resembled the <a href="/wiki/Malaria" title="Malaria">malaria</a> he had contracted while in Cuba fifteen years before.<sup id="cite_ref-oimjjac_306-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-oimjjac-306">&#91;304&#93;</a></sup> Because the bullet lodged in his chest from the assassination attempt in 1912 was never removed, his health worsened from the infection.<sup id="cite_ref-DeathNews_307-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-DeathNews-307">&#91;305&#93;</a></sup> This weakened Roosevelt so greatly that six weeks into the adventure, he had to be attended to day and night by the expedition's physician and his son Kermit. By then, he could not walk because of the infection in his injured leg and an infirmity in the other, which was due to a traffic accident a decade earlier. Roosevelt was riddled with chest pains, fighting a fever that soared to 103&#160;°F (39&#160;°C) and at times made him delirious, at one point constantly reciting the first two lines of <a href="/wiki/Samuel_Taylor_Coleridge" title="Samuel Taylor Coleridge">Samuel Taylor Coleridge</a>'s poem "<a href="/wiki/Kubla_Khan" title="Kubla Khan">Kubla Khan</a>": "In Xanadu did Kubla Khan / A stately pleasure dome decree". Regarding his condition as a threat to the survival of the others, Roosevelt insisted he be left behind to allow the poorly provisioned expedition to proceed as rapidly as it could, preparing to commit suicide with an overdose of <a href="/wiki/Morphine" title="Morphine">morphine</a>. Only an appeal by his son persuaded him to continue.<sup id="cite_ref-Millard,_2009_305-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Millard,_2009-305">&#91;303&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Despite Roosevelt's continued decline and loss of over 50 pounds (23&#160;kg), Colonel Rondon reduced the pace of the expedition to allow for his commission's mapmaking and other geographical tasks, which required regular stops to fix the expedition's position by sun-based survey. Upon Roosevelt's return to New York, friends and family were startled by his physical appearance and fatigue. Roosevelt wrote, perhaps prophetically, to a friend that the trip had cut his life short by ten years. For the rest of his few remaining years, he would be plagued by flare-ups of malaria and leg inflammations so severe as to require surgery.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEThayer19194–7_308-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThayer19194–7-308">&#91;306&#93;</a></sup> Before Roosevelt had even completed his sea voyage home, critics raised doubts over his claims of exploring and navigating a completely uncharted river over 625 miles (1,006&#160;km) long. When he had recovered sufficiently, he addressed a standing-room-only convention organized in Washington, D.C., by the <a href="/wiki/National_Geographic_Society" title="National Geographic Society">National Geographic Society</a> and satisfactorily defended his claims.<sup id="cite_ref-Millard,_2009_305-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Millard,_2009-305">&#91;303&#93;</a></sup><sup class="noprint Inline-Template" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing_sources" title="Wikipedia:Citing sources"><span title="This citation requires a reference to the specific page or range of pages in which the material appears. (September 2021)">page&#160;needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Final_years">Final years</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/Roosevelt%27s_World_War_I_volunteers" title="Roosevelt&#39;s World War I volunteers">Roosevelt's World War I volunteers</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:1914_-_Theodore_Roosevelt_on_balcony_of_Hotel_Allen.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f2/1914_-_Theodore_Roosevelt_on_balcony_of_Hotel_Allen.jpg/180px-1914_-_Theodore_Roosevelt_on_balcony_of_Hotel_Allen.jpg" decoding="async" width="180" height="214" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f2/1914_-_Theodore_Roosevelt_on_balcony_of_Hotel_Allen.jpg/270px-1914_-_Theodore_Roosevelt_on_balcony_of_Hotel_Allen.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f2/1914_-_Theodore_Roosevelt_on_balcony_of_Hotel_Allen.jpg/360px-1914_-_Theodore_Roosevelt_on_balcony_of_Hotel_Allen.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2307" data-file-height="2743" /></a><figcaption>Former President Theodore Roosevelt in Allentown, Pennsylvania, 1914</figcaption></figure>
<p>Roosevelt returned to the United States in May 1914. Though he was outraged by the <a href="/wiki/Presidency_of_Woodrow_Wilson" title="Presidency of Woodrow Wilson">Wilson Administration</a>'s conclusion of a treaty that expressed "sincere regret" for the way in which the United States had acquired the <a href="/wiki/Panama_Canal_Zone" title="Panama Canal Zone">Panama Canal Zone</a>, he was impressed by many of the reforms passed under Wilson. Roosevelt made several campaign appearances for the Progressives, but the <a href="/wiki/1914_United_States_elections" title="1914 United States elections">1914 elections</a> were a disaster for the fledgling third party.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992539–540_309-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992539–540-309">&#91;307&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt began to envision another campaign for president, this time with himself at the head of the Republican Party, but conservative party leaders remained opposed to Roosevelt.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992548–549_310-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992548–549-310">&#91;308&#93;</a></sup> In hopes of engineering a joint nomination, the Progressives scheduled the <a href="/wiki/1916_Progressive_National_Convention" title="1916 Progressive National Convention">1916 Progressive National Convention</a> at the same time as the <a href="/wiki/1916_Republican_National_Convention" title="1916 Republican National Convention">1916 Republican National Convention</a>. When the Republicans nominated Charles Evans Hughes, Roosevelt declined the Progressive nomination and urged his Progressive followers to support the Republican candidate.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992550–551_311-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992550–551-311">&#91;309&#93;</a></sup> Though Roosevelt had long disliked Hughes, he disliked Wilson even more, and he campaigned energetically for the Republican nominee. However, Wilson won the <a href="/wiki/1916_United_States_presidential_election" title="1916 United States presidential election">1916 election</a> by a narrow margin.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992552–553_312-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992552–553-312">&#91;310&#93;</a></sup> The Progressives disappeared as a party following the 1916 election, and Roosevelt and many of his followers permanently re-joined the Republican Party.<sup id="cite_ref-mmcgeary1_313-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-mmcgeary1-313">&#91;311&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="World_War_I">World War I</span></h4>
<p>When the <a href="/wiki/First_World_War" class="mw-redirect" title="First World War">First World War</a> began in 1914, Roosevelt strongly supported the <a href="/wiki/Allies_of_World_War_I" title="Allies of World War I">Allies</a> and demanded a harsher policy against Germany, especially regarding submarine warfare. Roosevelt angrily denounced the foreign policy of President Wilson, calling it a failure regarding the <a href="/wiki/Rape_of_Belgium" title="Rape of Belgium">atrocities in Belgium</a> and the violations of American rights.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997749–751,_806–809_314-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997749–751,_806–809-314">&#91;312&#93;</a></sup> In 1916, while campaigning for Hughes, Roosevelt repeatedly denounced Irish Americans and German Americans whom he described as unpatriotic, saying they put the interests of Ireland and Germany ahead of America's by supporting neutrality. He insisted that one had to be 100% American, not a "<a href="/wiki/Hyphenated_American" title="Hyphenated American">hyphenated American</a>" who juggled multiple loyalties. In March 1917, Congress gave Roosevelt the authority to raise a maximum of four divisions similar to the <a href="/wiki/Rough_Riders" title="Rough Riders">Rough Riders</a>, and Major <a href="/wiki/Frederick_Russell_Burnham" title="Frederick Russell Burnham">Frederick Russell Burnham</a> was put in charge of both the general organization and recruitment.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTERoosevelt1917347_315-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoosevelt1917347-315">&#91;313&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-NYT-1917-0313_316-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-NYT-1917-0313-316">&#91;314&#93;</a></sup> However, President Wilson announced to the press that he would not send Roosevelt and his volunteers to France, but instead would send an American Expeditionary Force under the command of General <a href="/wiki/John_J._Pershing" title="John J. Pershing">John J. Pershing</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-NYT-1917-0517_317-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-NYT-1917-0517-317">&#91;315&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt never forgave Wilson, and quickly published <i>The Foes of Our Own Household</i>, an indictment of the sitting president.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTERoosevelt1917_318-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoosevelt1917-318">&#91;316&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997781–784_319-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997781–784-319">&#91;317&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-320" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-320">&#91;318&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt's youngest son, Quentin, a pilot with the American forces in France, was killed when shot down behind German lines on July 14, 1918, at the age of 20. It is said that Quentin's death distressed Roosevelt so much that he never recovered from his loss.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDalton2002507_321-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDalton2002507-321">&#91;319&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="League_of_Nations">League of Nations</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <a href="/wiki/League_to_Enforce_Peace" title="League to Enforce Peace">League to Enforce Peace</a></div>
<p>Roosevelt was an early supporter of the modern view that there needs to be a global order. In his Nobel prize address of 1910, he said, "it would be a master stroke if those great Powers honestly bent on peace would form a League of Peace, not only to keep the peace among themselves, but to prevent, by force if necessary, its being broken by others."<sup id="cite_ref-322" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-322">&#91;320&#93;</a></sup> It would have executive power such as the <a href="/wiki/Hague_Conventions_of_1899_and_1907" title="Hague Conventions of 1899 and 1907">Hague Conventions of 1899 and 1907</a> lacked. He called for American participation.
</p><p>When World War I broke out, Roosevelt proposed "a World League for the Peace of Righteousness", in September 1914, which would preserve sovereignty but limit armaments and require arbitration. He added that it should be "solemnly covenanted that if any nations refused to abide by the decisions of such a court, then others draw the sword in behalf of peace and justice."<sup id="cite_ref-323" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-323">&#91;321&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-324" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-324">&#91;322&#93;</a></sup> In 1915 he outlined this plan more specifically, urging that nations guarantee their entire military force, if necessary, against any nation that refused to carry out arbitration decrees or violated rights of other nations. Though Roosevelt had some concerns about the impact on United States sovereignty, he insisted that such a league would only work if the United States participated as one of the "joint guarantors".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992562–564_325-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992562–564-325">&#91;323&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt referred to this plan in a 1918 speech as "the most feasible for...a league of nations".<sup id="cite_ref-326" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-326">&#91;324&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-327" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-327">&#91;325&#93;</a></sup> By this time Wilson was strongly hostile to Roosevelt and Lodge and developed his own plans for a rather different League of Nations. It became reality along Wilson's lines at the <a href="/wiki/Paris_Peace_Conference_(1919%E2%80%931920)" title="Paris Peace Conference (1919–1920)">Paris Peace Conference</a> in 1919. Roosevelt denounced Wilson's approach but died before it was adopted at Paris. However, Lodge was willing to accept it with serious reservations. In the end, on March 19, 1920, Wilson had Democratic Senators vote against the League with the <a href="/wiki/Lodge_Reservations" title="Lodge Reservations">Lodge Reservations</a> and the United States never joined the <a href="/wiki/League_of_Nations" title="League of Nations">League of Nations</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-328" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-328">&#91;326&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Final_political_activities">Final political activities</span></h4>
<p>Roosevelt's attacks on Wilson helped the Republicans win control of Congress in the midterm elections of 1918. He declined a request from New York Republicans to run for another gubernatorial term, but attacked Wilson's <a href="/wiki/Fourteen_Points" title="Fourteen Points">Fourteen Points</a>, calling instead for the unconditional surrender of Germany. Though his health was uncertain, he was seen as a leading contender for the 1920 Republican nomination, but insisted that, "If they take me, they'll have to take me without a single modification of the things that I have always stood for!" <sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992559_329-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992559-329">&#91;327&#93;</a></sup> He wrote <a href="/wiki/William_Allen_White" title="William Allen White">William Allen White</a>, "I wish to do everything in my power to make the Republican Party the Party of sane, constructive radicalism, just as it was under Lincoln." Accordingly, he told the 1918 state convention of the Maine Republican Party that he stood for old-age pensions, insurance for sickness and unemployment, construction of public housing for low-income families, the reduction of working hours, aid to farmers, and more regulation of large corporations.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992559_329-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992559-329">&#91;327&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>While his political profile remained high, Roosevelt's physical condition continued to deteriorate throughout 1918 due to the long-term effects of jungle diseases. He was hospitalized for seven weeks late in the year and never fully recovered.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller1992564–566_330-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1992564–566-330">&#91;328&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Death">Death</span></h2>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Theodore_and_Edith_Roosevelt_Grave.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ad/Theodore_and_Edith_Roosevelt_Grave.jpg/220px-Theodore_and_Edith_Roosevelt_Grave.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="165" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ad/Theodore_and_Edith_Roosevelt_Grave.jpg/330px-Theodore_and_Edith_Roosevelt_Grave.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ad/Theodore_and_Edith_Roosevelt_Grave.jpg/440px-Theodore_and_Edith_Roosevelt_Grave.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3000" data-file-height="2250" /></a><figcaption>Theodore and Edith Roosevelt's Grave at Youngs Memorial Cemetery</figcaption></figure>
<p>On the night of January 5, 1919, Roosevelt suffered breathing problems. After receiving treatment from his physician, Dr. George W. Faller, he felt better and went to bed. Roosevelt's last words were "Please put out that light, James" to his family servant <a href="/wiki/James_E._Amos" title="James E. Amos">James E. Amos</a>. Between 4:00 and 4:15 the next morning, Roosevelt died at the age of 60 in his sleep at <a href="/wiki/Sagamore_Hill_(house)" class="mw-redirect" title="Sagamore Hill (house)">Sagamore Hill</a> after a blood clot detached from a vein and traveled to his lungs.<sup id="cite_ref-DeathNews_307-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-DeathNews-307">&#91;305&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Upon receiving word of his death, his son Archibald telegraphed his siblings: "The old lion is dead."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDalton2002507_321-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDalton2002507-321">&#91;319&#93;</a></sup> Woodrow Wilson's vice president, <a href="/wiki/Thomas_R._Marshall" title="Thomas R. Marshall">Thomas R. Marshall</a>, said that "Death had to take Roosevelt sleeping, for if he had been awake, there would have been a fight."<sup id="cite_ref-331" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-331">&#91;329&#93;</a></sup> Following a private farewell service in the North Room at Sagamore Hill, a simple funeral was held at <a href="/wiki/Christ_Episcopal_Church_in_Oyster_Bay" class="mw-redirect" title="Christ Episcopal Church in Oyster Bay">Christ Episcopal Church in Oyster Bay</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMorris2010556_332-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorris2010556-332">&#91;330&#93;</a></sup> Vice President Thomas R. Marshall, Charles Evans Hughes, <a href="/wiki/Warren_G._Harding" title="Warren G. Harding">Warren G. Harding</a>, <a href="/wiki/Henry_Cabot_Lodge" title="Henry Cabot Lodge">Henry Cabot Lodge</a>, and <a href="/wiki/William_Howard_Taft" title="William Howard Taft">William Howard Taft</a> were among the mourners.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMorris2010556_332-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorris2010556-332">&#91;330&#93;</a></sup> The snow-covered procession route to <a href="/wiki/Youngs_Memorial_Cemetery" title="Youngs Memorial Cemetery">Youngs Memorial Cemetery</a> was lined with spectators and a squad of mounted policemen who had ridden from New York City.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMorris2010554,_556–557_333-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorris2010554,_556–557-333">&#91;331&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt was buried on a hillside overlooking Oyster Bay.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMorris2010554,_557_334-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorris2010554,_557-334">&#91;332&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Writer">Writer</span></h2>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Theodore_Roosevelt_bibliography" title="Theodore Roosevelt bibliography">Theodore Roosevelt bibliography</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1134653256"><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1096940132"><div class="side-box side-box-right listen noprint"><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1126788409">
<div class="side-box-flex">
<div class="side-box-image"><figure class="mw-halign-center" typeof="mw:File"><span><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg/50px-Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg.png" decoding="async" width="50" height="50" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg/75px-Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg/100px-Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="160" data-file-height="160" /></span><figcaption></figcaption></figure></div>
<div class="side-box-text plainlist"><div class="haudio">
<div class="listen-file-header"><a href="/wiki/File:Roosevelt_-_Address_to_the_Boys_Progressive_League.ogg" title="File:Roosevelt - Address to the Boys Progressive League.ogg">Address to the Boys Progressive League</a></div>
<div><span typeof="mw:File"><span><audio id="mwe_player_2" controls="" preload="none" class="mw-file-element" width="232" style="width:232px;" data-durationhint="92" data-mwtitle="Roosevelt_-_Address_to_the_Boys_Progressive_League.ogg" data-mwprovider="wikimediacommons"><source src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/a1/Roosevelt_-_Address_to_the_Boys_Progressive_League.ogg" type="audio/ogg; codecs=&quot;vorbis&quot;" data-title="Original Ogg file (97 kbps)" data-shorttitle="Ogg source" data-width="0" data-height="0" /><source src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/a/a1/Roosevelt_-_Address_to_the_Boys_Progressive_League.ogg/Roosevelt_-_Address_to_the_Boys_Progressive_League.ogg.mp3" type="audio/mpeg" data-title="MP3" data-shorttitle="MP3" data-transcodekey="mp3" data-width="0" data-height="0" /><track src="https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/api.php?action=timedtext&amp;title=File%3ARoosevelt_-_Address_to_the_Boys_Progressive_League.ogg&amp;lang=en&amp;trackformat=vtt&amp;origin=%2A" kind="subtitles" type="text/vtt" srclang="en" label="English ‪(en)‬" data-dir="ltr" /></audio></span></span></div>
<div class="description">A speech by Roosevelt as a former President</div></div></div></div>
<div class="side-box-abovebelow"><hr /><i class="selfreference">Problems playing this file? See <a href="/wiki/Help:Media" title="Help:Media">media help</a>.</i></div>
</div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:T_Rooosevelts_writings.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1d/T_Rooosevelts_writings.jpg/220px-T_Rooosevelts_writings.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="61" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1d/T_Rooosevelts_writings.jpg/330px-T_Rooosevelts_writings.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1d/T_Rooosevelts_writings.jpg/440px-T_Rooosevelts_writings.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3613" data-file-height="1007" /></a><figcaption>Part of the <i>Works of Theodore Roosevelt</i></figcaption></figure>
<p>Roosevelt was a prolific author, writing with passion on subjects ranging from foreign policy to the importance of the national park system. Roosevelt was also an avid reader of poetry. Poet <a href="/wiki/Robert_Frost" title="Robert Frost">Robert Frost</a> said that Roosevelt "was our kind. He quoted poetry to me. He knew poetry."<sup id="cite_ref-335" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-335">&#91;333&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>As an editor of <i><a href="/wiki/The_Outlook_(New_York_City)" title="The Outlook (New York City)">The Outlook</a></i>, Roosevelt had weekly access to a large, educated national audience. In all, Roosevelt wrote about 18 books (each in several editions), including his autobiography,<sup id="cite_ref-336" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-336">&#91;334&#93;</a></sup> <i>The Rough Riders</i>,<sup id="cite_ref-337" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-337">&#91;335&#93;</a></sup> <i>History of the Naval War of 1812</i>,<sup id="cite_ref-338" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-338">&#91;336&#93;</a></sup> and others on subjects such as ranching, explorations, and wildlife. His most ambitious book was the four-volume narrative <i>The Winning of the West</i>, focused on the <a href="/wiki/American_frontier" title="American frontier">American frontier</a> in the 18th and early 19th centuries. Roosevelt said that the American character—indeed a new "American race" (ethnic group) had emerged from the heroic wilderness hunters and Indian fighters, acting on the frontier with little government help.<sup id="cite_ref-339" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-339">&#91;337&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt also published an account of his 1909–1910 African expedition entitled <i>African Game Trails</i>.
</p><p>In 1905, Roosevelt became embroiled in a widely publicized literary debate known as the <a href="/wiki/Nature_fakers_controversy" title="Nature fakers controversy">nature fakers controversy</a>. A few years earlier, naturalist <a href="/wiki/John_Burroughs" title="John Burroughs">John Burroughs</a> had published an article entitled "Real and Sham Natural History" in the <i><a href="/wiki/Atlantic_Monthly" class="mw-redirect" title="Atlantic Monthly">Atlantic Monthly</a></i>, attacking popular writers of the day such as <a href="/wiki/Ernest_Thompson_Seton" title="Ernest Thompson Seton">Ernest Thompson Seton</a>, <a href="/wiki/Charles_G._D._Roberts" title="Charles G. D. Roberts">Charles G. D. Roberts</a>, and <a href="/wiki/William_J._Long" title="William J. Long">William J. Long</a> for their fantastical representations of wildlife. Roosevelt agreed with Burroughs's criticisms and published several essays of his own denouncing the booming genre of "naturalistic" animal stories as "yellow journalism of the woods". It was the President himself who popularized the negative term "nature faker" to describe writers who depicted their animal characters with excessive anthropomorphism.<sup id="cite_ref-340" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-340">&#91;338&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Character_and_beliefs">Character and beliefs</span></h2>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:SagamoreHill.JPG" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/98/SagamoreHill.JPG/220px-SagamoreHill.JPG" decoding="async" width="220" height="169" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/98/SagamoreHill.JPG/330px-SagamoreHill.JPG 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/98/SagamoreHill.JPG/440px-SagamoreHill.JPG 2x" data-file-width="2781" data-file-height="2134" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Sagamore_Hill" title="Sagamore Hill">Sagamore Hill</a>, Roosevelt's <a href="/wiki/Long_Island" title="Long Island">Long Island</a> estate</figcaption></figure>
<p>Roosevelt intensely disliked being called "Teddy", despite the widespread public association with said moniker, and was quick to point out this to those who referred to him as such, though it would become widely used by newspapers during his political career.
</p><p>He was an active <a href="/wiki/Freemason" class="mw-redirect" title="Freemason">Freemason</a><sup id="cite_ref-341" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-341">&#91;339&#93;</a></sup> and member of the <a href="/wiki/Sons_of_the_American_Revolution" title="Sons of the American Revolution">Sons of the American Revolution</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-342" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-342">&#91;340&#93;</a></sup> He was also a member of <a href="/wiki/The_Explorers_Club" title="The Explorers Club">The Explorers Club</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-343" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-343">&#91;341&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>British scholar <a href="/wiki/Marcus_Cunliffe" title="Marcus Cunliffe">Marcus Cunliffe</a> evaluates the liberal argument that Roosevelt was an opportunist, exhibitionist, and imperialist. Cunliffe praises Roosevelt's versatility, his respect for law, and his sincerity. He argues that Roosevelt's foreign policy was better than his detractors allege. Cunliffe calls him "a big man in several respects," ranking him below Washington, Lincoln, and Jefferson, and on the same level as Franklin D. Roosevelt.<sup id="cite_ref-344" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-344">&#91;342&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Strenuous_life">Strenuous life</span></h3>
<p>Roosevelt had a lifelong interest in pursuing what he called, in an 1899 speech, "<a href="/wiki/The_Strenuous_Life" title="The Strenuous Life">The Strenuous Life</a>". To this end, he exercised regularly and took up boxing, tennis, hiking, rowing, polo, and horseback riding. He also continued his habit of <a href="/wiki/Skinny-dipping" class="mw-redirect" title="Skinny-dipping">skinny-dipping</a> in the <a href="/wiki/Potomac_River" title="Potomac River">Potomac River</a> during the winter.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEThayer191922–24Chapter_XVII_345-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThayer191922–24Chapter_XVII-345">&#91;343&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-346" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-346">&#91;344&#93;</a></sup> As governor of New York, he boxed with sparring partners several times each week, a practice he regularly continued as president until being hit so hard in the face he became blind in his left eye (a fact not made public until many years later). As president, he practiced <a href="/wiki/Judo" title="Judo">judo</a> for two 2-month periods in 1902 and 1904, not attaining any rank.<sup id="cite_ref-347" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-347">&#91;345&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt began to believe in the utility of <a href="/wiki/Jiu-jitsu" class="mw-redirect" title="Jiu-jitsu">jiu-jitsu</a> training after training with <a href="/wiki/Yamashita_Yoshitsugu" title="Yamashita Yoshitsugu">Yoshitsugu Yamashita</a>. Concerned that the United States would lose its military supremacy to rising powers like Japan, Roosevelt began to advocate for jiu-jitsu training for American soldiers.<sup id="cite_ref-:0_348-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:0-348">&#91;346&#93;</a></sup> Feminists annoyed by the posturing of men like Roosevelt, insisted that women were just as capable of learning jiu-jitsu. To prove their point, Martha Blow Wadsworth and Maria Louise ("Hallie") Davis Elkins hired Fude Yamashita, a highly skilled jiu-jitsu instructor and the wife of Yoshitsugu Yamashita, to teach a jiu-jitsu class for women and girls in Washington, DC in 1904. Women had already begun training in boxing in the United States as a means of personal and political empowerment. Jiu-jitsu training thus soon also became popular with American women, coinciding with the origins of a women's self-defense movement.<sup id="cite_ref-349" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-349">&#91;347&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Roosevelt was an enthusiastic <a href="/wiki/Singlestick" title="Singlestick">singlestick</a> player and, according to <i><a href="/wiki/Harper%27s_Weekly" title="Harper&#39;s Weekly">Harper's Weekly</a></i>, showed up at a White House reception with his arm bandaged after a bout with General <a href="/wiki/Leonard_Wood" title="Leonard Wood">Leonard Wood</a> in 1905.<sup id="cite_ref-350" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-350">&#91;348&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt was an avid reader, reading tens of thousands of books, at a rate of several per day in multiple languages. Along with Thomas Jefferson, Roosevelt was the most well-read of all American presidents.<sup id="cite_ref-351" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-351">&#91;349&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Warrior">Warrior</span></h3>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:1905_cartoon_Theodore_Roosevelt_first_and_war_first_in_peace.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/6/68/1905_cartoon_Theodore_Roosevelt_first_and_war_first_in_peace.jpg/220px-1905_cartoon_Theodore_Roosevelt_first_and_war_first_in_peace.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="274" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/6/68/1905_cartoon_Theodore_Roosevelt_first_and_war_first_in_peace.jpg/330px-1905_cartoon_Theodore_Roosevelt_first_and_war_first_in_peace.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/6/68/1905_cartoon_Theodore_Roosevelt_first_and_war_first_in_peace.jpg/440px-1905_cartoon_Theodore_Roosevelt_first_and_war_first_in_peace.jpg 2x" data-file-width="481" data-file-height="598" /></a><figcaption>"The Man of the Hour" Roosevelt as Warrior in 1898 and Peacemaker in 1905 settling war between Russia and Japan</figcaption></figure>
<p>Historians have often emphasized Roosevelt's warrior persona.<sup id="cite_ref-352" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-352">&#91;350&#93;</a></sup> He took aggressive positions regarding war with Spain in 1898, <a href="/wiki/History_of_the_Panama_Canal" title="History of the Panama Canal">Colombia in 1903</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-353" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-353">&#91;351&#93;</a></sup> and especially with Germany, from 1915 to 1917. As a demonstration of American naval might, he sent the "<a href="/wiki/Great_White_Fleet" title="Great White Fleet">Great White Fleet</a>" around the world in 1907–1909.<sup id="cite_ref-354" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-354">&#91;352&#93;</a></sup> The implicit threat of the "big stick" of military power provided leverage to "speak softly" and quietly resolve conflict in numerous cases.<sup id="cite_ref-355" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-355">&#91;353&#93;</a></sup> He boasted in his autobiography:
</p>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r996844942"><blockquote class="templatequote"><p>When I left the Presidency I finished seven and a half years of administration, during which not one shot had been fired against a foreign foe. We were at absolute peace, and there was no nation in the world with whom a war cloud threatened, no nation in the world whom we had wronged, or from whom we had anything to fear. The cruise of the battle fleet was not the least of the causes which ensured so peaceful an outlook.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTERoosevelt1913602_356-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoosevelt1913602-356">&#91;354&#93;</a></sup></p></blockquote>
<p>Richard D. White Jr states, "Roosevelt's warrior spirit framed his views of national politics, [and] international relations."<sup id="cite_ref-357" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-357">&#91;355&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Historian <a href="/wiki/Howard_K._Beale" title="Howard K. Beale">Howard K. Beale</a> has argued:
</p>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r996844942"><blockquote class="templatequote"><p>He and his associates came close to seeking war for its own sake. Ignorant of modern war, Roosevelt romanticized war. ... Like many young men tamed by civilization into law-abiding but adventurous living, he needed an outlet for the pent-up primordial man in him and found it in fighting and killing, vicariously or directly, in hunting or in war. Indeed he had a fairly good time in war when war came. ... There was something dull and effeminate about peace. ... He gloried in war, was thrilled by military history, and placed warlike qualities high in his scale of values. Without consciously desiring it, he thought a little war now and then stimulated admirable qualities in men. Certainly preparedness for war did.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBeale195648_358-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBeale195648-358">&#91;356&#93;</a></sup></p></blockquote>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Religion">Religion</span></h3>
<p>Roosevelt attended church regularly and was a lifelong adherent of the <a href="/wiki/Reformed_Church_in_America" title="Reformed Church in America">Reformed Church in America</a>, the American affiliate of the <a href="/wiki/Dutch_Reformed_Church" title="Dutch Reformed Church">Dutch Reformed Church</a>. He often praised moral behavior but apparently never made a spiritual confession of his own faith. After the 1885 death of his wife, he almost never mentioned Jesus Christ in public or private. Dr. Benjamin J. Wetzel says, "There is little in Roosevelt suggestive of grace, mercy, or redemption."<sup id="cite_ref-359" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-359">&#91;357&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-360" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-360">&#91;358&#93;</a></sup> His rejection of dogma and spirituality, says biographer William Harbaugh, led to a broad tolerance. He campaigned among Protestants, Catholics and Jews, and appointed them to office. He was suspicious of Mormons until they renounced polygamy.<sup id="cite_ref-361" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-361">&#91;359&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In 1907, concerning the proposed motto "<a href="/wiki/In_God_We_Trust" title="In God We Trust">In God We Trust</a>" on money, he wrote, "It seems to me eminently unwise to cheapen such a motto by use on coins, just as it would be to cheapen it by use on postage stamps, or in advertisements." Roosevelt talked a great deal about religion. Biographer <a href="/wiki/Edmund_Morris_(writer)" title="Edmund Morris (writer)">Edmund Morris</a> states:
</p>
