<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r996844942"><blockquote class="templatequote"><p>When consoling bereaved people, he would awkwardly invoke 'unseen and unknown powers.' Aside from a few clichés of Protestant rhetoric, the gospel he preached had always been political and pragmatic. He was inspired less by the <a href="/wiki/Passion_of_Christ" class="mw-redirect" title="Passion of Christ">Passion of Christ</a> than by the Golden Rule—that appeal to reason amounting, in his mind, to a worldly rather than heavenly law.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMorris201062_362-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorris201062-362">&#91;360&#93;</a></sup></p></blockquote>
<p>Roosevelt publicly encouraged church attendance and was a conscientious churchgoer himself. When gas rationing was introduced during the First World War, he walked the three miles from his home at Sagamore Hill to the local church and back, even after a serious operation had made it difficult for him to travel by foot.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReisner1922355_363-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReisner1922355-363">&#91;361&#93;</a></sup> It was said that Roosevelt "allowed no engagement to keep him from going to church," and he remained a fervent advocate of the Bible throughout his adult life.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReisner1922305–323,_355_364-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReisner1922305–323,_355-364">&#91;362&#93;</a></sup> According to Christian F. Reisner, "Religion was as natural to Mr. Roosevelt as breathing,"<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReisner1922324_365-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReisner1922324-365">&#91;363&#93;</a></sup> and when the travel library for Roosevelt's famous <a href="/wiki/Smithsonian%E2%80%93Roosevelt_African_Expedition" title="Smithsonian–Roosevelt African Expedition">Smithsonian-sponsored African expedition</a> was being assembled, the Bible was, according to his sister, "the first book selected".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReisner1922306_366-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReisner1922306-366">&#91;364&#93;</a></sup> In an address delivered to the Long Island Bible Society in 1901, Roosevelt declared that:
</p>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r996844942"><blockquote class="templatequote"><p>Every thinking man, when he thinks, realizes what a very large number of people tend to forget, that the teachings of the Bible are so interwoven and entwined with our whole civic and social life that it would be literally—I do not mean figuratively, I mean literally—impossible for us to figure to ourselves what that life would be if these teachings were removed. We would lose almost all the standards by which we now judge both public and private morals; all the standards toward which we, with more or less of resolution, strive to raise ourselves. Almost every man who has by his lifework added to the sum of human achievement of which the race is proud, has based his lifework largely upon the teachings of the Bible ... Among the greatest men a disproportionately large number have been diligent and close students of the Bible at first hand.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReisner1922306_366-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReisner1922306-366">&#91;364&#93;</a></sup></p></blockquote>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Political_positions">Political positions</span></h2>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Political_positions_of_Theodore_Roosevelt" title="Political positions of Theodore Roosevelt">Political positions of Theodore Roosevelt</a></div>
<p>When he assumed the presidency, Roosevelt reassured many conservatives, stating that "the mechanism of modern business is so delicate that extreme care must be taken not to interfere with it in a spirit of rashness or ignorance."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTELeuchtenburg201530–31_367-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeuchtenburg201530–31-367">&#91;365&#93;</a></sup> The following year, Roosevelt asserted the president's independence from business interests by opposing the merger which created the <a href="/wiki/Northern_Securities_Company" title="Northern Securities Company">Northern Securities Company</a>, and many were surprised that any president, much less an unelected one, would challenge powerful banker <a href="/wiki/J.P._Morgan" class="mw-redirect" title="J.P. Morgan">J.P. Morgan</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTELeuchtenburg201532–33_368-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeuchtenburg201532–33-368">&#91;366&#93;</a></sup> In his last two years as president, Roosevelt became increasingly distrustful of <a href="/wiki/Big_business" title="Big business">big business</a>, despite its close ties to the Republican Party.<sup id="cite_ref-369" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-369">&#91;367&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt sought to replace the 19th-century <i><a href="/wiki/Laissez-faire" title="Laissez-faire">laissez-faire</a></i> economic environment with a new economic model which included a larger regulatory role for the federal government. He believed that 19th-century entrepreneurs had risked their fortunes on innovations and new businesses, and that these capitalists had been rightly rewarded. By contrast, he believed that 20th-century capitalists risked little but nonetheless reaped huge and, given the lack of risk, unjust, economic rewards. Without a redistribution of wealth away from the upper class, Roosevelt feared that the country would turn to radicals or fall to revolution.<sup id="cite_ref-370" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-370">&#91;368&#93;</a></sup> His <a href="/wiki/Square_Deal" title="Square Deal">Square Deal</a> domestic program had three main goals: conservation of natural resources, control of corporations, and consumer protection.<sup id="cite_ref-371" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-371">&#91;369&#93;</a></sup> The Square Deal evolved into his program of "<a href="/wiki/New_Nationalism_(Theodore_Roosevelt)" title="New Nationalism (Theodore Roosevelt)">New Nationalism</a>", which emphasized the priority of labor over capital interests and a need to more effectively control corporate creation and combination, and proposed a ban on corporate political contributions.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997675_243-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997675-243">&#91;241&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Foreign_policy_beliefs">Foreign policy beliefs</span></h3>
<p>In the analysis by <a href="/wiki/Henry_Kissinger" title="Henry Kissinger">Henry Kissinger</a>, Roosevelt was the first president to develop the guideline that it was the duty of the United States to make its enormous power and potential influence felt globally. The idea of being a passive "city on the hill" model that others could look up to, he rejected. Roosevelt, trained in biology, was a <a href="/wiki/Social_Darwinist" class="mw-redirect" title="Social Darwinist">social Darwinist</a> who believed in survival of the fittest. The international world in his view was a realm of violence and conflict. The United States had all the economic and geographical potential to be the fittest nation on the globe.<sup id="cite_ref-372" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-372">&#91;370&#93;</a></sup> The United States had a duty to act decisively. For example, in terms of the <a href="/wiki/Monroe_Doctrine" title="Monroe Doctrine">Monroe Doctrine</a>, America had to prevent European incursions in the Western Hemisphere. But there was more, as he expressed in his famous <a href="/wiki/Roosevelt_Corollary" title="Roosevelt Corollary">Roosevelt Corollary</a> to the Monroe Doctrine: the U.S. had to be the policeman of the region because unruly, corrupt smaller nations had to be controlled, and if United States did not do it, European powers would in fact intervene and develop their own base of power in the hemisphere in contravention to the Monroe Doctrine.<sup id="cite_ref-373" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-373">&#91;371&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>
Roosevelt was a realist and a conservative.<sup id="cite_ref-374" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-374">&#91;372&#93;</a></sup> He deplored many of the increasingly popular idealistic liberal themes, such as were promoted by <a href="/wiki/William_Jennings_Bryan" title="William Jennings Bryan">William Jennings Bryan</a>, the anti-imperialists, and <a href="/wiki/Woodrow_Wilson" title="Woodrow Wilson">Woodrow Wilson</a>. Kissinger says he rejected the efficacy of international law. Roosevelt argued that if a country could not protect its own interests, the international community could not help very much. He ridiculed disarmament proposals that were increasingly common. He saw no likelihood of an international power capable of checking wrongdoing on a major scale. As for world government:</p><blockquote><p> I regard the Wilson–Bryan attitude of trusting to fantastic peace treaties, too impossible promises, to all kinds of scraps of paper without any backing in efficient force, as abhorrent. It is infinitely better for a nation and for the world to have the <a href="/wiki/Frederick_the_Great" title="Frederick the Great">Frederick the Great</a> and <a href="/wiki/Otto_von_Bismarck" title="Otto von Bismarck">Bismarck</a> tradition as regards foreign policy than to have the Bryan or Bryan–Wilson attitude as a permanent national attitude.... A milk-and-water righteousness unbacked by force is...as wicked as and even more mischievous than force divorced from righteousness.<sup id="cite_ref-375" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-375">&#91;373&#93;</a></sup></p></blockquote>
<p>On his international outlook, Roosevelt favored <a href="/wiki/Spheres_of_influence" class="mw-redirect" title="Spheres of influence">spheres of influence</a>, whereby one great power would generally prevail, such as the United States in the Western Hemisphere or Great Britain in the Indian subcontinent. Japan fit that role and he approved. However, he had deep distrust of both Germany and Russia.<sup id="cite_ref-376" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-376">&#91;374&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Legacy">Legacy</span></h2>
<p>Historians credit Roosevelt for changing the nation's political system by permanently placing the "<a href="/wiki/Bully_pulpit" title="Bully pulpit">bully pulpit</a>" of the presidency at center stage and making <a href="/wiki/Character_(persona)" class="mw-redirect" title="Character (persona)">character</a> as important as the issues. His accomplishments include trust busting and conservationism. He is a hero to <a href="/wiki/Modern_liberalism_in_the_United_States" title="Modern liberalism in the United States">liberals</a> and <a href="/wiki/Progressivism_in_the_United_States" title="Progressivism in the United States">progressives</a> for his proposals in 1907–1912 that presaged the modern welfare state of the <a href="/wiki/New_Deal" title="New Deal">New Deal</a> Era, including <a href="/wiki/Direct_tax" title="Direct tax">direct federal taxation</a>, <a href="/wiki/Labour_movement" title="Labour movement">labor reforms</a>, and more <a href="/wiki/Direct_democracy" title="Direct democracy">direct democracy</a>, while <a href="/wiki/Conservationists" class="mw-redirect" title="Conservationists">conservationists</a> admire Roosevelt for putting the <a href="/wiki/Environmentalism" title="Environmentalism">environment</a> and <a href="/wiki/Altruism" title="Altruism">selflessness</a> towards future generations on the national agenda, and <a href="/wiki/Conservatism_in_the_United_States" title="Conservatism in the United States">conservatives</a> and <a href="/wiki/American_nationalism" title="American nationalism">nationalists</a> respect his commitment to <a href="/wiki/Law_and_order_(politics)" title="Law and order (politics)">law and order</a>, <a href="/wiki/Civic_engagement" title="Civic engagement">civic duty</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Military_history_of_the_United_States" title="Military history of the United States">military values</a>, as well as his personality of individual <a href="/wiki/Personal_responsibility" class="mw-redirect" title="Personal responsibility">self-responsibility</a> and hardiness. Dalton says, "Today he is heralded as the architect of the modern presidency, as a world leader who boldly reshaped the office to meet the needs of the new century and redefined America's place in the world."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDalton20024–5_377-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDalton20024–5-377">&#91;375&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Liberals and <a href="/wiki/History_of_the_socialist_movement_in_the_United_States" title="History of the socialist movement in the United States">socialists</a> have also criticized him for his <a href="/wiki/Intervention_(international_law)" title="Intervention (international law)">interventionist</a> and <a href="/wiki/American_imperialism" title="American imperialism">imperialist</a> approach to nations he considered "<a href="/wiki/Racism_in_the_United_States" title="Racism in the United States">uncivilized</a>". Conservatives and <a href="/wiki/Libertarianism_in_the_United_States" title="Libertarianism in the United States">libertarians</a> reject his vision of the welfare state and emphasis on the superiority of government over private action. <a href="/wiki/Historical_rankings_of_presidents_of_the_United_States" title="Historical rankings of presidents of the United States">Historians typically rank</a> Roosevelt among the top five presidents in American history.<sup id="cite_ref-378" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-378">&#91;376&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-379" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-379">&#91;377&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Persona_and_masculinity">Persona and masculinity</span></h3>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Many_Roles_of_Theodore_Roosevelt.JPG" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/61/Many_Roles_of_Theodore_Roosevelt.JPG/300px-Many_Roles_of_Theodore_Roosevelt.JPG" decoding="async" width="300" height="150" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/61/Many_Roles_of_Theodore_Roosevelt.JPG/450px-Many_Roles_of_Theodore_Roosevelt.JPG 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/61/Many_Roles_of_Theodore_Roosevelt.JPG/600px-Many_Roles_of_Theodore_Roosevelt.JPG 2x" data-file-width="1435" data-file-height="718" /></a><figcaption>1910 cartoon showing Roosevelt's many roles from 1899 to 1910</figcaption></figure>
<p>Dalton says Roosevelt is remembered as "one of the most picturesque personalities who has ever enlivened the landscape".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDalton20025_380-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDalton20025-380">&#91;378&#93;</a></sup> His friend, historian <a href="/wiki/Henry_Adams" title="Henry Adams">Henry Adams</a>, proclaimed: "Roosevelt, more than any other man... showed the singular primitive quality that belongs to ultimate matter—the quality that medieval theology assigned to God—he was pure act."<sup id="cite_ref-381" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-381">&#91;379&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Roosevelt's biographers have stressed his personality. <a href="/wiki/Henry_F._Pringle" title="Henry F. Pringle">Henry F. Pringle</a>, who won the <a href="/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize" title="Pulitzer Prize">Pulitzer Prize</a> in biography for his <i>Theodore Roosevelt</i> (1931) stated: "The Theodore Roosevelt of later years was the most adolescent of men... Failure to receive the Medal of Honor for his exploits [in Cuba] had been a grief as real as any of those which swamp childhood in despair. 'You must always remember,' wrote <a href="/wiki/Cecil_Spring_Rice" title="Cecil Spring Rice">Cecil Spring Rice</a> in 1904, 'that the President is about six.'"<sup id="cite_ref-382" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-382">&#91;380&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Cooper compared him with Woodrow Wilson and argued that both of them played the roles of warrior and priest.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECooper1983_383-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECooper1983-383">&#91;381&#93;</a></sup> Dalton stressed Roosevelt's strenuous life.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDalton2002_384-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDalton2002-384">&#91;382&#93;</a></sup> Sarah Watts examined the desires of the "Rough Rider in the White House".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2003_385-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2003-385">&#91;383&#93;</a></sup> Brands calls Roosevelt "the last <a href="/wiki/Romanticism" title="Romanticism">romantic</a>", arguing that his romantic concept of life emerged from his belief that "physical bravery was the highest virtue and war the ultimate test of bravery".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997x_386-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997x-386">&#91;384&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Roosevelt as the exemplar of American masculinity has become a major theme.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTETesti1995_387-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTETesti1995-387">&#91;385&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-388" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-388">&#91;386&#93;</a></sup> As president, he repeatedly warned men that they were becoming too office-bound, too complacent, too comfortable with physical ease and moral laxity, and were failing in their duties to propagate the race and exhibit masculine vigor.<sup id="cite_ref-389" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-389">&#91;387&#93;</a></sup> French historian <a href="/wiki/Serge_Ricard" title="Serge Ricard">Serge Ricard</a> says, "the ebullient apostle of the Strenuous Life offers ideal material for a detailed psycho-historical analysis of aggressive manhood in the changing socio-cultural environment of his era; McKinley, Taft, or Wilson would perhaps inadequately serve that purpose".<sup id="cite_ref-390" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-390">&#91;388&#93;</a></sup> He promoted competitive sports like boxing and jiu-jitsu for physically strengthening American men.<sup id="cite_ref-:0_348-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:0-348">&#91;346&#93;</a></sup> He also believed that organizations like the <a href="/wiki/Boy_Scouts_of_America" title="Boy Scouts of America">Boy Scouts of America</a>, founded in 1910, could help mold and strengthen the character of American boys.<sup id="cite_ref-391" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-391">&#91;389&#93;</a></sup> Brands shows that heroic displays of bravery were essential to Roosevelt's image and mission:
</p>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r996844942"><blockquote class="templatequote"><p> What makes the hero a hero is the romantic notion that he stands above the tawdry give and take of everyday politics, occupying an ethereal realm where partisanship gives way to patriotism, and division to unity, and where the nation regains its lost innocence, and the people their shared sense of purpose.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands1997372_392-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands1997372-392">&#91;390&#93;</a></sup></p></blockquote><p>In 1902, French artist <a href="/wiki/Th%C3%A9obald_Chartran" title="Théobald Chartran">Théobald Chartran</a> was commissioned to paint Roosevelt's likeness for his presidential portrait.<sup id="cite_ref-:2_393-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:2-393">&#91;391&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-394" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-394">&#91;392&#93;</a></sup> Roosevelt reportedly hid the portrait in a closet before having it destroyed because it made him look weak, like a "meek kitten".<sup id="cite_ref-:2_393-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:2-393">&#91;391&#93;</a></sup> In a letter to his son <a href="/wiki/Kermit_Roosevelt" title="Kermit Roosevelt">Kermit Roosevelt</a>, the elder Roosevelt plainly stated, "Chartran has been painting my picture. I do not particularly like it."<sup id="cite_ref-395" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-395">&#91;393&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/John_Singer_Sargent" title="John Singer Sargent">John Singer Sargent</a> was instead chosen by Roosevelt to paint his portrait.<sup id="cite_ref-:2_393-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:2-393">&#91;391&#93;</a></sup>
</p><h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Relations_with_Andrew_Carnegie">Relations with Andrew Carnegie</span></h3><p>
According to <a href="/wiki/David_Nasaw" title="David Nasaw">David Nasaw</a>, after 1898, when the United States entered a war with Spain, industrialist <a href="/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie" title="Andrew Carnegie">Andrew Carnegie</a> increasingly devoted his energy to supporting pacifism. He sold his steel company and now had the time and the dollars to make an impact. Carnegie strongly opposed the war with Spain and the subsequent imperialistic American takeover of the Philippines. When Roosevelt became president in 1901, Carnegie and Roosevelt were in frequent contact. They exchanged letters, communicated through mutual friends such as Secretary of State <a href="/wiki/John_Hay" title="John Hay">John Hay</a>, and met in person. Carnegie offered a steady stream of advice on foreign policy, especially on arbitration. Carnegie hoped that Roosevelt would turn the Philippines free, not realizing he was more of an imperialist and believer in warrior virtues than President McKinley had been. He saluted Roosevelt for forcing Germany and Britain to arbitrate their conflict with Venezuela in 1903, and especially for becoming the mediator who negotiated an end to the war between Russia and Japan in 1907–1908. Roosevelt relied on Carnegie for financing his expedition to <a href="/wiki/Smithsonian%E2%80%93Roosevelt_African_Expedition" title="Smithsonian–Roosevelt African Expedition">Africa in 1909</a>. In return he asked the ex-president to mediate the growing conflict between the two cousins who ruled Britain and Germany. Roosevelt started to do so but the scheme collapsed when king <a href="/wiki/Edward_VII" title="Edward VII">Edward VII</a> suddenly died.<sup id="cite_ref-396" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-396">&#91;394&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-397" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-397">&#91;395&#93;</a></sup> Nasaw argues that Roosevelt systematically deceived and manipulated Carnegie and held the elderly man in contempt. Nasaw quotes a private letter Roosevelt wrote to <a href="/wiki/Whitelaw_Reid" title="Whitelaw Reid">Whitelaw Reid</a> in 1905:<sup id="cite_ref-398" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-398">&#91;396&#93;</a></sup> </p><blockquote><p>[I have] tried hard to like Carnegie, but it is pretty difficult. There is no type of man for whom I feel a more contemptuous abhorrence than for the one who makes a God of mere money-making and at the same time is always yelling out that kind of utterly stupid condemnation of war which in almost every case springs from a combination of defective physical courage, of unmanly shrinking from pain and effort, and of hopelessly twisted ideals. All the suffering from Spanish war comes far short of the suffering, preventable and non-preventable, among the operators of the Carnegie steel works, and among the small investors, during the time that Carnegie was making his fortune....It is as noxious folly to denounce war per se as it is to denounce business per se. Unrighteous war is a hideous evil; but I am not at all sure that it is worse evil than business unrighteousness.</p></blockquote>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Memorials_and_cultural_depictions">Memorials and cultural depictions</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/Memorials_to_Theodore_Roosevelt" class="mw-redirect" title="Memorials to Theodore Roosevelt">Memorials to Theodore Roosevelt</a> and <a href="/wiki/Cultural_depictions_of_Theodore_Roosevelt" title="Cultural depictions of Theodore Roosevelt">Cultural depictions of Theodore Roosevelt</a></div>
<style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r1096954695/mw-parser-output/.tmulti">.mw-parser-output .tmulti .multiimageinner{display:flex;flex-direction:column}.mw-parser-output .tmulti .trow{display:flex;flex-direction:row;clear:left;flex-wrap:wrap;width:100%;box-sizing:border-box}.mw-parser-output .tmulti .tsingle{margin:1px;float:left}.mw-parser-output .tmulti .theader{clear:both;font-weight:bold;text-align:center;align-self:center;background-color:transparent;width:100%}.mw-parser-output .tmulti .thumbcaption{background-color:transparent}.mw-parser-output .tmulti .text-align-left{text-align:left}.mw-parser-output .tmulti .text-align-right{text-align:right}.mw-parser-output .tmulti .text-align-center{text-align:center}@media all and (max-width:720px){.mw-parser-output .tmulti .thumbinner{width:100%!important;box-sizing:border-box;max-width:none!important;align-items:center}.mw-parser-output .tmulti .trow{justify-content:center}.mw-parser-output .tmulti .tsingle{float:none!important;max-width:100%!important;box-sizing:border-box;text-align:center}.mw-parser-output .tmulti .tsingle .thumbcaption{text-align:left}.mw-parser-output .tmulti .trow>.thumbcaption{text-align:center}}</style><div class="thumb tmulti tright"><div class="thumbinner multiimageinner" style="width:224px;max-width:224px"><div class="trow"><div class="tsingle" style="width:222px;max-width:222px"><div class="thumbimage"><span typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:South_Dakota_-_Rushmore_American_Flag.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/South_Dakota_-_Rushmore_American_Flag.jpg/220px-South_Dakota_-_Rushmore_American_Flag.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="124" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/South_Dakota_-_Rushmore_American_Flag.jpg/330px-South_Dakota_-_Rushmore_American_Flag.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/South_Dakota_-_Rushmore_American_Flag.jpg/440px-South_Dakota_-_Rushmore_American_Flag.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1136" data-file-height="640" /></a></span></div><div class="thumbcaption">Theodore Roosevelt on Mount Rushmore (second from right)</div></div></div><div class="trow"><div class="tsingle" style="width:222px;max-width:222px"><div class="thumbimage"><span typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:MtRushmore_TR_close.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cb/MtRushmore_TR_close.jpg/220px-MtRushmore_TR_close.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="272" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cb/MtRushmore_TR_close.jpg/330px-MtRushmore_TR_close.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cb/MtRushmore_TR_close.jpg/440px-MtRushmore_TR_close.jpg 2x" data-file-width="707" data-file-height="875" /></a></span></div><div class="thumbcaption">A close-up of Roosevelt's face</div></div></div></div></div>
<p>Roosevelt was included with Presidents George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, and Abraham Lincoln at the <a href="/wiki/Mount_Rushmore" title="Mount Rushmore">Mount Rushmore Memorial</a>, designed in 1927 with the approval of Republican President <a href="/wiki/Calvin_Coolidge" title="Calvin Coolidge">Calvin Coolidge</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-399" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-399">&#91;397&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-400" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-400">&#91;398&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>For his gallantry at San Juan Hill, Roosevelt's commanders recommended him for the <a href="/wiki/Medal_of_Honor" title="Medal of Honor">Medal of Honor</a>. However, the initial recommendation lacked any eyewitnesses, and the effort was eventually tainted by Roosevelt's own lobbying of the War Department.<sup id="cite_ref-401" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-401">&#91;399&#93;</a></sup> In the late 1990s, Roosevelt's supporters again recommended the award, which was denied by the <a href="/wiki/Secretary_of_the_Army" class="mw-redirect" title="Secretary of the Army">Secretary of the Army</a> on basis that the decorations board determined "Roosevelt's bravery in battle did not rise to the level that would justify the Medal of Honor and, indeed, it did not rise to the level of men who fought in that engagement."<sup id="cite_ref-402" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-402">&#91;400&#93;</a></sup> Nevertheless, politicians apparently convinced the secretary to reconsider the award a third time and reverse himself, leading to the charge that it was a "politically motivated award".<sup id="cite_ref-403" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-403">&#91;401&#93;</a></sup> On January 16, 2001, President <a href="/wiki/Bill_Clinton" title="Bill Clinton">Bill Clinton</a> awarded Theodore Roosevelt the Medal of Honor posthumously for his charge on San Juan Hill.<sup id="cite_ref-MoH2001_109-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-MoH2001-109">&#91;107&#93;</a></sup> He is the only president to have received the Medal of Honor.<sup id="cite_ref-404" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-404">&#91;402&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The United States Navy named two ships for Roosevelt: the <a href="/wiki/USS_Theodore_Roosevelt_(SSBN-600)" title="USS Theodore Roosevelt (SSBN-600)">USS&#160;<i>Theodore Roosevelt</i>&#160;<span class="nowrap">(SSBN-600)</span></a>, a submarine that was in commission from 1961 to 1982, and the <a href="/wiki/USS_Theodore_Roosevelt_(CVN-71)" title="USS Theodore Roosevelt (CVN-71)">USS&#160;<i>Theodore Roosevelt</i>&#160;<span class="nowrap">(CVN-71)</span></a>, an <a href="/wiki/Aircraft_carrier" title="Aircraft carrier">aircraft carrier</a> that has been on active duty in the <a href="/wiki/United_States_Atlantic_Fleet" class="mw-redirect" title="United States Atlantic Fleet">Atlantic Fleet</a> since 1986.
</p><p>On November 18, 1956, the <a href="/wiki/United_States_Postal_Service" title="United States Postal Service">United States Postal Service</a> released a 6¢ <a href="/wiki/Liberty_Issue" title="Liberty Issue">Liberty Issue</a> postage stamp honoring Roosevelt. A 32¢ stamp was issued on February 3, 1998, as part of the <a href="/wiki/Celebrate_the_Century" title="Celebrate the Century">Celebrate the Century</a> stamp sheet series.<sup id="cite_ref-405" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-405">&#91;403&#93;</a></sup> In 2008, <a href="/wiki/Columbia_Law_School" title="Columbia Law School">Columbia Law School</a> awarded Roosevelt a <a href="/wiki/Juris_Doctor" title="Juris Doctor">Juris Doctor</a> degree, posthumously making him a member of the class of 1882.<sup id="cite_ref-406" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-406">&#91;404&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Roosevelt's "<a href="/wiki/Big_Stick_ideology" class="mw-redirect" title="Big Stick ideology">Speak Softly and Carry a Big Stick</a>" ideology is still quoted by politicians and columnists in different countries—not only in English, but also in translations to various other languages.<sup id="cite_ref-407" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-407">&#91;405&#93;</a></sup> Another lasting, popular legacy of Roosevelt is the stuffed toy bears—<a href="/wiki/Teddy_bear" title="Teddy bear">teddy bears</a>—named after him following an incident on a hunting trip in <a href="/wiki/Mississippi" title="Mississippi">Mississippi</a> in 1902.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTELeuchtenburg201530_408-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeuchtenburg201530-408">&#91;406&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Roosevelt has been portrayed in films and television series such as <i><a href="/wiki/Brighty_of_the_Grand_Canyon" title="Brighty of the Grand Canyon">Brighty of the Grand Canyon</a></i>, <i><a href="/wiki/The_Wind_and_the_Lion" title="The Wind and the Lion">The Wind and the Lion</a></i>, <i><a href="/wiki/Rough_Riders_(film)" class="mw-redirect" title="Rough Riders (film)">Rough Riders</a></i>, <i><a href="/wiki/My_Friend_Flicka_(TV_series)" title="My Friend Flicka (TV series)">My Friend Flicka</a></i>,<sup id="cite_ref-409" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-409">&#91;407&#93;</a></sup><i> and <a href="/wiki/Law_of_the_Plainsman" title="Law of the Plainsman">Law of the Plainsman</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-410" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-410">&#91;408&#93;</a></sup></i> <a href="/wiki/Robin_Williams" title="Robin Williams">Robin Williams</a> portrayed Roosevelt in the form of a wax <a href="/wiki/Mannequin" title="Mannequin">mannequin</a> that comes to life in <i><a href="/wiki/Night_at_the_Museum" title="Night at the Museum">Night at the Museum</a></i> and its sequels <i><a href="/wiki/Night_at_the_Museum:_Battle_of_the_Smithsonian" title="Night at the Museum: Battle of the Smithsonian">Night at the Museum: Battle of the Smithsonian</a></i> and <i><a href="/wiki/Night_at_the_Museum:_Secret_of_the_Tomb" title="Night at the Museum: Secret of the Tomb">Night at the Museum: Secret of the Tomb</a></i>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECullinane2017_411-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECullinane2017-411">&#91;409&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-412" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-412">&#91;410&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-413" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-413">&#91;411&#93;</a></sup> In 2017, it was announced that <a href="/wiki/Leonardo_DiCaprio" title="Leonardo DiCaprio">Leonardo DiCaprio</a> will portray Roosevelt in a biopic to be directed by <a href="/wiki/Martin_Scorsese" title="Martin Scorsese">Martin Scorsese</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-414" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-414">&#91;412&#93;</a></sup> Additionally, Roosevelt appears as the leader of the American civilization in the 2016 <a href="/wiki/Firaxis_Games" title="Firaxis Games">Firaxis Games</a>-developed video game <i><a href="/wiki/Civilization_VI" title="Civilization VI">Civilization VI</a></i>.<sup id="cite_ref-415" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-415">&#91;413&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p><a href="/wiki/Theodore_Roosevelt_National_Park" title="Theodore Roosevelt National Park">Theodore Roosevelt National Park</a> in the <a href="/wiki/U.S._state" title="U.S. state">state</a> of <a href="/wiki/North_Dakota" title="North Dakota">North Dakota</a> is named after him.<sup id="cite_ref-416" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-416">&#91;414&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/America_the_Beautiful_Quarters" class="mw-redirect" title="America the Beautiful Quarters">America the Beautiful Quarters</a> series features Roosevelt riding a horse on the national park's quarter.
</p><p>Asteroid <a href="/wiki/188693_Roosevelt" class="mw-redirect" title="188693 Roosevelt">188693 Roosevelt</a>, discovered by astronomers with the <a href="/wiki/Catalina_Sky_Survey" title="Catalina Sky Survey">Catalina Sky Survey</a> in 2005, was named after him.<sup id="cite_ref-MPC-object_417-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-MPC-object-417">&#91;415&#93;</a></sup> The official <a href="/wiki/Meanings_of_minor_planet_names:_188001%E2%80%93189000#693" title="Meanings of minor planet names: 188001–189000">naming citation</a> was published by the <a href="/wiki/Minor_Planet_Center" title="Minor Planet Center">Minor Planet Center</a> on November 8, 2019 (<span style="font-size:85%;"><a href="/wiki/Minor_Planet_Circulars" class="mw-redirect" title="Minor Planet Circulars">M.P.C.</a> 118221</span>).<sup id="cite_ref-MPC-Circulars-Archive_418-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-MPC-Circulars-Archive-418">&#91;416&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Robert_Peary" title="Robert Peary">Robert Peary</a> named the <a href="/wiki/Roosevelt_Range" title="Roosevelt Range">Roosevelt Range</a> and <a href="/wiki/Roosevelt_Land" title="Roosevelt Land">Roosevelt Land</a> after him.<sup id="cite_ref-419" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-419">&#91;417&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>For 80 years, <a href="/wiki/Equestrian_Statue_of_Theodore_Roosevelt_(New_York_City)" title="Equestrian Statue of Theodore Roosevelt (New York City)">an equestrian statue</a> of the former president, sitting above a <a href="/wiki/Native_Americans_in_the_United_States" title="Native Americans in the United States">Native American</a> and an <a href="/wiki/African_American" class="mw-redirect" title="African American">African American</a>, stood in front of New York's <a href="/wiki/American_Museum_of_Natural_History" title="American Museum of Natural History">American Museum of Natural History</a>. In January 2022, after years of lobbying by activists, the statue was removed. Museum president <a href="/wiki/Ellen_V._Futter" title="Ellen V. Futter">Ellen V. Futter</a> said the decision did not reflect a judgment about Roosevelt but was driven by the sculpture's "hierarchical composition".<sup id="cite_ref-420" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-420">&#91;418&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-pogrebin_421-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-pogrebin-421">&#91;419&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Audiovisual_media">Audiovisual media</span></h2>
<ul><li>Theodore Roosevelt was one of the first presidents whose voice was recorded for posterity. Several of his recorded speeches survive.<sup id="cite_ref-422" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-422">&#91;420&#93;</a></sup> A 4.6-minute voice recording,<sup id="cite_ref-423" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-423">&#91;421&#93;</a></sup> which preserves Roosevelt's lower timbre ranges particularly well for its time, is among those available from the <a href="/wiki/Michigan_State_University" title="Michigan State University">Michigan State University</a> libraries (this is the 1912 recording of <i>The Right of the People to Rule</i>, recorded by <a href="/wiki/Thomas_Edison" title="Thomas Edison">Thomas Edison</a> at <a href="/wiki/Carnegie_Hall" title="Carnegie Hall">Carnegie Hall</a>). The audio clip sponsored by the Authentic History Center includes his defense<sup id="cite_ref-424" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-424">&#91;422&#93;</a></sup> of the Progressive Party in 1912, wherein he proclaims it the "party of the people"&#160;– in contrast with the other major parties.</li></ul>

<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Notes">Notes</span></h2>
<style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r1011085734">.mw-parser-output .reflist{font-size:90%;margin-bottom:0.5em;list-style-type:decimal}.mw-parser-output .reflist .references{font-size:100%;margin-bottom:0;list-style-type:inherit}.mw-parser-output .reflist-columns-2{column-width:30em}.mw-parser-output .reflist-columns-3{column-width:25em}.mw-parser-output .reflist-columns{margin-top:0.3em}.mw-parser-output .reflist-columns ol{margin-top:0}.mw-parser-output .reflist-columns li{page-break-inside:avoid;break-inside:avoid-column}.mw-parser-output .reflist-upper-alpha{list-style-type:upper-alpha}.mw-parser-output .reflist-upper-roman{list-style-type:upper-roman}.mw-parser-output .reflist-lower-alpha{list-style-type:lower-alpha}.mw-parser-output .reflist-lower-greek{list-style-type:lower-greek}.mw-parser-output .reflist-lower-roman{list-style-type:lower-roman}</style><div class="reflist reflist-lower-alpha">
<div class="mw-references-wrap"><ol class="references">
<li id="cite_note-1"><span class="mw-cite-backlink"><b><a href="#cite_ref-1">^</a></b></span> <span class="reference-text">He was vice president under <a href="/wiki/William_McKinley" title="William McKinley">William McKinley</a> and became president upon <a href="/wiki/Assassination_of_William_McKinley" title="Assassination of William McKinley">McKinley's assassination</a> on September 14, 1901. This was prior to the adoption of the <a href="/wiki/Twenty-fifth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution" title="Twenty-fifth Amendment to the United States Constitution">Twenty-fifth Amendment</a> in 1967, and a vacancy in the office of vice president was not filled until the next election and inauguration.</span>
</li>
<li id="cite_note-6"><span class="mw-cite-backlink"><b><a href="#cite_ref-6">^</a></b></span> <span class="reference-text">His last name is, according to Roosevelt himself, "pronounced as if it was spelled 'Rosavelt.' That is in three syllables. The first syllable as if it was 'Rose.<span style="padding-right:.15em;">'</span>"<sup id="cite_ref-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-5">&#91;4&#93;</a></sup></span>
</li>
</ol></div></div>
